passages.text: When he had said these things, I replied, “Already I thank God, for just as I wished to be fully assured, so he has also granted it to me. Nevertheless, as far as I am concerned, be so free from worry that I will never doubt—to such an extent that, even if you yourself should ever wish to dislodge me from the prophetic position, being powerless, you will be unable to do so. So firmly do I know what I have received. And do not suppose that you are promising me anything great in this very thing, that I will never doubt. Rather, neither I myself nor any human being who has heard the discourse concerning a prophet will ever be able to doubt the true position, once he has first listened and understood what the truth of prophetic declaration is. Therefore, be confident in the doctrine willed by God, for every artifice of wickedness has been defeated. Against prophecy nothing has any power—neither arts of speech, nor devices of sophistries, nor reasonings, nor any other contrivance—provided, at least, that the person who has listened to a true prophet truly desires truth and is not looking around for something else under a pretext of truth. So, my lord Peter, do not lose heart as though you had bestowed the greatest good on someone insensible; for you bestowed it on someone who recognizes the favor and cannot be led astray from the truth that was given. For I know that it is possible both to receive quickly what one wants and not to obtain it after a long delay. I therefore know better than to despise, because of the speed with which it was given, what was given to me—something incomparable and alone secure.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to be fully assured
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive denotes being brought to full conviction or assurance, not merely receiving information.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the prophetic position
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόθεσις can denote a position, thesis, premise, subject, or doctrine; “position” fits something from which Clement might be dislodged while retaining the conceptual ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being powerless, you will be unable
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s emphatic repetition of the cognate ideas rather than smoothing one away.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μήτοι νόμιζέ μοι σὺ μέγα ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: do not suppose that you are promising me anything great
lexical_decisions.rationale: The explicit σὺ is taken as the subject of ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι and μοι as its recipient. Although “do not suppose that I am making a great claim” would fit the broader context, it would reverse the supplied pronouns.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what the truth of prophetic declaration is
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπαγγελία can mean a promise, profession, announcement, or declaration; “declaration” suits the discussion of prophetic discourse without restricting it to prediction of the future.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the doctrine willed by God
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεοβούλητος describes something intended or willed by God; the dative marks that in which Peter is to have confidence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: devices of sophistries
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίνοιαι denotes conceptions, inventions, or devices, while σοφίσματα denotes sophistic arguments or sophistries.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though ... on someone insensible
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναίσθητος here denotes someone unperceptive or unable to appreciate the gift, not necessarily someone physically unconscious.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ δυναμένῳ ἀπατηθῆναι ἀπὸ τοῦ δοθέντος ἀληθοῦς
lexical_decisions.chosen: cannot be led astray from the truth that was given
lexical_decisions.rationale: The separation expressed by ἀπό supports being deceived or led away from the bestowed true thing; “truth” gives natural English for the substantival neuter ἀληθοῦς.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἶδα γὰρ ὅτι ἔνεστιν ὧν βούλεταί τις καὶ ταχέως λαβεῖν καὶ βραδέως μὴ τυχεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For I know that it is possible both to receive quickly what one wants and not to obtain it after a long delay
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔνεστιν is taken impersonally as “it is possible,” governing the coordinated infinitives λαβεῖν and μὴ τυχεῖν. The rendering preserves μὴ τυχεῖν as nonattainment and expresses βραδέως idiomatically as “after a long delay.” The positive and negative members present prompt receipt both directly and by contrast with prolonged nonattainment. A less likely alternative takes ἔνεστιν existentially and attaches both infinitives to βούλεταί τις: “there are things one wants both to receive quickly and not to obtain after a delay.” That analysis makes both outcomes objects of desire and gives a less natural relation between ὧν and the two infinitives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ δοθέντος μοι διὰ τὸ τάχος ἀσυγκρίτου καὶ μόνου ἀσφαλοῦς
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of the speed with which it was given, what was given to me—something incomparable and alone secure
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσυγκρίτου and μόνου ἀσφαλοῦς agree with the substantival τοῦ δοθέντος, not with τάχος, and describe the gift as incomparable and uniquely secure.

passages.text: When I had said these things, Peter said, “I acknowledge my gratitude to God both for your salvation and for my own delight. For I truly rejoice, knowing that you have recognized what the greatness of prophecy really is. Since, then, as you said, even if I myself should ever wish—which may it never be!—to shift you to a different doctrine, I would not be able to persuade you, begin, from tomorrow onward, to be present with me in the disputations of those who oppose us. Tomorrow is my encounter with Simon the magician.” After saying this and himself partaking of food, he instructed me also to partake separately. After he had pronounced a blessing over the food and given thanks, once satiety had been reached and he had also explained to me the reason for this very thing, he continued, saying, “May God grant you to be made like me in every respect and, once baptized, to share the same table with me.” Having said these things, he instructed me to rest, for by then, I suppose, the body’s nature was also demanding sleep.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I acknowledge my gratitude to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase expresses thanksgiving while retaining the sense of ὁμολογῶ as acknowledgment rather than replacing it with an unrelated formula.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my own delight
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόλαυσις can mean enjoyment, delight, benefit, or fruition; the following ἥδομαι supports the affective sense, though “my own benefit” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: which may it never be!
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally the wish is that the contemplated event be far away; the English idiom preserves its optative rejection.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the disputations of those who oppose us
lexical_decisions.rationale: ζητήσεις may be inquiries, discussions, debates, or disputations. The substantival ἀντικείμενοι are opposing persons; “us” makes their contextual opposition explicit without identifying a different object.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔστι δέ μοι ἡ αὔριον πρὸς Σίμωνα μάγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Tomorrow is my encounter with Simon the magician
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek leaves the event after πρός implicit. “Encounter” preserves the adversarial relation without specifying whether it is formally a debate or contest, and μάγον is translated rather than retained as the Latinized “Magus.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τροφῆς αὐτὸς μεταλαβὼν ἰδία κἀμὲ μεταλαβεῖν ἐκέλευσεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: himself partaking of food, he instructed me also to partake separately
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰδία is taken adverbially with Clement’s partaking, which is supported by the later explanation about baptism and sharing Peter’s table. It could instead modify Peter’s partaking (“having partaken separately”) or, less likely, the manner of his instruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once satiety had been reached
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular passive infinitive does not state who was satisfied. The impersonal English preserves that ambiguity; “after he had eaten his fill” or “after I had eaten my fill” would choose an unstated subject.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτοῦ τούτου τὸν λόγον μοι ἀποδοὺς
lexical_decisions.chosen: he had also explained to me the reason for this very thing
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγον ἀποδιδόναι here means to give an account or explanation. The referent of “this very thing” is left open, though the separate partaking is the most immediate contextual explanation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: βαπτισθέντα τῆς αὐτῆς μοι μεταλαβεῖν τραπέζης
lexical_decisions.chosen: once baptized, to share the same table with me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The aorist participle makes baptism antecedent to sharing Peter’s table, while μεταλαβεῖν with the genitive denotes participation or sharing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for by then, I suppose
lexical_decisions.rationale: που softens the assertion with an inferential “I suppose” or “perhaps,” rather than functioning as a place adverb here.

passages.text: On the following day, then, I, Clement, woke while it was still night and learned that Peter was awake and discussing piety with those who were with him (they were sixteen; and I resolved to give their names too, after learning each one’s name in due course, so that you may also know who they were: the first was Zacchaeus, the former tax collector, and Sophonias his brother; Joseph and his childhood companion Micaiah; also the twins Thomas and Eliezer; as well as the priests Aeneas and Lazarus; furthermore Elisha and Benjamin son of Saphra; likewise the builders Roubilos and Zechariah; the Iammeans Ananias and Haggai; and finally the companions Nicetas and Aquila). At any rate, I went in, greeted them, and sat down at his direction.

source_issues.source_quote: οἱ ἰαμμηνοί
source_issues.issue: The printed ethnonym or group designation is uncommon, and its precise geographical identification is uncertain. The translation therefore preserves it by transliteration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after learning each one’s name in due course
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive ἑκάστου supplies the possessor of the previously mentioned “names,” while ἐξῆς χρόνου indicates their being learned successively over time.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his childhood companion Micaiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύντροφος denotes someone reared together with another and may alternatively be rendered “foster-brother” or “companion from youth.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Iammeans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The uncommon group designation is transliterated rather than silently identified with or emended to a better-known place-name.

lexical_decisions.chosen: greeted them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb here denotes addressing those present by way of greeting; the implied object is supplied from the surrounding company.

passages.text: He, however, interrupted the discourse under way and, as though defending himself, fully explained why he had not awakened me so that I could listen to the discussion, giving as his reason the exhaustion caused by the voyage. Wanting that exhaustion to be soothed for me, he had allowed me to rest. “For whenever the soul is occupied with what the body lacks, it does not receive the lessons being offered as they deserve. For this reason, I do not wish to converse with those who are deeply grieved by some misfortune, excessively angry, carried away into a frenzy of desire, physically worn down, buffeted by the concerns of daily life, or troubled by any other passions—passions under which the soul, as I said, falls and, sharing the suffering body’s pain, also keeps its own understanding occupied.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἐκεῖνον πεφθῆναί μοι θέλων
source_issues.issue: The compressed construction personifies the voyage-related exhaustion, and the exact nuance of πεφθῆναι is uncertain. Viable contextual senses include “be soothed,” “be worked off,” and “be overcome.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the exhaustion caused by the voyage
lexical_decisions.rationale: σκυλμός can denote trouble, strain, or weariness; the voyage and subsequent need for rest favor physical exhaustion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Wanting that exhaustion to be soothed for me
lexical_decisions.rationale: πεφθῆναι is taken in the sense of being softened, assuaged, or worked off. “Overcome for me” is a more literal but less natural alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ τὸ λεῖπον τῷ σώματι ἀσχολῆται
lexical_decisions.chosen: is occupied with what the body lacks
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the supplied λεῖπον, referring to a bodily deficiency or unmet need rather than replacing it with a conjectural expression for bodily suffering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: carried away into a frenzy of desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔρως may denote erotic passion or intense desire, while λύσσα supplies the image of frenzy or madness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: buffeted by the concerns of daily life
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιωθέω conveys being pushed or driven about, and βιωτικαὶ φροντίδες are concerns arising from ordinary worldly life.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἷς ἡ ψυχὴ (ὡς ἔφην) ὑποπίπτουσα καὶ τῷ σώματι πάσχοντι συναλγοῦσα, καὶ τὴν αὐτῆς φρόνησιν ἀσχολεῖ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: passions under which the soul, as I said, falls and, sharing the suffering body’s pain, also keeps its own understanding occupied
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative οἷς refers to the passions, while ὑποπίπτουσα and συναλγοῦσα are subordinate participles describing the soul. The finite predicate ἀσχολεῖ supplies the culminating assertion that the soul occupies its own understanding.

passages.text: And let no one say, “Then comfort and admonition should not be offered to those who are doing something wrong.” I say, “If someone achieves a result, let him offer them; but if not, let him yield to the occasion.” For I know that “everything has its own time.” Therefore, words that strengthen the soul must be given to people before adversity, so that, if anything bad should ever come, the mind, armed beforehand with right reasoning, may be able to withstand what has been brought upon it. For then, at the height of the battle, the mind knows how to come to the aid of the one who has helped it through good counsel.

source_issues.source_quote: ὁ νοῦς. προωπλισμένος
source_issues.issue: The printed full stop separates the subject ὁ νοῦς from the participle προωπλισμένος and the later verb δυνηθῇ, although they can form one continuous construction. The translation provisionally treats the stop as editorial punctuation rather than as evidence of omitted wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who are doing something wrong
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative object with πράττουσιν indicates committing or doing something bad, rather than merely faring badly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If someone achieves a result
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνύει is used absolutely for accomplishing something or producing an effect; the result of the offered counsel is implicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let him yield to the occasion
lexical_decisions.rationale: καιρός denotes the suitable or opportune time, and εἴκω means to give way or defer to it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: before adversity
lexical_decisions.rationale: κάκωσις can denote affliction, harm, or distress; “adversity” fits the subsequent image of something bad coming upon the mind.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at the height of the battle
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκμή denotes the culminating or most intense point. The phrase is attached here to the mind’s coming to aid; it could alternatively modify the earlier helping through good counsel.

passages.text: “However, I have learned, Clement, that in Alexandria Barnabas thoroughly expounded to you the discourse about prophecy. Or did he not?” And I answered, “Yes, and very well.” Peter said, “Accordingly, it is not necessary to spend the present time, which can serve us for other teachings that you do not know, attending to those you do know.” And I said, “You are right, Peter. But grant me this, since I have resolved always to remain with you: continue to guide me through the discourse about the prophet, as I gladly listen. For without him, as I learned from Barnabas, it is impossible to learn the truth.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the discourse about prophecy
lexical_decisions.rationale: προφητεία denotes prophecy or the subject of prophetic revelation; the rendering does not replace it with the later and distinct phrase “about the prophet.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἑτέρους λόγους οὓς οὐκ ἐπίστασαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: for other teachings that you do not know
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγοι here refers to subjects of instruction or discourses rather than merely individual spoken words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the discourse about the prophet
lexical_decisions.rationale: The definite τοῦ προφήτου is retained without adding “true,” which is not present in the supplied Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: continue to guide me through
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφηγεῖσθαι can mean to guide, instruct, or expound, while συνεχῶς gives the continuing character of the requested instruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For without him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine pronoun is taken as referring to “the prophet,” which best fits learning the truth through him. Grammatically, reference to the masculine λόγος, “discourse,” remains possible, yielding “without it.”

passages.text: Peter, greatly pleased at this, answered, “Your being set right has now reached completion, now that you have recognized the greatness of unerring prophecy, without which it is impossible for anyone to obtain what is supremely beneficial. For although many and diverse good things exist among the things that are or can come to be, the most blessed of all—whether it is eternal life, lasting health, perfect intellect, light, joy, incorruptibility, or any other thing that exists or can exist as a surpassing good in the nature of beings—cannot be acquired in any other way unless one first knows the things that exist as they are. And that knowledge cannot be attained in any other way unless one first recognizes the prophet of truth.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἡ πρὸς σὲ διόρθωσις τέλος εἴληφεν, ἐπεγνωκότα
source_issues.issue: The accusative participle ἐπεγνωκότα has no explicit accusative head following the nominative clause. It can defensibly be understood by sense as referring back to σὲ, hence “now that you have recognized”; the construction is anacoluthic but intelligible, so the printed wording is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: your being set right
lexical_decisions.rationale: διόρθωσις can mean correction, reform, or rectification; the passive English wording makes Peter’s addressee the person corrected without implying that he performs the correction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of unerring prophecy
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπταίστος denotes freedom from stumbling or error; “unerring” preserves the epistemic emphasis, though “infallible prophetic revelation” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what is supremely beneficial
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes the beneficial thing that stands preeminent, rather than merely something advantageous.

lexical_decisions.chosen: lasting health
lexical_decisions.rationale: παράμονος describes something enduring or abiding; “lasting” avoids suggesting that ordinary health is necessarily permanent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things that exist as they are
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the ontological wording of τὰ ὄντα and the claim that they must be known according to their actual state.

passages.text: A prophet of truth is one who always knows all things: things past as they happened, things occurring as they occur, and things to come as they will be; he is free from error, merciful, and the only one entrusted to set forth the truth. Read, and you will find those who supposed they had discovered the truth on their own....... For this is distinctive of a prophet: to disclose the truth, just as it is distinctive of the sun to bring the day. For this reason, all who ever desired to know the truth but were not fortunate enough to learn it from him came to the end of their lives still seeking and without finding. For how could someone who seeks the truth obtain it from his own ignorance? Even if he finds it, because he does not know it, he passes it by as though it did not exist. Nor, for that matter, will he be able to grasp truth from someone else (someone who likewise, out of ignorance, claims to possess knowledge), except only with respect to conduct—and even then only that conduct which can be recognized because it is reasonable, and which, from each person’s not wishing to be wronged, presents to him the knowledge that he must not wrong another.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀναγίνωσκε, καὶ εὑρήσεις τοὺς ἀπὸ ἑαυτῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν εὑρεῖν νομίσαντας.......
source_issues.issue: The seven printed periods after νομίσαντας mark a verified lacuna. The surviving wording announces that the reader will find those who supposed they had discovered the truth on their own, but the gap leaves the continuation of that thought unavailable and fragmentary. The translation preserves all seven periods and supplies no restoration. Because every surviving word and the printed gap are represented under the selected-edition coverage scope, this lacuna does not itself block publication of that scoped text, although the passage must not be presented as an unbroken original or as recovering the lost wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: free from error
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean “sinless” or “infallible”; the surrounding description of comprehensive knowledge and truthful instruction favors freedom from error.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the only one entrusted to set forth the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφηγεῖσθαι can mean to guide, explain, or set forth, while πεπιστευμένος presents the prophet as uniquely entrusted with this task.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἀπὸ ἑαυτῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν εὑρεῖν νομίσαντας
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who supposed they had discovered the truth on their own
lexical_decisions.rationale: The aorist infinitive εὑρεῖν in this indirect statement permits the retrospective sense “had discovered.” A prospective or capacity-oriented interpretation, “those who thought they could discover the truth by themselves,” is also contextually possible, but the clause does not explicitly contain δύνασθαι; the following printed gap may conceal context relevant to the nuance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ ὁμοίως ἐξ ἀγνωσίας γνῶσιν ἔχειν ἐπαγγελλομένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone who likewise, out of ignorance, claims to possess knowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐξ ἀγνωσίας is taken with the act of claiming, emphasizing the claimant’s ignorance; alternatively, it may be heard as the paradoxical “claims to possess knowledge derived from ignorance.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: except only with respect to conduct
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία may denote conduct, a way of life, or civic order. The following rule against wronging another indicates moral conduct here; “with respect to” expresses the sphere in which truth remains attainable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: which can be recognized because it is reasonable
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸ εὔλογον denotes the conduct’s reasonable or rationally evident character rather than knowledge received through prophetic disclosure; “which can be recognized by its reasonableness” is also possible.

passages.text: All, then, who ever sought what is true, trusting themselves to be able to find it, were ensnared. This is precisely what the Greek philosophers and the more earnest among the barbarians have suffered. For, drawing on conjectures as they applied themselves to visible things, they pronounced on things unseen, supposing that whatever happened in any way to present itself to them was true. For, as though they knew the truth, those who are still seeking the truth reject some of the notions that present themselves to them and confirm others, as though they knew, although they do not know which are true and which are false. And those searching for truth lay down doctrines about truth, not knowing that one who seeks truth cannot learn it from his own error. For, as I said, he cannot even recognize it when it is present, since it is the very thing he does not know.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were ensnared
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb evokes being caught by an ambush or trap; “ensnared” preserves that image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ στοχασμῶν γὰρ ἐπιβάλλοντες τοῖς ὁρατοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: drawing on conjectures as they applied themselves to visible things
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιβάλλειν with the dative can describe directing or applying oneself to something. “Drawing on conjectures” preserves ἐκ στοχασμῶν without claiming that the visible things themselves are conjectural.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever happened in any way to present itself to them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁπώσποτε stresses the indeterminate manner in which a notion occurs, while παραστάν depicts it as presenting itself.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπολήψεων ἃ μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζουσιν, ἃ δὲ κρατύνουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: notions that present themselves to them ... reject some ... and confirm others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόληψις here denotes a conception or supposition, and κρατύνειν means to strengthen, establish, or confirm it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: lay down doctrines about truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: δογματίζειν means to formulate or assert authoritative opinions; “lay down doctrines” preserves its force without importing a later ecclesiastical sense.

passages.text: But what persuades each person who seeks to learn from himself is not invariably what is true, but what is pleasing. Since, then, one thing pleases one person and another thing another, a different thing holds sway over each as true. But what is true is what the prophet holds to be true, not what is pleasant to each person. For the one would be many if what is pleasing were true, which is impossible. This is also why the word-lovers among the Greeks (not wisdom-lovers), having approached matters through conjectures, laid down many different doctrines. They supposed that the internal coherence of their hypotheses was truth, not knowing that, once they had defined false starting points for themselves, their conclusion had indeed come into agreement with their starting point.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ πάντως τὸ ἀληθές, ἀλλὰ τὸ τέρπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: not invariably what is true, but what is pleasing
lexical_decisions.rationale: οὐ πάντως can deny universality, yielding “not invariably” or “not necessarily,” and the argument contrasts truth with pleasure as the independent seeker’s persuasive criterion. A materially stronger reading, “not at all what is true” or “by no means what is true,” is also possible and would make the denial emphatic rather than qualified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a different thing holds sway over each as true
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρατεῖ with the genitive portrays each person as governed by a different purported truth; an alternative is “each holds a different thing as true.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: what the prophet holds to be true
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοκεῖν may mean “seem,” “appear good,” or “judge.” The contrast with each person’s pleasure favors the prophet’s judgment, while “to be true” supplies the contextual complement.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλὰ γὰρ ἂν ἦν τὸ ἕν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one would be many
lexical_decisions.rationale: The deliberately abstract contrast between the one and the many is retained; context identifies “the one” with truth, but the Greek does not repeat the noun.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the word-lovers among the Greeks (not wisdom-lovers)
lexical_decisions.rationale: The etymological rendering preserves the author’s contrast between φιλόλογοι and φιλόσοφοι; the neutral modern term “philologists” would obscure the wordplay.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the internal coherence of their hypotheses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκολουθία denotes logical sequence or consistency, while οἰκεία marks it as belonging intrinsically to the hypotheses; “proper sequence” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ψευδεῖς ἀρχὰς ἑαυτοῖς ὁρισαμένων, τῇ μὲν ἀρχῇ αὐτῶν τὸ τέλος συμφωνίαν εἴληφεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: once they had defined false starting points for themselves, their conclusion had indeed come into agreement with their starting point
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχή and τέλος are rendered as logical starting point and conclusion, preserving the claim that consistency with false premises does not establish truth.

passages.text: Therefore, setting everything else aside, one must entrust oneself only to the prophet of truth, and all of us can judge whether he is a prophet, even if we are entirely uneducated, laypeople in sophistical arguments, inexperienced in geometry, and uninitiated in music. For God has made discovering him easier for everyone (as guardian of all), so that neither barbarians are too weak to find him nor Greeks are unable to find him. Discovering him, then, is easy. This is how:

lexical_decisions.chosen: setting everything else aside
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle denotes passing over or setting aside everything; “else” makes the implied contrast with the one prophet explicit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μόνῳ τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας πιστεύειν ἑαυτὸν προφήτῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: entrust oneself only to the prophet of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: πιστεύειν ἑαυτόν with the dative means committing or entrusting oneself to someone, not merely believing a statement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: laypeople in sophistical arguments
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰδιῶται denotes people without specialist training; σοφισμοί may be “sophistical arguments,” “subtle reasonings,” or “sophisms.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: as guardian of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: κηδεμών describes one who cares for, protects, or acts as guardian of others.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα μήτε βάρβαροι ἐξασθενῶσιν αὐτὸν μήτε Ἕλληνες ἀδυνατῶσιν εὑρεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that neither barbarians are too weak to find him nor Greeks are unable to find him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first coordinated member is compressed; “to find him” is understood with ἐξασθενῶσιν from the explicit εὑρεῖν and αὐτόν in the whole construction. A less idiomatic alternative is “neither barbarians prove too weak for him.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: discovering him
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὕρεσις here concerns identifying or finding the prophet; “the discovery concerning him” would be more formally literal.

passages.text: If he is a prophet and can know how the world came into being, the things happening within it, and the things that will be until the end, then if he has foretold to us something that we have learned ultimately came to pass, we rightly believe him, on the basis of what has already happened, that the things yet to be will happen—not only as one who knows, but also as one who foreknows. To whom, then, who has even a little understanding, is it not evident that this man should be trusted above everyone else regarding what has seemed good to God, since he alone, unlike all other human beings, knows even without having learned? Therefore, if someone is unwilling to grant that such a person (I mean one who has foreknowledge because of the divinity of the spirit within him) knows the truth, to what other person could he concede knowledge and not be deficient in understanding, when he has assigned to a non-prophet the things he was unwilling to grant a prophet to know?

lexical_decisions.chosen: how the world came into being
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς introduces the manner in which the world originated, rather than merely asserting that it originated.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things that will be until the end
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰς τέλος can indicate extension to the end; “the things that will be at the end” is also possible but less suited to the broad sequence of past, present, and future events.

lexical_decisions.chosen: something that we have learned ultimately came to pass
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here εἰς τέλος is taken temporally as “ultimately” or “in the end”; it could also emphasize complete fulfillment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καλῶς αὐτῷ ἐκ τῶν ἤδη γεγενημένων καὶ τὰ ἐσόμενα ἔσεσθαι πιστεύομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we rightly believe him, on the basis of what has already happened, that the things yet to be will happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative αὐτῷ identifies the person believed, while the accusative-and-infinitive construction gives the content accepted on the evidence of fulfilled events.

lexical_decisions.chosen: should be trusted above everyone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρά with the comparative force of the context marks preference over all other people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what has seemed good to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes what God has approved or determined; “God’s decisions” is a smoother alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃς μόνος παρὰ πάντας ἀνθρώπους καὶ μὴ μαθὼν ἐπίσταται
lexical_decisions.chosen: since he alone, unlike all other human beings, knows even without having learned
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρὰ πάντας marks him as exceptional in comparison with everyone else, and μὴ μαθών emphasizes knowledge not acquired through instruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ τοῦ πνεύματος θειότητα
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of the divinity of the spirit within him
lexical_decisions.rationale: θειότης is “divinity” or “divine nature.” Lowercase “spirit” avoids deciding by capitalization whether the author intends a distinct personal title; “Spirit” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not be deficient in understanding
lexical_decisions.rationale: φρένες here denotes mental sense or understanding; alternatives include “judgment” and “wits.”

passages.text: Therefore, before everything else, one must seek out the prophet with full discernment by means of the prophetic promise; once one has recognized him, one must follow without hesitation the remaining words of his teaching; and, confident about the things hoped for, one must conduct one’s life in accordance with the initial judgment, knowing, then, that the one who said these things is not naturally disposed to lie. Therefore, if from then on anything said by him seems to us not to have been said well, one must know that it was not badly said by him; rather, we failed to understand it, though it is sound. For ignorance does not judge knowledge correctly (since indeed not even knowledge is naturally capable of judging foreknowledge truly); rather, foreknowledge supplies knowledge to those who are ignorant.

lexical_decisions.chosen: before everything else ... with full discernment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρὸ πάντων gives priority to the search, while πάσῃ κρίσει is taken as complete or full exercise of judgment; “using every test” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by means of the prophetic promise
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπαγγελία ordinarily means “promise” or “announcement”; in this context it may specifically denote a prophetic prediction tested by its fulfillment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once one has recognized him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The prophet is the understood object, and the participle refers to recognizing or identifying him after the preceding test.

lexical_decisions.chosen: conduct one’s life in accordance with the initial judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεύεσθαι concerns one’s manner of life, while τῇ πρώτῃ κρίσει refers to the first determination that the speaker is a prophet; “the primary criterion” is a possible alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὸ ψεύσασθαι φύσιν οὐκ ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: is not naturally disposed to lie
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording describes a lack of natural disposition toward falsehood; “cannot lie by nature” would state the implication more strongly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from then on
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive phrase functions adverbially. It may alternatively mean “as for the rest,” referring to the remainder of the prophet’s statements.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸ ἡμεῖς καλῶς ἔχον οὐκ ἐνοήσαμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: rather, we failed to understand it, though it is sound
lexical_decisions.rationale: καλῶς ἔχον describes the statement as being in a good, right, or sound condition despite the hearers’ misunderstanding.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε γνῶσις πρόγνωσιν ἀληθῶς κρίνειν πέφυκεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not even knowledge is naturally capable of judging foreknowledge truly
lexical_decisions.rationale: πέφυκεν expresses natural constitution or capacity, maintaining the contrast between ordinary knowledge and foreknowledge.

passages.text: Therefore, my friend Clement, if indeed you wish to know the things pertaining to God, you can learn them from this man alone, because he alone knows the truth. For if any of the others knows anything, he has it by receiving it from this man or from his disciples. And this is both his purpose and his true proclamation: there is one God, whose work the world is, and who, being just, will certainly repay each person someday according to their deeds.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my friend Clement
lexical_decisions.rationale: The vocative φίλε is a direct, friendly address; “dear Clement” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things pertaining to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes matters concerning God; it may also be understood as “the things that matter to God.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you can learn them from this man alone
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχεις with the infinitive expresses ability or available means, while παρά identifies the source of instruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρὰ τούτου ἢ τῶν τούτου μαθητῶν λαβὼν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: he has it by receiving it from this man or from his disciples
lexical_decisions.rationale: λαβὼν ἔχει combines reception and continued possession of the knowledge.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τό τε βούλημα καὶ ἀληθὲς κήρυγμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: both his purpose and his true proclamation
lexical_decisions.rationale: βούλημα can mean “purpose,” “intention,” or “will,” while κήρυγμα is the content publicly proclaimed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: there is one God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase makes a monotheistic assertion; “God is one” is an equally possible formal rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whose work the world is
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concise nominal clause identifies the world as God’s work without adding a separate creation verb.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντως ἑκάστῳ πρὸς τὰς πράξεις ἀποδώσει ποτέ
lexical_decisions.chosen: will certainly repay each person someday according to their deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως conveys certainty, ποτέ retains the indefinite future time, and ἀποδώσει denotes rendering or repaying in correspondence with each person’s actions.

passages.text: For it is absolutely necessary that one who says God is just by nature should also believe that human souls are immortal. Otherwise, where is his justice, when some who lived devoutly, after sometimes being mistreated, were violently killed, while others who had become exceedingly impious, after luxuriating in an affluent life, died the death common to human beings? Since, then, beyond all dispute God is good and just, yet he will be recognized as just in no other way unless the soul is immortal after its separation from the body, so that the evil person, having entered Hades, since he received good things here, may there be punished for the sins he committed, while the good person, having been punished here for the sins he committed, may there be established as an heir of good things, as though in the bosoms of the just—therefore, since God is just, it is evident to us both that judgment takes place and that souls are in fact immortal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For it is absolutely necessary
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom expresses complete necessity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: died the death common to human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the contrast between an ordinary human death and the violent deaths previously mentioned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since he received good things here
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς is understood as giving the basis for the punishment; it may alternatively be rendered more literally, “as one who received good things here.” The clause remains in its Greek position between entering Hades and being punished there.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though in the bosoms of the just
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the plural bodily image and understands δικαίων substantivally as just people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: therefore, since God is just
lexical_decisions.rationale: This first ὅτι is read causally, while the following ὅτι introduces what is evident.

lexical_decisions.chosen: souls are in fact immortal
lexical_decisions.rationale: τυγχάνω with the predicate adjective emphasizes their actual state; “turn out to be immortal” is also possible.

passages.text: But if anyone (as Simon the Samaritan thinks) is unwilling to grant God the attribute of being just, to whom else can anyone grant this—or even the ability to become just? For if the root of all things does not possess this, it is absolutely necessary to understand that it is impossible to find it in human nature, as in the fruits. But if it can be found among human beings, how much more in God? And if what is just can be found nowhere (neither with God nor with human beings), then assuredly neither can what is unjust. But what is just does exist; for when justice exists, the unjust is spoken of, just as, when justice is compared with it and found to stand in opposition, the term “injustice” is used.

lexical_decisions.chosen: God the attribute of being just
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitival expression denotes God’s being just as an attribute granted to him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνι ἔτι τοῦτό τις δοῦναι δύναται ἢ καὶ τὸ γενέσθαι δύνασθαι;
lexical_decisions.chosen: to whom else can anyone grant this—or even the ability to become just?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative τίνι is taken as governing both grants, with the recipient as the implicit subject of γενέσθαι and “just” understood from the preceding δικαίῳ εἶναι. Alternatively, justice itself may be understood as the implicit subject: “or even grant that it is capable of coming into being.” The recipient-and-capacity reading is preferred because it continues the question “to whom?” and the preceding predicate “just.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: For if the root of all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the root-and-fruit analogy between the source of all things and human nature.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what is just
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjective may also be rendered abstractly as “justice.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ παραβαλλομένης τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὐτῇ καὶ ἐναντίως ἔχειν εὑρισκομένης ἀδικία λέγεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: just as, when justice is compared with it and found to stand in opposition, the term “injustice” is used
lexical_decisions.rationale: The referent of αὐτῇ and the implicit subject of λέγεται are compressed. The rendering leaves “it” open while taking the final clause as naming the opposed condition; alternatively, “what stands opposed to justice is called injustice.”

passages.text: Hence, then, God, in teaching human beings with a view to the truth of existing things, though himself one, divided all the things at the extremes in two and as opposites. Being himself from the beginning the one and only God, he made heaven and earth, day and night, light and fire, sun and moon, life and death. But among these he made the human being alone self-determining, with the capacity to become just or unjust. For the human being he also reversed the patterns of the pairs, setting before him the first members as small and the second as great—for example, the world and the age. (For the present world is temporary, but the one to come is eternal.) Ignorance is first, knowledge second. In this way he also arranged the leaders of prophecy. For since the present world is female, like a mother of children giving birth to souls, while the coming age is male, like a father receiving his own children, for this reason prophets accordingly make their appearance in this world as sons of the coming age, possessing knowledge of human beings. If people who live in reverence for God had understood this mystery, they would never have gone astray, but even now they would know that Simon, who is now throwing everyone into confusion, is a collaborator of the weak left hand. The account of the prophetic rule runs as follows:

lexical_decisions.chosen: with a view to the truth of existing things
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός is taken as expressing the aim of the teaching; it could also be understood as “concerning the truth of existing things.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διχῶς καὶ ἐναντίως διεῖλεν πάντα τὰ τῶν ἄκρων
lexical_decisions.chosen: divided all the things at the extremes in two and as opposites
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the twofold division and the opposition without specifying more precisely what τὰ τῶν ἄκρων comprises.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μόνον δὲ ἐν τούτοις αὐτεξούσιον τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐποίησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: But among these he made the human being alone self-determining
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνον is taken with “the human being,” making humanity alone αὐτεξούσιος among the listed creations. A possible alternative attachment is “only in these matters he made the human being self-determining.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ᾧ καὶ τὰς τῶν συζυγιῶν ἐνήλλαξεν εἰκόνας
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the human being he also reversed the patterns of the pairs
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative pronoun refers to the human being. εἰκόνας literally means “images,” while “patterns” conveys the exemplary correspondences in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: (ὁ μὲν γὰρ παρὼν κόσμος πρόσκαιρος, ὁ δὲ ἐσόμενος ἀΐδιος.)
lexical_decisions.chosen: (For the present world is temporary, but the one to come is eternal.)
lexical_decisions.rationale: No noun is expressed after ὁ δὲ ἐσόμενος. “The one to come” preserves the ellipsis. The balanced construction can supply κόσμος, “the world to come,” while the immediately preceding κόσμον, αἰῶνα and the later ὁ ἐσόμενος αἰών also support “the coming age.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: arranged the leaders of prophecy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context emphasizes their ordering; “appointed the leaders of prophecy” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: prophets accordingly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπομένως is taken inferentially as “accordingly”; it may also suggest that the prophets follow in the corresponding order.

lexical_decisions.chosen: possessing knowledge of human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive is understood objectively. Alternatives include “possessing human knowledge” and “possessing the knowledge belonging to human beings.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: of the weak left hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjective may denote the left hand or left side; “hand” anticipates the right-and-left image in the following section.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ λόγος τοῦ προφητικοῦ κανόνος οὕτως ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: The account of the prophetic rule runs as follows
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος is taken as the formulation or account that follows; κανών denotes the governing rule or pattern.

passages.text: Just as in the beginning God, being one, first made heaven, like the right hand, and then earth, like the left, and in this way constituted all the pairs in succession, with human beings, however, it is no longer this way; instead, he reverses all the pairs. For while the first things from him are better and the second inferior, among human beings we find the opposite: the first inferior and the second better. Thus, to begin with, from Adam, who came into being according to God’s image, there arose one who was first and unjust, Cain, and a second who was just, Abel. Again, from the one you call Deucalion, two images of spirits were sent out—I mean of an unclean spirit and a clean one—the black raven and, second, the white dove. From Abraham, the founder of our nation, two came into being first: first Ishmael, then Isaac, who was blessed by God. And from Isaac himself, likewise, again two arose: the impious Esau and the devout Jacob. Thus, in order, first—as firstborn for the world—is the high priest, and then the lawgiver.

source_issues.source_quote: (ὡς γὰρ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τὰ πρῶτα κρείττονα, τὰ δεύτερα ἥττονα
source_issues.issue: The supplied text prints an opening parenthesis before ὡς but no matching closing parenthesis within section 2.16, so its intended scope remains uncertain. This is a confirmed editorial-punctuation feature, not an unreadable Greek construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: like the right hand ... like the left
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjectives can denote the right and left hand or side; the rendering maps them respectively to heaven and earth according to the stated order.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with human beings, however
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπί marks the sphere in which the ordering is reversed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς γὰρ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τὰ πρῶτα κρείττονα, τὰ δεύτερα ἥττονα
lexical_decisions.chosen: For while the first things from him are better and the second inferior
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical Greek is supplied with an English copula. ὡς may alternatively be taken causally as “since.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐγένετό τις πρῶτος ἄδικος Κάιν, δεύτερος δίκαιος Ἄβελ
lexical_decisions.chosen: there arose one who was first and unjust, Cain, and a second who was just, Abel
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the ordinal contrast and the moral predicates without smoothing them into a familiar narrative formula.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one you call Deucalion
lexical_decisions.rationale: καθ’ ὑμᾶς marks the addressees’ terminology or tradition rather than simply presenting Deucalion as the author’s own designation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: two images of spirits were sent out
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the explicit description of the raven and dove as images representing the two spirits.

lexical_decisions.chosen: two came into being first
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine plural πρῶτοι is compressed and no noun such as “sons” is expressed. The rendering avoids supplying that noun; “two first ones came into being” is more formally literal but less intelligible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as firstborn for the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative can express relation or perspective. Alternatives include “as firstborn in the world” and “as firstborn from the world’s standpoint.”

passages.text: For likewise the pairing connected with Elijah, though due to come, was willingly left behind until another time, having decided to take it up on another suitable occasion. Therefore the one “among those born of women” came first; then the one among the sons of men came second. By following this sequence, it was possible to understand whose Simon is—the one who, before me, was first to come to the Gentiles—and whose I am, I who have come after him and come upon him as light upon darkness, as knowledge upon ignorance, as healing upon disease. So then, just as the true prophet told us, a false gospel must first come from a certain deceiver, and only then, after the destruction of the holy place, must a true gospel be sent out secretly to set right the heresies that will arise. After these things, toward the end, the Antichrist must again come first, and then our Jesus, who is truly the Messiah, must appear; and after that, when eternal light has risen, everything belonging to darkness must disappear.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the pairing connected with Elijah
lexical_decisions.rationale: συζυγία denotes a conjunction or paired counterpart in the author’s sequence of paired figures; “connected with” leaves the precise relationship open.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to take it up on another suitable occasion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The referent of αὐτήν is not explicit. “Take it up” reflects ἀπολαβεῖν while allowing the pairing or its deferred fulfillment to be intended; “receive it” or “recover it” are possible alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνος ἐστὶν Σίμων, ὁ πρὸ ἐμοῦ εἰς τὰ ἔθνη πρῶτος ἐλθών, καὶ τίνος ὢν τυγχάνω
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose Simon is—the one who, before me, was first to come to the Gentiles—and whose I am
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated τίνος expresses affiliation or belonging within the paired sequence; specifying a particular owner, side, or spiritual source would resolve an ambiguity the Greek leaves open.

lexical_decisions.chosen: our Jesus, who is truly the Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χριστός functions as a title here, emphasized by ὄντως, rather than merely as part of a conventional personal name.

passages.text: Since, then, as I said, some people are ignorant of the rule of pairing, for this reason they do not know who Simon, the one who went ahead of me, actually is. For if he were known, he would not have been believed. But now, because he is unknown, he has wrongly been believed. The one who does what haters do has been loved; the enemy has been welcomed as a friend; though he is death, he has been desired as one who saves; though he is fire, he has been regarded as light; and though he is a deceiver, he is listened to as one who speaks the truth. When I, Clement, heard these things, I said, “Who, then, is this man, such a great deceiver? I would like to know.” Peter said, “If you wish to learn, it is within your reach to find out from those from whom I too accurately learned everything concerning him.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the rule of pairing
lexical_decisions.rationale: κανών is the governing pattern or rule, while συζυγία continues the author’s technical language of paired figures.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who does what haters do
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek literally refers to doing “the things of those who hate.” This rendering preserves that unusual expression; “the deeds of hatred” is a smoother but less formally exact alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: though he is death, he has been desired as one who saves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast identifies him with death and presents him as falsely desired in the role of a saving figure; “as a savior” would be an idiomatic alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it is within your reach to find out
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression states that the opportunity or means of knowing is available to Clement, not merely that knowledge is physically present.

passages.text: There is among us a certain Justa, a Syrophoenician and a Canaanite by ancestry, whose little daughter was afflicted by a severe disease. She approached our Lord, crying out and pleading that he heal her little daughter. But he, when appealed to by us as well, said, “It is not permitted to heal the Gentiles, who resemble dogs because they use different foods and practices, since the table corresponding to the royal one has been allotted to the sons of Israel.” When she heard this, wishing, like a dog, to partake as well of crumbs falling from that same table, she changed what she had been by living in the same way as the sons of the kingdom, and obtained, as she had requested, healing for her little daughter. For had she remained a Gentile—being a Gentile and continuing in the same way of life—he would not have healed her, since in the first place it was not permitted to heal her as a Gentile.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀποδεδομένης τῆς κατὰ τὴν βασίλειον τραπέζης τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ.
source_issues.issue: The verified printed construction is unusual but permits a provisional unaltered-text analysis: τραπέζης can be the head of the genitive absolute, while τὴν βασίλειον is substantival or elliptical, with another “table” understood. Changing τραπέζης to τράπεζαν would produce a different construction and support an allotted portion or provisions at the royal table, but that remains a conjecture rather than the supplied reading.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἀποδεδομένης τῆς κατὰ τὴν βασίλειον τράπεζαν τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ.

source_issues.source_quote: τῆς βασιλείας .υἱοῖς
source_issues.issue: The verified printed full stop interrupts the noun phrase. It is provisionally treated as non-syntactic or stray editorial punctuation because taking it as a sentence boundary does not yield a defensible construction here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a Syrophoenician and a Canaanite by ancestry
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first term identifies her regional or ethnic designation, while τὸ γένος explicitly marks Canaanite descent or ancestry.

lexical_decisions.chosen: little daughter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The diminutive form is retained as “little daughter.” It may be affectionate or lexicalized rather than a precise statement of age.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ καὶ ὑφ’ ἡμῶν ἀξιωθεὶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: But he, when appealed to by us as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this context ἀξιωθείς describes his being petitioned or entreated by the disciples; the more literal “deemed worthy by us” would not fit the following response as naturally.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀποδεδομένης τῆς κατὰ τὴν βασίλειον τραπέζης τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the table corresponding to the royal one has been allotted to the sons of Israel
lexical_decisions.rationale: This provisionally retains τραπέζης as the head of the genitive absolute and takes τὴν βασίλειον substantivally or elliptically, with another “table” understood after it. The construction is unusual; a conjectural change of τραπέζης to τράπεζαν would instead support a sense such as “what belongs at the royal table,” but that is not the supplied reading.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς τραπέζης ὡς κύων ψιχίων ἀποπιπτόντων συνμεταλαμβάνειν βουλομένη
lexical_decisions.chosen: wishing, like a dog, to partake as well of crumbs falling from that same table
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνμεταλαμβάνειν conveys sharing or partaking along with others, while the genitives associate the crumbs with their falling from the table.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μεταθεμένη ὅπερ ἦν, τῷ ὁμοίως διαιτᾶσθαι τοῖς τῆς βασιλείας .υἱοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: she changed what she had been by living in the same way as the sons of the kingdom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive with the dative article expresses the means by which the change occurred. διαιτᾶσθαι concerns manner of life, including the foods and practices just mentioned; the printed full stop before υἱοῖς is treated provisionally as non-syntactic punctuation and disclosed separately.

passages.text: This very woman, then, after adopting a way of life according to law, was driven from her own home, together with her healed daughter, by her own husband, who held opinions opposed to ours. But she, remaining faithful to her agreements and having abundant means, herself remained a widow, while she arranged her daughter’s marriage to a certain man who was favorably disposed toward the true faith and was poor. Then, being deprived also of her daughter because of the marriage, she bought two boys, educated them, and had them in place of sons. Having been educated together with Simon the magician from childhood, they learned thoroughly everything concerning him; for their friendship with him was so close that they were even closely joined to him in every matter in which he wished to unite with them.

source_issues.source_quote: οἷς βούλοιτο αὐτοῖς ἐνοῦν
source_issues.issue: The printed ἐνοῦν and its construction with οἷς and αὐτοῖς are unusual. It can defensibly be understood as corresponding in sense to ἑνοῦν, “to unite,” yielding “in every matter in which he wished to unite with them.” The alternative sense “in which he wished them to be present” requires the conjectural alteration αὐτοῖς ἐνοῦν to αὐτοὺς ἐνεῖναι and is not another reading of the unchanged words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after adopting a way of life according to law
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία denotes a manner of life or conduct, and νόμιμον connects it with law-observant practice rather than merely describing it as socially respectable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: remaining faithful to her agreements
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes honorable fidelity toward established agreements, probably her marital commitments in context; “marriage covenant” is possible but more specific than the Greek itself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being deprived also of her daughter because of the marriage
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can indicate the occasion or stated reason, not necessarily a deceptive pretext. The sense is that the daughter’s marriage deprived Justa of her presence or companionship.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she bought two boys
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὠνησαμένη explicitly describes purchase, while the following statement that she treated them as sons supports taking παῖδας as boys rather than generically as children.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοσαύτη γὰρ αὐτῶν ἦν ἡ φιλία, ὡς καὶ συνοστεῦσαι αὐτῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: for their friendship with him was so close that they were even closely joined to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνοστεῦσαι expresses close association or intimate attachment, more strongly than merely keeping company. “Were intimate with him” is possible but could carry an unintended sexual implication in modern English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν πᾶσιν οἷς βούλοιτο αὐτοῖς ἐνοῦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in every matter in which he wished to unite with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering provisionally understands the printed ἐνοῦν as corresponding in sense to ἑνοῦν, “unite,” with αὐτοῖς identifying those with whom Simon wished to join. A conjectural alteration to αὐτοὺς ἐνεῖναι would instead mean “in everything in which he wished them to be present.”

passages.text: These men met Zacchaeus while he was staying here and, through him, shared in the word of truth. Having regretted their initial innovations, they quickly condemned Simon. Since they had shared knowledge of everything with him, as soon as I arrived here they approached me together with the woman who had raised them. They were introduced to me by Zacchaeus, and from then on they have always remained with me, benefiting from the teachings of the truth. After Peter said this, he sent for them and ordered them to set out for me precisely everything concerning Simon. They called God as witness that they would tell no lie, and began their account.

source_issues.source_quote: ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ συσταθέντες μοι
source_issues.issue: The pronoun can grammatically refer to more than one previously mentioned man. The main text chooses Zacchaeus because he had instructed them locally and could naturally introduce them to Peter; reference to Simon is contextually less likely.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Having regretted their initial innovations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb expresses regret over their earlier innovations; the context does not require the policy term “reorient.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Since they had shared knowledge of everything with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction can denote being privy to everything together with Simon; “knowing everything about him” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: together with the woman who had raised them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle identifies a woman, and the verb denotes bringing up or rearing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: They were introduced to me by Zacchaeus
lexical_decisions.rationale: Zacchaeus is the contextually preferable antecedent of the pronoun, and the verb here denotes presenting or introducing someone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: benefiting from the teachings of the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle can mean enjoying, partaking of, or benefiting from the instruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: They called God as witness that they would tell no lie
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction invokes God as witness to the truthfulness of the account they are about to give.

passages.text: Of these, Aquila was the first and began to speak as follows: “Listen, brother dearest to us, so that you may know precisely everything concerning the man—whose son he is, who he is and where he comes from, what things he does, and how and why. This Simon’s father is Antonius and his mother Rachel. He is a Samaritan by nationality, from Geththon, a village six schoeni from the city. Having been in Alexandria in Egypt, he thoroughly trained himself in Greek learning, became very powerful in magic, and grew conceited. He wants to be regarded as some supreme power, higher even than the God who created the world. At times, while also hinting that he himself is the Messiah, he calls himself ‘the Standing One.’ He uses this designation on the ground that he will always stand and has no cause of decay that would make his body fall. Nor does he say that the God who created the world is supreme. He does not believe that the dead will be raised. He repudiates Jerusalem and advances Mount Gerizim in opposition to it. In place of our actual Messiah, he proclaims himself. He allegorizes the provisions of the Law according to his own preconception. He says that there will be a judgment, but he does not expect it; for if he were convinced that he would be judged by God, he would not have dared to act impiously even against God himself. Consequently, some people, unaware that he uses reverence for God as a veil and stealthily pilfers what belongs to the truth, perish as people faithfully believing in the hope and judgment that he says will somehow come to pass.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τῇ πρὸς Αἴγυπτον γεγονώς
source_issues.issue: The participle can describe having been or lived in Alexandria, but it can also denote having been born there. The main wording leaves that distinction open.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ τὴν ὁπώσποτε ὑπὸ αὐτοῦ ἐλπίδα καὶ κρίσιν λεγομένην ἔσεσθαι, ὡς πιστῶς πιστεύοντες ἀπόλλυνται
source_issues.issue: The syntax is compressed. The main text takes the hope and judgment as the content of πιστεύοντες, but they may instead be included among the things of truth that Simon stealthily appropriates. The placement of ὁπώσποτε permits either “which he says will somehow occur” or “which he somehow says will occur.” The main text takes ὡς as characterizing the people as faithful believers; it may instead present their stance as supposed: “as though believing faithfully.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Listen, brother dearest to us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording explicitly preserves the group relationship expressed by ἡμῖν, presenting the addressed brother as dear to Aquila and his companions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνος τε ὢν καὶ τίς καὶ πόθεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son he is, who he is and where he comes from
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first expression concerns family origin here, as the immediately following identification of Simon’s parents indicates.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a Samaritan by nationality
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase identifies Simon’s ethnic or national affiliation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from Geththon, a village
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Geththon” directly represents the printed place name; Gitta and Gittha are possible conventional forms.

lexical_decisions.chosen: six schoeni
lexical_decisions.rationale: The schoenus was an ancient unit of variable length, so retaining it avoids an unsupported modern conversion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τῇ πρὸς Αἴγυπτον γεγονώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Having been in Alexandria in Egypt
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the broad force of the expression without deciding whether it denotes residence, presence, or birth; “having been born in Alexandria in Egypt” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνωτάτη τις εἶναι δύναμις καὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον κτίσαντος θεοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: some supreme power, higher even than the God who created the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive associated with the superlative presents Simon’s claimed power as surpassing even the creator God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hinting that he himself is the Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes suggesting indirectly, while χριστός functions independently as a title.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he calls himself ‘the Standing One’
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle functions as a designation and begins the section’s repeated standing-and-falling imagery.

lexical_decisions.chosen: advances Mount Gerizim in opposition to it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb means to bring forward as a counterclaim or substitute; Jerusalem is the contextual point of opposition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: In place of our actual Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle contrasts the real or actual Messiah with Simon’s self-proclamation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δὲ τοῦ νόμου ἰδίᾳ προλήψει ἀλληγορεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: He allegorizes the provisions of the Law according to his own preconception
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a prior assumption or preconceived notion governing his allegorical treatment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he uses reverence for God as a veil
lexical_decisions.rationale: Reverence for God is presented as a covering or façade.

lexical_decisions.chosen: perish as people faithfully believing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering represents ὡς as characterizing the capacity or stance in which they perish and renders the adverb and verb as “faithfully believing.” The alternative “perish as though believing faithfully” takes ὡς as marking a supposed or represented stance.

passages.text: The way he slipped into the doctrine of reverence for God came about as follows: There was a certain John, a daily baptizer, who, according to the principle of pairing, also became the forerunner of our Lord Jesus. Just as our Lord had twelve apostles, bearing the number of the sun’s twelve months, so John too had thirty leading men, fulfilling the moon’s monthly reckoning. Within that number there was one woman named Helena, so that not even this might lie outside the ordered scheme. For the woman, being half a man, made the count of the thirty incomplete, just as the moon’s count is incomplete, since the moon’s journey does not complete its course during the month. Of these thirty, Simon was first and most highly approved by John. The reason he did not assume leadership after John’s death was this:

source_issues.source_quote: μία τις ἦν γυνὴ λεγομένη Ἑλένη
source_issues.issue: The source has just described the numbered group as thirty ἄνδρες but then states that one member was a woman. The following explanation deliberately develops this numerical tension, so no correction is warranted.

source_issues.source_quote: ἧς ἡ πορεία τοῦ μηνὸς οὐ τέλειον ποιεῖται τὸν δρόμον
source_issues.issue: The genitive τοῦ μηνός may be temporal, as in the main text, or may attach to τὸν δρόμον, yielding “whose movement does not cover the month’s course in full.” This is an attachment ambiguity rather than evidence of source corruption.

source_issues.source_quote: τῷ Ἰωάννῃ πρῶτος καὶ δοκιμώτατος ἦν ὁ Σίμων
source_issues.issue: The dative may present Simon as first and most approved in John’s estimation or place him first within the group associated with John. The main text combines rank within the group with John’s approval.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ παρεισελθεῖν αὐτὸν τὸν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: The way he slipped into the doctrine of reverence for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb suggests intrusive or surreptitious entry, while λόγος here denotes a body of teaching.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a daily baptizer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound describes one who practices daily baptism; “Hemerobaptist” would be a possible technical transliteration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: according to the principle of pairing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a pairing or paired correspondence within the work’s conceptual scheme.

lexical_decisions.chosen: became the forerunner
lexical_decisions.rationale: The predicate noun concerns going forth or going before and identifies John’s precursor role.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν τοῦ ἡλίου δώδεκα μηνῶν φέροντες τὸν ἀριθμόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: bearing the number of the sun’s twelve months
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source explicitly correlates the twelve apostles with the twelve solar months.

lexical_decisions.chosen: had thirty leading men
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes chiefs or leading persons. The following sentences explicitly include one woman within this numbered group.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that not even this might lie outside the ordered scheme
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective describes something unarranged or outside an ordering plan.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥμισυ γὰρ ἀνδρὸς οὖσα ἡ γυνὴ
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the woman, being half a man
lexical_decisions.rationale: The author’s gendered numerical claim is translated directly without endorsement or mitigation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀτελῆ τὸν τῆς τριακοντάδος τέθεικεν ἀριθμόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: made the count of the thirty incomplete
lexical_decisions.rationale: Within the author’s calculation, Helena’s inclusion produces an incomplete total corresponding to the lunar course.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἧς ἡ πορεία τοῦ μηνὸς οὐ τέλειον ποιεῖται τὸν δρόμον
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the moon’s journey does not complete its course during the month
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τοῦ μηνός temporally, setting the period during which the moon’s journey fails to complete its course. It may instead modify τὸν δρόμον: “whose movement does not cover the month’s course in full.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρῶτος καὶ δοκιμώτατος ἦν ὁ Σίμων
lexical_decisions.chosen: Simon was first and most highly approved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative can mean most approved, esteemed, tested, or qualified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not assume leadership
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb here concerns taking the leading position after John rather than merely beginning an action.

passages.text: For while Simon was away in Egypt to advance his training in magic, John was killed. A certain Dositheus, who coveted the leadership, falsely announced Simon’s death and succeeded to the sect. Simon returned not long afterward and, though he laid strong claim to the position as his own, when he met Dositheus he did not demand it back, knowing that the person who first secures the leadership is not deposed against his will. Therefore, under a pretense of friendship, he submitted himself for a little while to second place under Dositheus. After not many days, once he had been ranked among the thirty fellow disciples, he began secretly to disparage Dositheus, alleging that he was not transmitting the teachings authentically. He said that Dositheus did this not out of envy but out of ignorance. At one point Dositheus perceived that Simon’s artful disparagement was destroying the estimation in which the majority held him, so that he was thought not to be the Standing One. He came in anger to their customary session and, finding Simon, struck him with a staff; but the staff seemed to pass through Simon’s body as though it were smoke. Astonished at this, Dositheus said to him, “If you are the Standing One, then I worship you.” When Simon said, “I am,” Dositheus recognized that he himself was not the Standing One, fell down, and worshiped him. He lowered himself to the level of the twenty-nine chief disciples and made Simon stand in the place in their estimation that had been his own. And so, after not many days, while Simon stood, Dositheus himself fell and died.

source_issues.source_quote: ταγεὶς δὲ μετ’ οὐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας τοῖς τριάκοντα συμμαθηταῖς
source_issues.issue: The dative with the participle permits Simon to be assigned among or to the thirty fellow disciples, or possibly appointed over them. The main rendering chooses ranking among them because the preceding sentence places him second under Dositheus.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῦ μὴ αὐτὸν εἶναι νομίζειν τὸν ἑστῶτα
source_issues.issue: The main text takes μή as negating the embedded identification: Dositheus was thought not to be the Standing One. It may instead have wider scope over νομίζειν, giving “so that people would no longer think him to be the Standing One.” The alternatives differ between a negative judgment and the cessation of a positive judgment, but both are defensible from the construction.

source_issues.source_quote: Εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ ἑστώς, καὶ προσκυνῶ σε
source_issues.issue: The conjunction may introduce the consequence, “then I worship you,” or carry additive force, “I too worship you.” The main text adopts the consequential reading.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῖς εἰκοσιεννέα ἑξάρχοις συγκαταβαλὼν ἑαυτὸν
source_issues.issue: The phrase may mean that Dositheus lowered himself to the rank of the twenty-nine chiefs or that he cast himself down together with them. The main rendering chooses the rank relation because he is surrendering his leadership position.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ τῆς ὑπονοίας τόπον ἔστησε τὸν Σίμωνα
source_issues.issue: The expression is unusual. The main rendering takes it as Dositheus making Simon stand in the place Dositheus had occupied in the group’s estimation. Alternatively, it may denote Dositheus’s supposed status or the position he himself believed he held. Rendering ἔστησε as “made stand” preserves the explicit standing motif without resolving the genitive phrase beyond what the context supports.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to advance his training in magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes continued practice, training, or cultivation of an ability.
