lexical_decisions.chosen: falsely announced Simon’s death
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronoun most naturally refers to the absent Simon, whose supposed death would remove his claim to succeed John.

lexical_decisions.chosen: succeeded to the sect
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes taking over in succession, while αἵρεσις here refers to the organized school or sect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ τόπου ὡς ἰδίου μεγάλως ἀντεχόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: though he laid strong claim to the position as his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: The “place” is the leadership position, and the verb expresses holding firmly to or asserting a claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is not deposed against his will
lexical_decisions.rationale: The prepositional phrase is understood as removal contrary to the officeholder’s choice; “regardless of preference” is less likely.

lexical_decisions.chosen: under a pretense of friendship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression presents friendship as assumed or feigned.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν δεύτερον τοῦ Δοσιθέου τόπον δίδωσιν ἑαυτόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he submitted himself for a little while to second place under Dositheus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase places Simon in a subordinate, second-ranking position relative to Dositheus.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταγεὶς δὲ μετ’ οὐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας τοῖς τριάκοντα συμμαθηταῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: After not many days, once he had been ranked among the thirty fellow disciples
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative is taken as the group to which Simon was assigned, though appointment in relation to or over them is also grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he began secretly to disparage Dositheus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound denotes covert or insinuating slander.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μὴ παραδιδόντα γνησίως τὰ μαθήματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: alleging that he was not transmitting the teachings authentically
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb can mean genuinely, faithfully, or authentically.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the estimation in which the majority held him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun is taken as the opinion or supposition about Dositheus among the wider group; “suspicion” is possible lexically but less suitable here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ ὥσπερ καπνοῦ τοῦ Σίμωνος διελθεῖν ἔδοξε σῶμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: but the staff seemed to pass through Simon’s body as though it were smoke
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun refers back to the staff, while the smoke comparison characterizes Simon’s apparently insubstantial body.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ ἑστώς, καὶ προσκυνῶ σε
lexical_decisions.chosen: If you are the Standing One, then I worship you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conjunction is taken with apodotic force; “I too worship you” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He lowered himself to the level of the twenty-nine chief disciples
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle depicts Dositheus lowering himself into the rank associated with the twenty-nine leaders.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ τῆς ὑπονοίας τόπον ἔστησε τὸν Σίμωνα
lexical_decisions.chosen: made Simon stand in the place in their estimation that had been his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: Rendering ἔστησε as “made stand” preserves the sustained standing-and-falling imagery. The unusual genitive phrase is taken as Dositheus’s former place in the group’s estimation, though it may instead concern his supposed status or the position he believed himself to hold.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while Simon stood, Dositheus himself fell and died
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal standing-and-falling contrast concludes the wordplay surrounding the designation “the Standing One.”

passages.text: Simon, however, took Helen with him and travels about everywhere, and to this very day—as you see—he throws the crowds into turmoil. He says that he has brought Helen herself down from the highest heavens to the world, she being mistress, as an all-mother essence and wisdom. For her sake, he says, Greeks and barbarians fought, having imagined an image of the reality; for she who truly existed was then with the very first God. Nevertheless, by giving a plausible allegorical interpretation to certain such things concocted together with Greek myths, he deceives many, especially by performing many monstrous wonders—so much so that, if we did not know that he does these things by magic, we ourselves would also have been deceived. But since we were his associates at first, when in doing such things he did not harm the cause of reverence toward God, we have now left him, when, having gone far into madness, he began trying to deceive those who live in reverence toward God.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰκόνα φαντασθέντες ἀληθείας· ἣ γὰρ ὄντως οὖσα τότε παρὰ τῷ πρωτίστῳ ὑπῆρχεν θεῷ
source_issues.issue: The feminine relative ἣ can be heard as resuming Helen, while its proximity to ἀληθείας permits a reference to truth or reality. The translation takes it as the real Helen, in contrast with her image; “for the truth, which really existed, was then with the very first God” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: travels about everywhere
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound describes Simon’s continued movement from place to place.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κυρίαν οὖσαν, ὡς παμμήτορα οὐσίαν καὶ σοφίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: she being mistress, as an all-mother essence and wisdom
lexical_decisions.rationale: This retains the predication of sovereignty and the unusual description of Helen as both universal maternal essence and wisdom.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having imagined an image of the reality
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between the image over which people fought and the real Helen said to be with God. “An image of truth” is also lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: giving a plausible allegorical interpretation
lexical_decisions.rationale: πιθανῶς may describe the interpretation as plausible or Simon’s manner as persuasive; the rendering preserves its deceptive plausibility.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐξαιρέτως πολλὰ τερατώδη θαυμάσια ποιῶν, ὡς εἰ μὴ ᾔδειμεν ὅτι μαγείᾳ· ταῦτα ποιεῖ, ἠπατήθημεν ἂν καὶ αὐτοί
lexical_decisions.chosen: especially by performing many monstrous wonders—so much so that, if we did not know that he does these things by magic, we ourselves would also have been deceived
lexical_decisions.rationale: The consequential expression “so much so that” makes explicit the connection marked by ὡς between the wonders’ deceptive force and the hypothetical deception of the speakers.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τῆς θεοσεβείας οὐκ ἠδίκει μέρος
lexical_decisions.chosen: did not harm the cause of reverence toward God
lexical_decisions.rationale: μέρος literally denotes the part or sphere belonging to θεοσέβεια; “cause” gives its contextual institutional sense without importing ecclesiastical terminology.

passages.text: For he even began committing murder, as he himself disclosed to friends while he was still a friend: he had separated a child’s soul from its own body by secret oaths, to serve as an assistant in manifesting whatever he pleased; and after depicting the child in a picture, he keeps the picture set up in an inner room where he himself sleeps. He claims that he once formed him out of air through divine transformations, delineated his shape, and then returned him to the air. He explains that he carried out the operation in this way: first, he says, the human spirit, after being changed into the nature of heat, compresses the air surrounding it, drawing it in like a cupping vessel; then it turns the air into water once that air has come inside the form of the spirit. Next, he said, it changes the air within it—which cannot be poured out because of the spirit’s cohesion—into the nature of blood; the blood, upon coagulating, makes flesh; and thus, once the flesh has solidified, it brings forth a human being not from earth but from air. Having thus convinced himself that he could make a new human being, he said that, by undoing the transformations, he had returned him to the air again. While telling these things to others, he was believed, but we who were present with him at the rite piously disbelieved him. Therefore, having condemned him for impiety, we left him.

source_issues.source_quote: παιδίου ψυχὴν τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος χωρίσας, ἀπορρήτοις ὅρκοις συνεργὸν πρὸς τὴν τῶν αὐτῷ δοκούντων φαντασίαν
source_issues.issue: The construction is compressed: no separate verb meaning “make” or “bind” is printed with συνεργόν, and ἀπορρήτοις ὅρκοις may attach either to the soul’s separation or to its service as an assistant. The translation treats συνεργόν as the resulting function of the separated soul and attaches the oaths to the separation.

source_issues.source_quote: εἶτα ἔνδοθεν τῆς τοῦ πνεύματος ἰδέας γενόμενον αὐτὸν τρέψαι εἰς ὕδωρ. ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς συνεχείας τοῦ πνεύματος χυθῆναι μὴ δυνάμενον εἰς αἵματος φύσιν μετατρέπειν ἔφασκεν τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ ἀέρα
source_issues.issue: The subjects of τρέψαι and μετατρέπειν are implicit, and the reference of αὐτῷ is not uniquely fixed. The main translation continues the spirit as the agent, understands χυθῆναι μὴ δυνάμενον as describing the enclosed air, and takes αὐτῷ as referring to the spirit, favoring continuity with the preceding spirit-agent construction. Alternatively, the neuter χυθῆναι μὴ δυνάμενον may resume the previously mentioned water as the subject of μετατρέπειν, with αὐτῷ referring to that water: the water, unable to flow out because of the spirit’s cohesion, changes the air within itself into blood. This is interpretive ambiguity rather than demonstrated source corruption.

lexical_decisions.chosen: committing murder
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb literally evokes blood-defilement but contextually denotes murderous bloodshed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπορρήτοις ὅρκοις συνεργὸν πρὸς τὴν τῶν αὐτῷ δοκούντων φαντασίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by secret oaths, to serve as an assistant in manifesting whatever he pleased
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνεργόν presents the separated soul as Simon’s assistant, while φαντασία denotes producing an appearance or manifestation. The attachment of “by secret oaths” is compressed and could instead qualify how the soul was made his assistant.

lexical_decisions.chosen: depicting the child in a picture
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαγράφω denotes drawing or delineating, and the subsequent feminine participle points back to the implicitly understood picture.

lexical_decisions.chosen: compresses the air
lexical_decisions.rationale: The uncommon verb describes pressing or condensing the surrounding air after drawing it inward.

lexical_decisions.chosen: drawing it in like a cupping vessel
lexical_decisions.rationale: A σικύα is a medical cupping vessel that draws material inward by suction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς συνεχείας τοῦ πνεύματος χυθῆναι μὴ δυνάμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: which cannot be poured out because of the spirit’s cohesion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes συνέχεια as cohesion or enclosing continuity and understands the clause as describing the enclosed air. The neuter wording also permits the previously mentioned water to be the substance unable to flow out.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were present with him at the rite
lexical_decisions.rationale: τελετή can denote a rite or an initiation; “rite” avoids deciding whether a formal initiation is specifically meant.

passages.text: After Aquila said these things, his brother Nicetas said, “It is necessary, our brother Clement, for me to recall what Aquila omitted. First, God is witness that we did not collaborate with him in anything impious, but that we observed what he did. As long as he showed himself doing harmless things, we too were entertained; but when he said that he did by divinity the things that are done by magic, in order to deceive those who revere God, we no longer tolerated him, although he promised us many things: first, that statues of us would be judged worthy of temples, that we would be regarded as gods, worshiped by crowds, glorified by kings, judged worthy of public honors, and enriched with boundless wealth.”

source_issues.source_quote: αὐτοῦ πράσοντος ἱστορήσαμεν
source_issues.issue: The supplied edition prints πράσοντος with one sigma, an apparent orthographic irregularity understood contextually as “doing.” The conventional πράσσοντος is offered only as a possible orthographic normalization, not as the supplied reading or as a demonstrated correction of source corruption.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what Aquila omitted
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative identifies Aquila as the person responsible for the omission; “what was left for Aquila” is grammatically possible but does not fit Nicetas’s supplementation as well.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we did not collaborate with him in anything impious
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes working jointly with someone, while ἀσεβές supplies the impious object or result denied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we observed what he did
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω can mean investigating, learning by inquiry, or observing. Here it contrasts witnessing Simon’s actions with participating in them. The printed πράσοντος is contextually understood as “doing.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: he did by divinity the things that are done by magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording deliberately contrasts the actual means, magic, with Simon’s claimed means, divine power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: statues of us would be judged worthy of temples
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual promise is that their statues would merit placement or honor in temples; the rendering preserves the source’s genitive construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: enriched with boundless wealth
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπεριόριστος denotes what is unlimited or without bounds.

passages.text: “He promised us both these things and the things reckoned with them, on the sole condition that we stay with him and keep silent about the evil of his undertaking, so that the business of deception might prosper for him. Yet we did not agree. Instead, we even advised him to cease from such folly, saying to him, ‘Simon, remembering our friendship with you from childhood and caring for you, we advise you of what is beneficial: Stop such audacity. You cannot be a god. Fear the one who really is God. Know that you are a human being and that your span of life is short. Even if you possess great wealth or even become king, in the short span of your life little is available for enjoyment; and what is acquired impiously, though it immediately vanishes, secures eternal punishment for the one who has dared it. Therefore we advise you to fear God, by whom each person’s soul is to be judged for what it did here.’”

source_issues.source_quote: ταῦτά τε καὶ τὰ τούτοις νομιζόμενα
source_issues.issue: The relation expressed by the dative τούτοις with νομιζόμενα is semantically compressed. The main rendering takes it as things reckoned together with the preceding promises; “things regarded as comparable to these” or more idiomatically “similar promises” is also defensible. No alteration of the printed text is required.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things reckoned with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is compressed and literally concerns things regarded or reckoned in relation to the preceding promises. “Things considered comparable to these” and “similar promises” are viable contextual alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μόνον ἵνα συνόντες αὐτῷ τὸ τῆς ἐγχειρήσεως κακὸν σιωπῶμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: on the sole condition that we stay with him and keep silent about the evil of his undertaking
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνον ἵνα introduces the condition attached to Simon’s promises, while συνόντες denotes continuing in his company.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα αὐτῷ τὰ τῆς ἀπάτης προκόπτῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that the business of deception might prosper for him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural expression denotes the affairs or enterprise of deception; its singular verb is natural with a neuter plural subject.

lexical_decisions.chosen: such folly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόνοια can denote madness, desperation, or reckless folly; the context emphasizes Simon’s irrationally audacious course.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεὸς εἶναι οὐ δύνασαι· φοβήθητι τὸν ὄντως θεόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: You cannot be a god. Fear the one who really is God.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὄντως qualifies θεόν and reinforces the contrast between Simon, who cannot be a god, and the one who really is God. “Fear the real God” is a more compact alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν μεγάλα πλουτῇς ἢ καὶ βασιλεύσῃς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if you possess great wealth or even become king
lexical_decisions.rationale: μεγάλα πλουτεῖν describes being wealthy in great possessions, while βασιλεύειν means reigning or holding kingship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς ζωῆς σου μικρῷ χρόνῳ ὀλίγα τυγχάνει πρὸς ἀπόλαυσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the short span of your life little is available for enjoyment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause stresses that even great wealth or royal power provides only limited enjoyment during a short life.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀσεβῶς πορισθέντα, εὐθέως φεύγοντα, αἰωνίαν κόλασιν περιποιεῖται τῷ τετολμηκότι
lexical_decisions.chosen: what is acquired impiously, though it immediately vanishes, secures eternal punishment for the one who has dared it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival participles describe ill-gotten gains as transient yet productive of lasting punishment. The object of “has dared” remains implicit in Greek and is represented by “it.”

passages.text: But when he heard this, he laughed. When we said, “Why are you laughing at us when we are advising you about what is to your advantage?” he replied, “I am laughing at your foolish supposition, because you believe that the human soul is immortal.” And I said, “We are not surprised, Simon, that you are trying to deceive us, but we are astonished at the reasoning by which you deceive even yourself. Tell me, Simon: even if no one else has been fully assured that the soul is immortal, at least you and we have—you because you separated it from a human body, conversed with it, and commanded it; and we because we were there with you, heard the command, and clearly witnessed what it was commanded to do.” Simon said, “I know what you are saying, but you do not know what matters you are discussing.” Nicetas said, “Since you know, tell us. But if you do not know, do not imagine that you can deceive us by saying that you know while we do not. We are not so childish that you can plant in us the cunning suspicion that you know something of the secret matters, and then take us into your power and keep us there while we are tormented by desire.”

source_issues.source_quote: ὅτι πιστεύετε ἀθάνατον εἶναι τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ψυχήν
source_issues.issue: ὅτι can be read causally, as in the translation, or as introducing an explanation or the content of the preceding expression. The causal reading avoids representing Simon as ridiculing a second-order supposition that the others believe something, while preserving πιστεύετε as the verb governing the claim that the soul is immortal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Γελῶ ὑμῶν τὴν μωρὰν ὑπόληψιν, ὅτι πιστεύετε ἀθάνατον εἶναι τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ψυχήν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I am laughing at your foolish supposition, because you believe that the human soul is immortal.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὅτι is taken causally, so Simon ridicules their supposition on account of their belief in the soul’s immortality. Taking it as introducing the content of ὑπόληψιν would awkwardly make their believing, rather than the soul’s immortality, the content of the supposition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: has been fully assured
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive expresses settled assurance, not merely having heard or believed a claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: clearly witnessed what it was commanded to do
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω can mean ascertain, observe, or report; their stated presence favors direct witnessing of the commanded event.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the secret matters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression denotes things withheld or not to be disclosed; alternatives include “hidden things” and “mysteries.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: take us into your power and keep us there
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποχείριος literally describes someone under another’s hand and hence under that person’s control.

passages.text: Simon said, “I know that you know I separated a soul from a human body. But I also know that you do not know this: it is not the dead person’s soul that renders service—since it does not exist—but some demon that acts while itself pretending to be a soul.” Nicetas said, “We have heard many unbelievable things in this life, but we did not expect to hear any statement more senseless than this one. For if a demon pretends to be the dead person’s soul, what need is there for the soul to be separated from the body? Were we not ourselves there and did we not hear you adjuring the soul of the corpse? How, moreover, when one is adjured, does another that was not adjured obey as though frightened? And when you yourself were once questioned by us as to why the spirit-attendances sometimes cease, did you not say, ‘Once a soul has completed the time above ground that it was destined to spend in a body, it goes to Hades’? Did you not also add that the souls of those who died a natural death, because they went there into Hades and are kept under guard, are not readily permitted to come?”

source_issues.source_quote: αἱ παρεδρίαι
source_issues.issue: The exact English value of this technical magical plural is uncertain. It can denote attendances or services of assisting spirits and, by extension, their manifestations or sessions. “Spirit-attendances” preserves the underlying attendance terminology without selecting one narrower reconstruction of the practice.

source_issues.source_quote: αὐτόθι εἰς ᾅδην χωρήσασαι
source_issues.issue: αὐτόθι may be locative, as in the main rendering, with Hades as the place meant by “there.” It also has an attested temporal use and may mean “then and there,” “forthwith,” or “straightaway,” giving the alternative “because, having gone straightaway into Hades, they are kept under guard.” This is an ordinary interpretive ambiguity and does not require altering the supplied Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: renders service
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb describes acting in a subordinate or assisting capacity without specifying whom the being serves.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the soul of the corpse
lexical_decisions.rationale: σκῆνος literally means a tent or bodily dwelling; in this necromantic setting it refers to the dead body.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the spirit-attendances
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural denotes magical attendance or assistance associated with an attending spirit; possible contextual renderings include “spirit manifestations,” “séances,” or “familiar-spirit services.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who died a natural death
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “those who ended by their own/proper death”; the context contrasts completing one’s allotted embodied lifetime with dying prematurely.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because they went there into Hades
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes αὐτόθι locatively, referring to the place just mentioned, Hades. The word can also have temporal force such as “then and there,” “forthwith,” or “straightaway,” yielding the alternative “because, having gone straightaway into Hades, they are kept under guard.”

passages.text: After Nicetas said this, Aquila himself spoke again: “I wanted to learn just this from you, Simon: whether what is adjured is a soul or a demon, what does it fear, so that it does not disregard the oaths?” Simon said, “For it knows that it will suffer punishment if it disobeys.” Aquila said, “Accordingly, if a soul comes when adjured, judgment also takes place. If, then, souls prove to be immortal and judgment certainly takes place, so that even those adjured to an evil deed would be condemned for disobeying, how have you not been afraid to compel them, when those being compelled are punished for disobedience? The fact that you have not yet suffered for what you did is no wonder, since judgment has not yet taken place—the judgment in which you are to pay the penalty for those you compelled, while the one compelled is to come under pardon as having given priority to the oath over the evil deed.” When he heard this, he became angry and threatened us with death unless we kept silent about the things he was doing.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰ οὖν αἱ ψυχαὶ ἀθάνατοι γίνονται καὶ κρίσις πάντως γίνεται, ὥστ’ ἂν καὶ τοὺς ἐπὶ κακῇ πράξει ὁρκισθέντας καταδικασθῆναι παρακούσαντας: πῶς οὐ πεφόβησαι σὺ ἀναγκάζειν, τῶν ἀναγκαζομένων ἐπὶ παρακοῇ κολαζομένων;
source_issues.issue: The scope of καὶ κρίσις πάντως γίνεται is syntactically open. The translation joins immortality and judgment as a compound condition leading to the πῶς question, in keeping with the printed colon after παρακούσαντας. Alternatively, καὶ may be apodotic: “If souls prove to be immortal, then judgment also certainly takes place,” followed by the question. No alteration of the supplied Greek is required.

source_issues.source_quote: περὶ ὧν ἠνάγκασας
source_issues.issue: The gender and referent of ὧν are not explicit in context. It may mean “for those whom you compelled” or, with an elliptical complement, “for what you compelled them to do.” The main rendering follows the personal referent continued by τὸ ἀναγκασθέν.

source_issues.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ἀναγκασθὲν ὑπὸ συγγνώμην γένηται ὡς τῆς κακῆς πράξεως τὸν ὅρκον προτιμήσαν
source_issues.issue: The compressed comparison does not explicitly state whether prioritizing the oath caused compliance with the evil deed or amounted to preferring the oath instead of the deed. The translation preserves the comparison rather than supplying either unstated relationship.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the oaths
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this magical context the oaths function as binding adjurations; “the adjurations” is a viable contextual alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Κόλασιν γὰρ παρακούσασα οἶδεν μέλλειν παθεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For it knows that it will suffer punishment if it disobeys
lexical_decisions.rationale: The aorist participle expresses disobedience preceding the threatened punishment and is naturally represented as a condition in English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ οὖν αἱ ψυχαὶ ἀθάνατοι γίνονται καὶ κρίσις πάντως γίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: If, then, souls prove to be immortal and judgment certainly takes place
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation treats immortality and judgment as the joined conditions leading to the subsequent question and explicitly represents καὶ as “and.” An apodotic reading, “then judgment also certainly takes place,” is grammatically possible but less consistent with the printed clause sequence and punctuation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: souls prove to be immortal
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally the souls “become immortal,” but in the argument γίνονται can present immortality as the conclusion demonstrated by their continued activity; “become immortal” remains a possible more literal rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for those you compelled
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative may refer to the beings Simon compelled. It could alternatively be understood as an elliptical reference to what he compelled them to do.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς κακῆς πράξεως τὸν ὅρκον προτιμήσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: having given priority to the oath over the evil deed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the explicit comparison between the binding oath and the evil act without supplying an unstated object such as avoiding or performing the act.

passages.text: After Aquila said these things, I, Clement, asked what, then, were the wonders he performed. They told me, “He makes statues walk; when he rolls onto fire, he is not burned; sometimes he even flies; he makes loaves out of stones; he becomes a snake; he is transformed into a goat; he becomes double-faced; he turns into gold; he opens closed doors; he dissolves iron; at dinners he presents images in forms of every kind; and he causes the utensils in a house to be seen being carried for service as though on their own, while those carrying them are not seen.” As I listened to them saying these things, I was amazed. They also testified that they themselves had been present and had witnessed many such things.

lexical_decisions.chosen: statues
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes statues or sculpted human figures.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he becomes double-faced
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound literally indicates having two faces; “double-faced” preserves the physical marvel here rather than the modern figurative sense of deceitfulness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he dissolves iron
lexical_decisions.rationale: λύω can mean loosen, release, undo, or dissolve. With generic “iron,” dissolving or breaking it apart best fits the list of physical marvels, though “loosens iron” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: images in forms of every kind
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἴδωλα can denote images, apparitions, or phantasms; the following phrase emphasizes their varied visible forms.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being carried for service as though on their own
lexical_decisions.rationale: The objects appear self-moving, although the following clause indicates that unseen bearers actually carry them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they themselves had been present and had witnessed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their personal presence supports the observational sense of ἱστορέω rather than merely reporting information received from others.

passages.text:
When these things had been said in this way, the good Peter himself also began to speak:

“Brothers, you must grasp the truth of the rule of pairing. Anyone who does not depart from it cannot be led astray. For since, as we have said, we see that all things are arranged twofold and in opposition—first night, then day; first ignorance, then knowledge; and first disease, then healing—so the things of error come into life first, and afterward the truth comes upon it, as the physician comes upon the disease. For instance, when our God-loving nation was about to be delivered from its mistreatment by the Egyptians, first the diseases arose through the staff that had been turned into a snake, the staff given to Aaron, and afterward the healings were brought about through Moses’s prayers. And now too, when the nations are about to be delivered from the religion centered on idols, evil once again, as itself holding sway, acted in advance and first sent its own ally, like a snake—the Simon whom you see—who performs wonders for astonishment and deception, not healing signs for turning and salvation. Therefore, from the marvels being performed, you must discern those who perform them: who is whose worker. If someone performs useless marvels, he is a servant of evil; but if he does beneficial things, he is a leader of the good.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἡ κακία πάλιν, ὡς αὐτὴ βασιλεύουσα
source_issues.issue: The force of ὡς with the participle is interpretively open. It can present evil as holding sway in an attributed role, give the reason “since it itself held sway,” or introduce the comparison “as though it itself were reigning.” The main rendering adopts the attributed-role sense without altering the supplied text.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἐστὶν ἡγεμών
source_issues.issue: The substantival τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ may be neuter, “the good,” or masculine, “the Good One.” The main rendering adopts the former, but a personified or divine referent remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the rule of pairing
lexical_decisions.rationale: συζυγία denotes coupling or paired arrangement and here introduces the author’s sequence of opposed pairs.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ μὴ ἀφιστάμενός τις οὐκ ἔχει πλανηθῆναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: Anyone who does not depart from it cannot be led astray
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative οὗ complements ἀφιστάμενος: the person who does not depart from the rule has no possibility of being led astray.

lexical_decisions.chosen: twofold and in opposition
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves both the division into two and the opposition between the paired members.

lexical_decisions.chosen: our God-loving nation
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεοφιλής can mean loving God or beloved by God; the active sense suits the description here, though “our nation beloved by God” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the staff that had been turned into a snake
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle presents the staff as having been made into or transformed into a snake.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ κακία πάλιν, ὡς αὐτὴ βασιλεύουσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: evil once again, as itself holding sway
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering presents the role or circumstance attributed to personified evil without making its reign merely apparent. The construction may alternatively be causal, “since it itself held sway,” or comparative and provisional, “as though it itself were reigning.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: for turning and salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιστροφή denotes a turning or return; the Greek does not explicitly state the destination of the turning.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he is a leader of the good
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive can mean “of the good” or, with a masculine personal referent, “of the Good One.” The main text preserves the formally possible neuter sense.

passages.text: Accordingly, the useless signs are all the things that you yourselves have said Simon performed. I mean his making statues walk, his rolling on burning coals, his becoming a dragon, being transformed into a goat, flying into the air, and whatever other things there are of this kind. Since they are not done for the healing of human beings, they are naturally apt to deceive many besides. The signs of compassionate truth, however, are benevolent: you heard that the Lord had performed them and that I, after him, accomplish them through prayers. Most of you have stood present for these—some freed from diseases of every kind, others from demons; some having had their hands straightened, others their feet; some having recovered their eyes, and others their hearing—and also for whatever other things a person can do after becoming one who belongs to a benevolent spirit.

source_issues.source_quote: οἱ δὲ τὰς ἀκοὰς καὶ ἄλλα ὅσα ἄνθρωπος ποιεῖν δύναται, φιλανθρώπου πνεύματος ἴδιος γενόμενος
source_issues.issue: The syntax shifts from the healed people in the repeated οἱ δέ clauses to the singular generic ἄνθρωπος with γενόμενος. The main translation takes καὶ ἄλλα as extending the signs for which the audience stood present; it could instead resume the things Peter accomplishes through prayer.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they are naturally apt to deceive many besides
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom φύσιν ἔχει describes a natural tendency, while προσαπατάω can convey deceiving additional people as well.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δὲ τῆς οἰκτίρμονος ἀληθείας σημεῖά ἐστι φιλάνθρωπα
lexical_decisions.chosen: The signs of compassionate truth, however, are benevolent
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive associates the signs with compassionate truth, while φιλάνθρωπα describes them as humane or benevolent toward people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that I, after him, accomplish them through prayers
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετ’ ἐκεῖνον places Peter after the Lord, while κατορθόω presents the deeds as successfully accomplished.

lexical_decisions.chosen: others their hearing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle ἀπολαβόντες, “having recovered,” is understood elliptically from the preceding clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after becoming one who belongs to a benevolent spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιος with a genitive can describe someone as belonging to another. The phrase can also be rendered “after becoming the possession of a benevolent spirit”; the Greek does not explicitly identify the spirit.

passages.text:
After Peter had said these things, Zacchaeus came in to us toward daybreak, greeted us, and said to Peter:

“Simon postpones the debate until tomorrow, for today happens to be his sabbath, the one occurring every eleven days.”

Peter answered him, “Tell Simon, ‘Observe it as you wish, knowing that we are ready to meet you whenever you wish, by God-loving providence.’”

After hearing this, Zacchaeus went out to deliver the reply in return.

source_issues.source_quote: ἡ γὰρ σήμερον τὸ δι’ ἕνδεκα ἡμερῶν αὐτοῦ τυγχάνει σάββατον
source_issues.issue: The initial feminine article ἡ has no explicitly printed noun; ἡμέρα, “day,” is naturally understood from σήμερον. The construction remains translatable without altering the supplied reading.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Simon postpones the debate
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνατίθεται here means putting off or deferring the scheduled inquiry or disputation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δι’ ἕνδεκα ἡμερῶν αὐτοῦ τυγχάνει σάββατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: happens to be his sabbath, the one occurring every eleven days
lexical_decisions.rationale: διά with the temporal expression is taken as marking a recurring eleven-day interval. “His sabbath after eleven days” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Observe it as you wish
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperative can mean perform, complete, or observe. The sabbath is the likely unexpressed object, though the wording could more generally mean “Carry on as you wish.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by God-loving providence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective is translated in its active sense. It may alternatively mean providence that is beloved or favored by God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: went out to deliver the reply in return
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound verb conveys returning or conveying an answer in response.

passages.text:
Seeing that I was disheartened, he asked the reason and learned from me that it came from no other source than the postponement of the debate. He said:

“Clement, my friend, anyone who has already grasped that the world is governed by God’s good providence is not himself distressed over circumstances that arise, however they may, since he has acknowledged that under the administration of the superior one circumstances reach their outcome beneficially. Therefore, because he recognizes the superior one as just and lives with a good conscience, he knows how to shake from his soul, by sound reasoning, the painful event that befalls him, because it is bound to come about as something brought to completion by some unknown good. And now, do not let Simon the magician’s postponement of the debate distress you; for perhaps it has happened through God’s providence for your benefit. Therefore, since you are one of my own, I will not hesitate to speak.”

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ·πράγματα
source_issues.issue: The printed centered dot occurs between the article and its noun, where it does not function as ordinary sentence punctuation. The translation provisionally treats it as a non-semantic editorial mark rather than as a break in the construction.

source_issues.source_quote: πρὸς ἀγαθοῦ τινὸς ἀγνώστου συντελούμενον ἐλθεῖν ἔχει
source_issues.issue: The genitive after πρός supports source or agency, yielding “by some unknown good,” while the providential argument also supports the intended sense “for the sake of some unknown good.” Both interpretations are defensible without changing the printed text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: anyone who has already grasped that the world is governed
lexical_decisions.rationale: προλαμβάνω here describes grasping or accepting something beforehand as a governing conviction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: under the administration of the superior one
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομία denotes ordering or administration, while the substantival comparative refers to one who is superior or better, contextually God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because he recognizes the superior one as just
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronoun most naturally resumes “the superior one.” A reflexive interpretation, “recognizes himself as righteous,” is less likely because the Greek does not use a reflexive pronoun.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ἀγαθοῦ τινὸς ἀγνώστου συντελούμενον ἐλθεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: it is bound to come about as something brought to completion by some unknown good
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός with the genitive can mark source or agency, while συντελούμενον presents the event as being brought to completion. In context, the phrase may instead be intended teleologically: “for the sake of some unknown good.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: since you are one of my own
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιος describes Clement as personally belonging to Peter’s intimate circle rather than merely receiving private information.

passages.text: Some of our companions associate with Simon under false pretenses, as though they had been persuaded by his most godless error, so that, by learning his plans, they may disclose them to us, enabling us to adapt ourselves appropriately to a formidable man. And now I have learned from them the question about which he intends to deliver his arguments. When I learned this, I thanked God and counted you blessed because of the debate’s postponement; for, having been equipped by me before the debate, you will be able to hear without stumbling the arguments that he is going to present for the testing of those who do not know.

source_issues.source_quote: τῶν γὰρ μελλόντων λόγων ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ πρὸς διάκρισιν τῶν ἀγνοούντων λέγεσθαι σὺ πρὸ τῆς ζητήσεως ἐφοδιασθεὶς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ ἄπτωτος ἀκροατὴς γενέσθαι δυνήσει.
source_issues.issue: The fronted genitive τῶν ... λόγων is most naturally attached to ἀκροατής, yielding the arguments Clement will hear without stumbling. Attachment to ἐφοδιασθείς, “equipped with the arguments,” is grammatically conceivable but less direct and is not adopted. In addition, πρὸς διάκρισιν τῶν ἀγνοούντων may mean “for the testing of those who do not know,” as translated, or “to unsettle those who do not know,” with διάκρισις emphasizing doubt or perplexity. The latter is contextually supported by 2.39 and by διακριθῆναι in 2.40. These are attachment and lexical ambiguities, not evidence of source corruption.

lexical_decisions.chosen: associate ... under false pretenses
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb indicates that their apparent association or agreement with Simon is feigned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his most godless error
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the superlative force of ἀθεωτάτῃ and the sense of πλάνη as religious error or deception.

lexical_decisions.chosen: adapt ourselves appropriately to a formidable man
lexical_decisions.rationale: συναρμόζομαι conveys fitting or adapting oneself, while δεινός may describe someone formidable, dangerous, or highly capable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἧς μέλλει ζητήσεως ποιεῖσθαι τοὺς λόγους
lexical_decisions.chosen: the question about which he intends to deliver his arguments
lexical_decisions.rationale: ζητήσεως identifies the disputed question or debate topic, while ποιεῖσθαι τοὺς λόγους refers to presenting arguments about it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν γὰρ μελλόντων λόγων ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ πρὸς διάκρισιν τῶν ἀγνοούντων λέγεσθαι ... ἄπτωτος ἀκροατὴς γενέσθαι δυνήσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: you will be able to hear without stumbling the arguments that he is going to present for the testing of those who do not know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The fronted genitive τῶν ... λόγων is taken with ἀκροατής as the content heard. διάκρισις can denote differentiation or judgment and is rendered “testing” because the clause presents Simon’s arguments as a means of exposing uninstructed hearers to a trial. Unlike the explicit πειρασμός, “test” or “trial,” in 2.39, however, διάκρισις may emphasize the resulting division, doubt, or perplexity. The alternative “to unsettle those who do not know” is supported by Simon’s attempt to alienate hearers in 2.39 and by διακριθῆναι, rendered “to waver,” in 2.40.

passages.text: For the writings took on many false statements against God for this reason: when the prophet Moses, by God’s counsel, had handed down the law together with its interpretations to some chosen persons, seventy in number, so that they too might equip those among the people who wished it, not long afterward, once the law had been put into writing, it took on some false statements against the sole God, who created heaven and earth and everything in them, because the evil one dared to bring this about for a certain just reason. And this happened with reason and judgment, so that it might be shown who dare eagerly to listen to the things written against God, and who, out of affection for him, dare not only to disbelieve the things said against him but even to refuse to tolerate hearing them at all, even if they should happen to be true, judging it much safer to take a risk for reverent faith than to live with a troubled conscience over blasphemous words.

source_issues.source_quote: κἂν ἀληθῆ τυγχάνῃ; πολλῷ κρίναντες ἀσφαλέστερον· περὶ εὐφήμου πίστεως κινδυνεύειν ἢ ἐπὶ βλασφήμοις λόγοις δυσσυνειδήτως βιοῦν.
source_issues.issue: The supplied punctuation places a question mark after τυγχάνῃ and a middle dot after ἀσφαλέστερον, although κρίναντες and the following comparative infinitives form a coherent continuation of the preceding description. The translation treats the punctuation as editorial and follows the grammatical connection without altering the supplied Greek wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the writings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes the authoritative written corpus under discussion without importing the boundaries or capitalization of a later canon.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by God’s counsel
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνώμη may mean judgment, purpose, decision, or counsel; “counsel” presents Moses’ transmission as occurring by divine determination.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some chosen persons, seventy in number
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves both the indefinite force of τισίν and the stated number without making “some seventy” sound approximate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for a certain just reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase grammatically accompanies the evil one’s action. The difficult claim that his action occurred for a just reason is retained rather than reassigned to another agent.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ γραφέντα φιληκόως ἔχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: eagerly to listen to the things written against God
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιληκόως expresses fondness for hearing or eagerness to listen, contrasting with the following group’s refusal even to hear such statements.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνες τολμῶσιν τὰ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ γραφέντα φιληκόως ἔχειν τίνες τε στοργῇ τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸν τὰ κατ’ αὐτοῦ λεγόμενα μὴ μόνον ἀπιστεῖν, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀκούειν ἀνέχεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: who dare eagerly to listen to the things written against God, and who, out of affection for him, dare not only to disbelieve the things said against him but even to refuse to tolerate hearing them at all
lexical_decisions.rationale: The predicate τολμῶσιν governs both coordinated τίνες clauses. Repeating “dare” in English preserves the boldness attributed both to those who welcome the accusations and to those who reject them; “even to refuse” conveys the emphatic escalation of μηδὲ with the negative sense of ἀνέχεσθαι.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even if they should happen to be true
lexical_decisions.rationale: The antecedent is the things said against God. Greek permits the singular verb with the neuter plural predicate, and the author’s striking concession is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to take a risk for reverent faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὔφημος concerns favorable or reverent speech, in contrast with the blasphemous words that follow. An alternative is “to take a risk for faith that speaks well of God.”

passages.text: Simon, then, as I learn, intends to come into the midst and recite the very passages against God that were added to the writings for the sake of testing, so that he may be able to detach from affection for God as many wretched people as he can. For we do not wish to say publicly that these passages have been added to the books, since by alarming unlearned crowds we would be doing the will of the wicked Simon himself. Because they do not yet possess the ability to discern, they will either flee from us as impious or, supposing that falsity is not confined to the blasphemous passages, withdraw from the teaching. We are therefore compelled, while assenting to the false passages and asking him counterquestions about them, to bring him into perplexity, but privately, after a test of faith, to provide fair-minded people with the explanation of the passages spoken against God. That explanation has one brief path. It is this:

source_issues.source_quote: ἢ ὡς οὐ μόνον τῶν βλασφήμων περικοπῶν ψευδῶν οὐσῶν ἀποστήσονται τοῦ λόγου
source_issues.issue: The coordination is elliptical because οὐ μόνον has no expressed corresponding member. The translation understands an implied extension of falsity beyond the blasphemous passages to the larger teaching. The supplied wording nevertheless admits a defensible contextual translation and need not be emended.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ εὐγνωμονοῦσιν τῶν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ῥηθεισῶν περικοπῶν μετὰ πεῖραν πίστεως ἰδίᾳ παρέχειν τὴν ἐπίλυσιν
source_issues.issue: The genitive τῶν ... περικοπῶν may specify τὴν ἐπίλυσιν, “the explanation of the passages,” as adopted in the translation, or it may depend on εὐγνωμονοῦσιν, describing people who judge sensibly concerning those passages. This is an ordinary attachment ambiguity rather than source corruption.

lexical_decisions.chosen: added ... for the sake of testing
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόσκειμαι indicates that the passages were attached or added, while πειρασμός denotes a trial or test in this context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: come into the midst and recite
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the image of Simon entering the midst of the assembly and speaking the passages publicly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by alarming unlearned crowds
lexical_decisions.rationale: πτύρω means to frighten or alarm, and ἀμαθής describes people lacking instruction or learning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ ὡς οὐ μόνον τῶν βλασφήμων περικοπῶν ψευδῶν οὐσῶν ἀποστήσονται τοῦ λόγου
lexical_decisions.chosen: or, supposing that falsity is not confined to the blasphemous passages, withdraw from the teaching
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unexpressed counterpart to οὐ μόνον is understood as an extension of perceived falsity beyond the blasphemous passages to the larger teaching. A more formally literal rendering is “or, supposing that not only the blasphemous passages are false, they will withdraw from the teaching.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: while assenting to the false passages
lexical_decisions.rationale: The speakers accept the passages as the basis of the public argument; the wording does not require that they affirm the passages as true.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ εὐγνωμονοῦσιν τῶν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ῥηθεισῶν περικοπῶν μετὰ πεῖραν πίστεως ἰδίᾳ παρέχειν τὴν ἐπίλυσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: privately, after a test of faith, to provide fair-minded people with the explanation of the passages spoken against God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive τῶν ... περικοπῶν is attached to τὴν ἐπίλυσιν, specifying what is explained. Alternatively, it may attach to εὐγνωμονοῦσιν: “to those who judge sensibly concerning the passages spoken against God.”

passages.text: Everything said or written against God is false. That we say this truly, not merely for reverence’s sake but also for truth’s, I will fully demonstrate when the discussion has advanced a little. Therefore you, my dearest Clement, ought not to be grieved that Simon has postponed the debate for a single day—the present one. For since today, before the debate, you are being equipped in advance concerning the passages added to the writings, you ought not to waver during the debate concerning the sole and good God, who also made the world. Instead, during the debate you will even marvel at how the impious pass over the many things said in the writings on God’s behalf, yet look around for the things said against him and joyfully bring them forward. Thus the hearers, because of ignorance, believe the things said against God and become excluded from his kingdom. Therefore, having learned the mystery of the writings on the occasion of the postponement and having gained the benefit of not sinning against God, you will show favor beyond compare.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀπαραβλήτως χαρίσῃ
source_issues.issue: The supplied χαρίσῃ can be read as a future middle form of χαρίζω, but its benefactive sense is contextually difficult because no recipient or object is expressed. The main translation therefore remains provisional and preserves the printed verb’s sense without supplying a recipient. The conjecture χαρήσῃ would straightforwardly mean “you will rejoice beyond compare,” but it is not the supplied reading and is not used to justify the translation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for reverence’s sake
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐφημία here concerns speaking favorably or reverently of God, in contrast with the surrounding blasphemous statements.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ βραχὺ προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου πληροφορήσω
lexical_decisions.chosen: I will fully demonstrate when the discussion has advanced a little
lexical_decisions.rationale: πληροφορέω conveys providing full assurance or establishing something fully, while λόγος denotes the developing discussion or argument.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ τοῦ μόνου καὶ ἀγαθοῦ θεοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: concerning the sole and good God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves μόνος and ἀγαθός as coordinated descriptions. An alternative is “concerning the only God, who is good.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to waver
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this context διακρίνω denotes divided judgment, doubt, or uncertainty rather than analytical discernment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ πλήθη τῶν ὑπὲρ θεοῦ εἰρημένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the many things said ... on God’s behalf
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the contrast between the abundance of favorable statements and the selectively cited statements against God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κατ’ αὐτοῦ εἰρημένα περιβλεπόμενοι χαίροντες φέρουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: look around for the things said against him and joyfully bring them forward
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιβλέπομαι retains the image of looking around or searching, χαίροντες supplies their delight, and φέρουσιν describes bringing the selected statements forward.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the occasion of the postponement
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις may mean occasion, stated reason, or pretext. “On the occasion” presents the delay as the opportunity for instruction without requiring deceptive intent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will show favor beyond compare
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation follows the ordinary benefactive force of χαρίζομαι and leaves the recipient unexpressed, as in the supplied Greek. It does not import the meaning “rejoice” from the conjectural χαρήσῃ.

passages.text: And when I, Clement, heard this, I said, “Truly I rejoice and acknowledge my gratitude to God, the benefactor in every respect. Yet he himself knows that I shall not be able to think anything except to think about everything in God’s favor. Therefore, do not suppose that I am asking because I doubt what has been said by God or even what will yet be said, but so that, once I too have learned, I may be able to teach another who wishes to learn in a fair-minded way. So tell me what false things have been added to the Scriptures and how they prove to be actually false.” And Peter answered, “Even if you had not asked me, as I proceeded through the arguments in their proper order, I would have supplied the demonstration I promised. Nevertheless, hear how the Scriptures tell many falsehoods about him, as you will discover when you read them.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: God, the benefactor in every respect
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ πάντα presents God as beneficent in every respect, rather than merely identifying him as the benefactor of all things.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to think about everything in God’s favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπὲρ θεοῦ indicates thought favorable to or in defense of God; an alternative is “to hold every opinion in defense of God.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who wishes to learn in a fair-minded way
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐγνωμόνως can describe a reasonable, well-disposed, or appreciative manner; “fair-minded” suits the prospective learner’s disposition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what false things have been added to the Scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσκείμενα describes material placed alongside or added to the writings; the context treats γραφαί as authoritative Scriptures.

lexical_decisions.chosen: how they prove to be actually false
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual combination πῶς ὅτι is understood as asking how the alleged additions turn out in fact to be false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Scriptures tell many falsehoods about him
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταψεύδομαι with the genitive means to speak falsely about or against someone; “him” refers contextually to God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when you read them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐντυγχάνω with writings commonly means to encounter them by reading; a more literal alternative is “when you engage with them.”

passages.text: The things about to be said will suffice by way of example. I do not think, my friend Clement, that anyone who retains even a little affection and gratitude toward God will be able to accept, or so much as hear, the things said against him. But how is it possible for anyone to have a soul devoted to one sovereign and to become devout after having assumed beforehand that there are many gods and not one? And even if there is one, who, finding him amid many absurdities, will strive to become devout, in the hope that the origin of all things, because of the absurdities inherent in his own nature, will not pursue the wrongdoings of others?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ οἶμαι δέ, ὦ φίλε Κλήμης, εἰ δυνήσεταί τις
lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not think, my friend Clement, that anyone ... will be able
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although εἰ can formally introduce “whether,” after negative οἶμαι the contextual force is an emphatic doubt that anyone could do so.

lexical_decisions.chosen: affection and gratitude
lexical_decisions.rationale: στοργή denotes affectionate attachment, while εὐγνωμοσύνη here naturally denotes grateful appreciation toward God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a soul devoted to one sovereign
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “a monarchic soul,” the phrase describes a disposition affirming sole divine sovereignty; “monotheistic soul” is possible but would replace the author’s monarchy imagery.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having assumed beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle denotes adopting a prior conception or assumption.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even if there is one
lexical_decisions.rationale: “God” is elliptically understood from the preceding contrast between many gods and one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: finding him amid many absurdities
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase portrays God as being found in or associated with numerous incongruities; “finding him implicated in many absurdities” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the origin of all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχή may mean origin, first principle, or ruler; “origin” fits God as the source of everything, while “ruler of all” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will not pursue the wrongdoings of others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπέρχομαι can mean to come against, visit, or pursue; the context may specifically imply calling others to account or punishing their wrongdoings.

passages.text: Therefore, far be it from us to believe either that the Master of all, “who created heaven and earth” and everything in them, shares sovereignty with others, or that he lies—for if he lies, who then tells the truth?—or that he “tests” as though ignorant—and who then has foreknowledge? If he “deliberates” and “changes his mind,” who then is perfect in understanding and steadfast in purpose? If he “is jealous,” who then is beyond comparison? If he “hardens hearts,” who then makes wise? If there are blind and deaf people, who then has granted sight and hearing? If he advises defrauding, who then lays down justice as law? If he “mocks,” who then is sincere? If he is unable, who then can do all things? If he acts unjustly, who then is just? If he “creates evils,” who then will do good things? If he does evil things, who then does good things?

source_issues.source_quote: εἰ δὲ τυφλοὶ καὶ κωφοί
source_issues.issue: The clause has plural predicate adjectives but no expressed subject or finite verb. It is defensibly read as an elliptical nominal clause, though the context may imply an omitted action such as making people blind and deaf. No restoration is inserted into the translation.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐνπαίζει
source_issues.issue: The supplied print uses the unassimilated spelling ἐνπαίζει where the normalized spelling is commonly ἐμπαίζει. The printed form remains intelligible and is not altered.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ ’ τίς ἀγαθὰ πράξει;
source_issues.issue: An isolated high mark appears between καὶ and τίς. It has no evident syntactic function and is most plausibly editorial or typographical punctuation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: far be it from us to believe
lexical_decisions.rationale: The impersonal optative expresses emphatic rejection; “from us” is supplied by the conventional English construction without identifying a narrower subject.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shares sovereignty with others
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνάρχω means to rule jointly with others, not merely to coexist with them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: “tests”
lexical_decisions.rationale: πειράζω may mean test or tempt; the accompanying comparison with ignorance makes testing to discover unknown information the relevant idea.

lexical_decisions.chosen: “deliberates”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean considers, reflects, or deliberates; “deliberates” highlights the alleged lack of already perfected understanding.

lexical_decisions.chosen: “changes his mind”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb may mean regrets or changes one’s mind; the contrast with being steadfast in purpose favors the latter here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If there are blind and deaf people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek contains plural adjectives without an expressed noun or verb. This rendering treats them substantivally and supplies only the English existential construction; context may instead imply “if [he makes people] blind and deaf.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: lays down justice as law
lexical_decisions.rationale: The transitive νομιτεύει has legislative force here: it presents justice as something prescribed or established as law. “Practices justice” would shift the predicate from law-setting to conduct, while “regards justice as law” would shift it toward an attitude rather than prescription.

lexical_decisions.chosen: “mocks”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes mocking or making sport of someone; “deceives” is possible in some contexts but is not required here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is unable
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes inability; the following contrast is with the one who can do all things.

lexical_decisions.chosen: “creates evils”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the creation verb and the plural substantive κακά rather than generalizing the claim as merely “causes evil.”

passages.text: If he desires “the fat mountain,” to whom do all things belong? If he lies, who then tells the truth? If he dwells in a tent, who then is uncontainable? If he longs for fat-smoke and sacrifices and sacrificial victims and libations, who then needs nothing, and who is holy, and who is pure, and who is perfect? If he delights in lamps and lampstands, who then set the luminaries in heaven? If he is present in thick gloom and darkness and tempest and smoke, who then, being light, illuminates the greatest age? If he approaches with trumpets and loud cries and missiles and arrows, who then is the calm awaited by all? If he himself loves wars, who then desires peace? If he himself “creates” “the evils,” who then fashions good things? If he himself is without affection, who then loves humanity? If he himself is not faithful concerning what he promises, who then will be trusted? If he himself loves wicked people and adulterers and murderers, who then will be a just judge? If he himself “changes his mind,” who then is steadfast? If he himself chooses evil people, who then welcomes good people?

lexical_decisions.chosen: “the fat mountain”
lexical_decisions.rationale: πῖον literally describes something fat or rich and may imply a fertile or luxuriant mountain; the concrete “fat” image is retained because the phrase is quoted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to whom do all things belong
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “and whose are all things?” the question challenges the attribution of desire to the one who owns everything.

lexical_decisions.chosen: uncontainable
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective denotes one who cannot be contained, confined, or accommodated within a place.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fat-smoke
lexical_decisions.rationale: κνίση denotes the greasy smoke or savor rising from burning fat; the compact rendering preserves both the material and sacrificial imagery.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κνίσης καὶ θυσιῶν καὶ θυμάτων καὶ προσχύσεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: fat-smoke and sacrifices and sacrificial victims and libations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated conjunctions and the distinction between sacrifices, victims, and poured offerings are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν γνόφῳ καὶ σκότῳ καὶ θυέλλῃ καὶ καπνῷ σύνεστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: is present in thick gloom and darkness and tempest and smoke
lexical_decisions.rationale: The locative ἐν governs all four atmospheric nouns, while σύνεστιν means “is with” or “is present.” “Is present in” preserves the setting expressed by ἐν and avoids conflating σύνεστιν with the earlier οἰκεῖ, “dwells.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the greatest age
lexical_decisions.rationale: αἰών may denote an age, eternity, or a world-order. “Age” is the most direct rendering, while “the greatest world” remains a possible contextual interpretation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: missiles and arrows
lexical_decisions.rationale: βολίδες are thrown projectiles or bolts, while τοξεύματα are things shot from a bow; the two images are kept distinct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the calm awaited by all
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσδόκιμος means expected or awaited, and τῶν ὅλων can refer either to everyone or collectively to all things.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ „τὰ κακὰ“ αὐτὸς „κτίζει“, καὶ τίς ἀγαθὰ δημιουργεῖ;
lexical_decisions.chosen: If he himself “creates” “the evils,” who then fashions good things?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied edition separately marks both τὰ κακὰ and κτίζει as quoted expressions; the English preserves both sets of quotation marks while adopting natural English word order.

lexical_decisions.chosen: without affection
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective denotes absence of natural or familial affection; “unloving” is a broader alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If he himself “changes his mind,” who then is steadfast?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb may also mean “regrets,” but the contrast with βέβαιος, one who is stable or steadfast, favors “changes his mind”; the quotation marking in the supplied edition is preserved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: welcomes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean admits, receives, or accepts; “welcomes” provides a natural contrast with choosing evil people.

passages.text: Therefore, child Clement, be on guard not to think anything about God other than that he alone is God and Lord and Father, good and just, creator, patient, merciful, nourisher, benefactor, practicing benevolence toward humanity, counseling purity, eternal and making people eternal, incomparable, dwelling in the souls of the good, uncontainable yet contained; the one who fixed the great world within the boundless like a center point, who spread out heaven and compressed the earth, stored up water, arranged stars in heaven, made springs gush in the earth, made fruits spring up, raised mountains, set bounds around the sea, and ordered winds and spirits; the one who secured the encompassing body in a boundless sea by “spirit of counsel.”

source_issues.source_quote: φιλανθρωπίαν’ νομιτεύων
source_issues.issue: The supplied print has an apostrophe after φιλανθρωπίαν, but no elision or syntactic function for it is evident, and νομιτεύων is rare. The clause remains defensibly renderable as printed; interpreting the apostrophe as an editorial or typographical oddity is provisional.

lexical_decisions.chosen: practicing benevolence toward humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rare νομιτεύων is understood in the sense of observing or practicing something as customary; alternatively, the phrase could mean “making benevolence toward humanity his rule.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: eternal and making people eternal
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first adjective describes God, while the masculine plural αἰωνίους supplies an implied personal object for the participle.

lexical_decisions.chosen: uncontainable yet contained
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the source’s deliberate paradox; χωρούμενος may also carry the sense “received” or “comprehended.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐν ἀπείρῳ τὸν μέγαν αἰῶνα ὡς κέντρον πήξας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who fixed the great world within the boundless like a center point
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although αἰών can mean “age” or “aeon,” the spatial language of fixing it in the boundless as a κέντρον supports the cosmological rendering “world.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: compressed the earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: πιλόω depicts pressing or compacting, with an underlying image of material being felted together.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and ordered winds and spirits
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεύματα can denote spirits, but in coordination with “winds” within this sequence of physical creation it may instead mean “breaths,” “blasts,” or “gusts of air”; thus “and ordered winds and gusts of air” is a materially relevant alternative. “Spirits” is retained because it preserves the broader sense of πνεύματα and allows the coordinated nouns to identify distinct created entities rather than two near-synonymous kinds of moving air.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ περιέχον σῶμα ἐν ἀπείρῳ πελάγει „πνεύματι βουλῆς“ ἀσφαλισάμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: secured the encompassing body in a boundless sea by “spirit of counsel”
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεύματι is taken instrumentally and ἐν ἀπείρῳ πελάγει locally. The participle περιέχον may describe a body that encompasses or surrounds all things.

passages.text: He is our judge. Looking to him, we must set our own souls right, considering everything with reference to him, praising him, and being convinced that, while by his patience he brings everyone’s recklessness into the open, he alone is good. And at the end of all things, he will take his seat before each of those who have dared what they should not have as a just judge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: considering everything with reference to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: With νοεῖν, ὑπέρ can identify the reference or concern governing one’s thought, supporting the chosen broad rendering. It may also mean “considering everything in his favor,” especially in light of the surrounding discussion of statements made against God, or “considering everything for his sake.” The main text retains the referential sense because the construction does not by itself require an explicitly favorable or defensive posture.

lexical_decisions.chosen: praising him
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐφημέω literally concerns speaking well of someone and here functions as praise directed to God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ αὐτοῦ μακροθυμίᾳ πάντων τὴν προπέτειαν εἰς φανερὸν ἄγων
lexical_decisions.chosen: while by his patience he brings everyone’s recklessness into the open
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative may be instrumental, “by his patience,” or modal, “in his patience.” The participle is rendered circumstantially without making its precise logical relationship exclusively causal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at the end of all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῦ παντός can denote the totality of things or the universe; the final-judgment context supports “all things,” while “at the end of the universe” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will take his seat ... as a just judge
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb presents the judge as being seated before those judged; “will preside as judge” is a smoother alternative.

passages.text: After hearing these things, I, Clement, said, “Truly, this is reverence for God; this truly is piety.” Then I said again, “So I would like to learn why the books were written in this way. For I remember you saying that it was to expose those who would dare to believe anything said against God. Still, since you graciously allow us to question you as we wish, we venture to question you, since you have instructed us to do so. If someone should wish, dearest Peter, to say to us, ‘What has been written is true, even if what has been said against God seems false to you,’ how are we to answer him?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: reverence for God ... piety
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering distinguishes explicit reverence directed toward God from the broader quality of devout or pious conduct.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἔλεγχον τῶν μελλόντων τολμᾶν πιστεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to expose those who would dare to believe
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔλεγχος can denote exposure, testing, refutation, or conviction. “Expose” fits the claim that such readers reveal themselves by believing statements against God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χαρίζῃ ἡμῖν πυνθάνεσθαί σου ὡς βουλόμεθα
lexical_decisions.chosen: you graciously allow us to question you as we wish
lexical_decisions.rationale: χαρίζῃ presents the permission as a favor, while ὡς βουλόμεθα describes the freedom with which they may ask.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν σοὶ ψευδῆ δοκῇ τὰ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ῥηθέντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if what has been said against God seems false to you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the concessive force of κἄν and the subjective appearance expressed by σοὶ ... δοκῇ, rather than asserting directly that the statements are false.

passages.text: Peter answered, “You did well to ask, for it will be for your security. But listen. Since many things have been said against God by the writings, in view of the hour’s urgency because of the evening, ask about whichever one statement you wish, and I will resolve it, showing it to be false not merely because it has been stated against God, but because it is actually false.” And I replied, “I want to learn how, when the writings say that God does not know, you can prove that he does know.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: things ... said ... by the writings
lexical_decisions.rationale: γραφαί can be rendered “Scriptures,” but “writings” preserves the lexical form without imposing a capitalization or canonical designation not marked by the Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὸ ἐπεῖγον τῆς ὥρας διὰ τὴν ἑσπέραν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in view of the hour’s urgency because of the evening
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase attributes the pressure of the available time to the evening; a smoother alternative is “since evening makes the time pressing.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: ask about whichever one statement you wish
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος here denotes a particular assertion or passage to be questioned rather than speech in general.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐχ ὅτι μόνον κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ εἴρηται, ἀλλ’ ὅτι ὄντως ψευδής ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not merely because it has been stated against God, but because it is actually false
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast denies that opposition to God alone is the ground for rejection and promises a demonstration of the statement’s actual falsehood.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγνοεῖν λεγουσῶν τὸν θεὸν ... γινώσκοντα αὐτὸν ἀποδεῖξαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: say that God does not know ... prove that he does know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated English verb preserves the direct contrast between ἀγνοεῖν and γινώσκοντα without supplying an unstated object of God’s knowledge.

passages.text: And Peter replied, “You have put before us something that can easily be refuted. Nevertheless, hear how God is ignorant of nothing and even foreknows. But first answer me this question of mine: Was the one who wrote the books and said how the world was created and that God does not foreknow a human being or not?” And I said, “A human being.” Peter replied, “Since he was a human being, then, how was it possible for him to know without error how the world was created and that God does not foreknow?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: You have put before us something that can easily be refuted
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival neuter participle leaves the object unnamed; “something” preserves that lack of specification rather than supplying “argument.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲν ἀγνοεῖ θεός, ἀλλὰ καὶ προγινώσκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: God is ignorant of nothing and even foreknows
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the contrast between lacking no knowledge and possessing knowledge in advance; “knows beforehand” is also possible for προγινώσκει.
