lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃ δὲ πυνθάνομαί σου; πρῶτον ἀπόκριναί μοι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: But first answer me this question of mine
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative expression is taken with the following command. The editorial question mark could instead yield the more abrupt “But what I ask you? Answer me first,” but that is less natural English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to know without error
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀψευδῶς denotes knowing truly or infallibly; “without error” avoids implying merely personal honesty.

passages.text: And I, already perceiving the solution, said with a slight smile, “Because he was a prophet.” Peter said, “If, then, the prophet, though a human being, was ignorant of nothing because he had received foreknowledge from God, how could the very one who gave a human being the ability to foreknow, being God, have been ignorant?” And I said, “You spoke correctly.” Then Peter said, “Join me, then, in examining this very point further. Since we have agreed that God foreknows everything, it is absolutely necessary that the scriptures which say he is ignorant are false, while those which say he knows are true.” And I said, “It must be so.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: already perceiving the solution, said with a slight smile
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίλυσις is the solution or resolution of the difficulty, while ὑπομειδιῶν indicates a restrained or slight smile.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ ἀπὸ θεοῦ εἰληφέναι τὴν πρόγνωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: because he had received foreknowledge from God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive gives the reason, and πρόγνωσις denotes advance knowledge rather than a prediction uttered by the prophet.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸς ὁ δεδωκὼς ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ προγινώσκειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the very one who gave a human being the ability to foreknow
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτός emphasizes the giver himself, and the articular infinitive denotes the capacity or act of knowing in advance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἔτι οὖν, ἔφη, εἰς αὐτὸ συνδιαπόρησόν μοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: Then Peter said, “Join me, then, in examining this very point further”
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνδιαπορέω invites joint consideration of a difficulty. “Join me in questioning” is possible, but “examining” is more idiomatic in context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those which say he knows
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτόν is construed as the accusative subject of γινώσκειν in contrast with the preceding claim that he is ignorant. Its position also permits the formal alternative “say that someone knows him,” but that leaves the subject unstated and disrupts the explicit contrast.

passages.text: And Peter said, “If, then, some things in the scriptures are true and others false, our teacher had good reason to say, ‘Become approved money changers,’ since some of the statements in the scriptures are genuine while others are counterfeit. And to those being led astray by the false scriptures, he appropriately revealed the cause of their error by saying, ‘This is why you go astray: you do not know what is true in the scriptures; for this reason you are also ignorant of the power of God.’” And I said, “Very good.”

source_issues.source_quote: μὲν-ἐστὶν
source_issues.issue: The supplied, image-checked reading prints a hyphen between μὲν and ἐστίν. It appears to be an editorial or typographic separator without semantic force; the translation construes the two printed words separately.

source_issues.source_quote: τῶν γραφῶν ἃ μὲν-ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ, ἃ δὲ ψευδῆ
source_issues.issue: If ἃ and ἀληθῆ directly modified the feminine γραφῶν, their neuter gender would be unexpected. They can defensibly be understood substantivally as “some things” or contents among the scriptures, especially in light of the following reference to λόγοι, so no correction is required.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν γραφῶν ἃ μὲν-ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ, ἃ δὲ ψευδῆ
lexical_decisions.chosen: some things in the scriptures are true and others false
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter forms ἃ and ἀληθῆ are read substantivally of contents or statements within the feminine γραφαί. “Some of the scriptures are true and others false” is contextually possible but would not preserve the printed gender distinction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Become approved money changers
lexical_decisions.rationale: τραπεζῖται are money changers or bankers, and δόκιμοι means tested, approved, or reliable. “Discerning money changers” would express the contextual function but less directly render the adjective.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τινῶν μὲν δοκίμων ὄντων λόγων, τινῶν δὲ κιβδήλων
lexical_decisions.chosen: some of the statements in the scriptures are genuine while others are counterfeit
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγοι here are statements or passages. δοκίμων and κιβδήλων continue the coin-testing image with genuine versus counterfeit material.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ψευδῶν γραφῶν πλανωμένοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: to those being led astray by the false scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπό marks the false writings as the source of the error; “because of the false scriptures” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what is true in the scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter substantive denotes the true contents or portions of the writings, not simply acquaintance with the writings as a whole.

passages.text: And Peter replied, “Therefore I have good reason to believe nothing against either God or the righteous people recorded in the law, taking reverent thought as my starting point. For, as I am convinced, Adam was not a transgressor, he who was gestated by the hands of God; nor was Noah a drunkard, he who was found righteous beyond the entire world; nor did Abraham live with three women at once, he who was deemed worthy of many children because of self-control; nor did Jacob have relations with four women, two of whom also happened to be sisters, he who, being the father of twelve tribes, also signaled that the presence of our teacher would come. Moses was not a murderer, and he did not learn to judge from a priest of an idol, he who prophesied God’s law for the entire age and, because of right understanding, was attested as a ‘faithful steward.’”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πιστεύω οὔτε κατὰ τῶν ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ἀναγραφέντων δικαίων
lexical_decisions.chosen: I have good reason to believe nothing against either God or the righteous people recorded in the law
lexical_decisions.rationale: With κατά and the genitive, πιστεύω concerns accepting something adverse to the named persons. “Nothing” supplies the object required by natural English without specifying a particular accusation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: taking reverent thought as my starting point
lexical_decisions.rationale: προλαμβάνων presents reverent judgment as an antecedent presumption or principle. “Presupposing that one should think reverently” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ χειρῶν κυοφορηθείς
lexical_decisions.chosen: he who was gestated by the hands of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: κυοφορέω ordinarily depicts carrying in the womb or gestation. The deliberately striking image is retained rather than reduced to the more general “formed.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ὑπὲρ πάντα τὸν κόσμον δίκαιος εὑρεθείς
lexical_decisions.chosen: he who was found righteous beyond the entire world
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπέρ gives a comparative or surpassing sense. “Above the whole world” is more literal, while “more righteous than everyone in the world” makes the comparison explicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: live with three women at once
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύνειμι with the dative can mean associate or cohabit and may carry a sexual or marital implication here. “Have relations with” is a possible stronger rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: nor did Jacob have relations with four women
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοινωνέω can mean share or associate with and, in this marital context, have relations with. “Women” is supplied from the preceding clause and confirmed by the feminine relative ὧν and ἀδελφαί.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν τοῦ διδασκάλου ἡμῶν παρουσίαν ἐσήμανεν ἐλθεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: signaled that the presence of our teacher would come
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρουσία is retained as “presence,” while ἐλθεῖν separately expresses its coming; translating only “the coming of our teacher” would collapse the source’s wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ Μωϋσῆς φονεὺς ἦν, καὶ παρὰ ἱερέως εἰδώλου κρίνειν ἐμάνθανεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Moses was not a murderer, and he did not learn to judge from a priest of an idol
lexical_decisions.rationale: The single οὐ is taken as governing both coordinated allegations, as required by the surrounding sequence of denials. A formally possible reading that affirms the second predicate would conflict with that structure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παντὶ τῷ αἰῶνι τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ νόμον προφητεύσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: prophesied God’s law for the entire age
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative is read temporally or as indicating the age for which the prophecy was given. “To the entire age” and, if αἰών is spatially extended, “to the whole world” are possible alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: faithful steward
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονόμος denotes one entrusted with managing a household or its affairs; “manager” is a possible modern alternative.

passages.text: Nevertheless, at the proper time I will also give you an explanation of these matters together with similar ones. But for now, as you see, since evening has overtaken us, let the things said today be sufficient. On another occasion, if you wish, feel free to ask us about whatever you want, and we will gladly explain them without hesitation. After saying this, he got up. And so, after partaking of food, we turned to sleep, for night had overtaken us.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως. τροφῆς μεταλαβόντες
source_issues.issue: The printed full stop leaves καὶ οὕτως as an elliptical sentence or separates an adverb naturally attachable to the following participial clause. The translation adopts the latter attachment; alternatively the print may be represented as “And so it was. After partaking of food ...” This is an editorial punctuation ambiguity, not unreadable or missing text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an explanation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can denote an explanation or solution; the context concerns resolving the hearer's questions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: But for now
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase can mean “for the rest,” “for the remaining time,” or “henceforth.” The evening context supports taking it as a transition that closes the present session.

lexical_decisions.chosen: feel free to ask us
lexical_decisions.rationale: This expresses the participle’s call for confidence in idiomatic modern English while retaining the invitation to inquire.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we will gladly explain them without hesitation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle χαίροντες conveys gladness, ἀόκνως readiness or lack of hesitation, and ἐπιλύσομεν the explaining or resolving of the matters raised.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he got up
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect is used in the narrative sequence for the completed action of rising.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we turned to sleep
lexical_decisions.rationale: This retains the source’s image of turning toward sleep rather than replacing it with the less transparent “went to bed.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: for night had overtaken us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the pluperfect force and the image of night catching or overtaking the group; “us” is implicit from the context.

passages.text: So, when two days had passed and the third was beginning to dawn, I, Clement, awoke for the debate with Simon, and together with the companions who were with me, at the second calls of the roosters, we found the lamp still shining and Peter on his knees praying. When he had finished his petition, he turned, saw that we were ready to listen, and said:

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the debate with Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαλέγεσθαι can denote discussion or debate; the planned public dispute supports “debate.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τὰς δευτέρας τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων φωνάς
lexical_decisions.chosen: at the second calls of the roosters
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the reference to the second round of rooster calls rather than replacing it with a conventional time designation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Peter on his knees praying
lexical_decisions.rationale: γονυκλινής describes a kneeling posture.

passages.text: “I want you to know that those who, under our direction, associate with Simon so that, as they learn his plans, they may report them to us, enabling us to adapt ourselves to the variety of his wickedness, have themselves sent word and informed us, saying: ‘Today Simon, just as he arranged, is ready to come before everyone and demonstrate from the Scriptures that this one is not the highest God—he “who created heaven and earth” and all things in them—but that there is some other unknown and highest one, as one existing among secret mysteries, a God of gods. He sent two gods, of whom one is the one who created the world, while the other is the one who gave the law. Simon schemes to say these things so that he may undermine beforehand the right faith of those who are going to worship the one and only God, “who created heaven and earth.”’”

source_issues.source_quote: μὴ τοῦτον εἶναι·θεὸν ἀνώτατον
source_issues.issue: The printed high point interrupts the infinitive construction between εἶναι and its predicate θεὸν ἀνώτατον. The surviving words permit a clear construction if the punctuation is provisionally disregarded.

source_issues.source_quote: τῶν τὸν ἕνα καὶ μόνον μελλόντων. σέβειν θεόν
source_issues.issue: The printed full stop separates μέλλειν from its complementary infinitive σέβειν. The translation provisionally treats this as intrusive editorial punctuation without changing the surviving words.
source_issues.proposed_reading: τῶν τὸν ἕνα καὶ μόνον μελλόντων σέβειν θεόν

lexical_decisions.chosen: under our direction
lexical_decisions.rationale: In context πρόνοια refers to the deliberate arrangement by which the informants remain with Simon; “by our foresight” is also lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὴν τῆς κακίας αὐτοῦ ποικιλίαν ἁρμόσασθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: adapt ourselves to the variety of his wickedness
lexical_decisions.rationale: ποικιλία denotes variety or versatility, while ἁρμόζεσθαι expresses adjustment to it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐν ἀπορρήτοις ὄντα θεὸν θεῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: as one existing among secret mysteries, a God of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόρρητα can denote secrets, mysteries, or esoteric teachings. Here ὡς introduces the characterization attributed to Simon; alternatives include “supposedly existing among secret things as God of gods.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: may undermine beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound verb indicates loosening or weakening in advance.

passages.text: “When I heard these things, how could I not have been disheartened? Therefore I also wanted you, the brothers who are with me, to know that my soul is in no small pain, as I observe that the evil one is vigilant for the testing of human beings, while human beings are utterly neglectful of their own salvation. For he has contrived to introduce notions of many other gods among those from the nations who are about to be persuaded that the earthly carved images are not gods, so that, if they cease from the polytheistic madness below, they will be deceived into speaking in another way—or even worse—against God’s sole sovereignty, so that, never having preferred what belongs to that sole sovereignty, they may never at any time be able to obtain mercy. For this audacious undertaking Simon approaches us for battle, armed with the false passages of the Scriptures. And what is worse, on the basis of prophets in whom he has not believed, he has not feared to teach such doctrines against the God who is truly God.”

source_issues.source_quote: κατὰ τῆς· τοῦ θεοῦ μοναρχίας
source_issues.issue: The printed high point separates the article τῆς from its dependent genitive τοῦ θεοῦ and is syntactically intrusive. The translation provisionally reads the phrase as a continuous construction while preserving all surviving words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: utterly neglectful of their own salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάνυ intensifies the stated neglect and is retained rather than softened.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the earthly carved images
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξόανα are carved cult images; “earthly” preserves the contrast expressed by ἐπίγειος.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the polytheistic madness below
lexical_decisions.rationale: The spatial image of κάτω is retained; alternatives include “earthbound polytheistic madness” and “polytheistic madness down here.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s sole sovereignty
lexical_decisions.rationale: μοναρχία here denotes the rule or sovereignty of the one God. The rendering provisionally disregards the printed high point but does not alter the surviving words.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα μηδέποτε τὰ τῆς μοναρχίας προτιμήσαντες οὐπώποτε ἐλέους τυχεῖν δυνηθῶσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that, never having preferred what belongs to that sole sovereignty, they may never at any time be able to obtain mercy
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both negative expressions, μηδέποτε and οὐπώποτε, are preserved rather than reducing their apparent repetition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the God who is truly God
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὄντως qualifies the designation θεός by marking this one as genuinely God. Alternatives include “the real God” and “the one who really is God”; the phrase is not treated as a separate assertion of existence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the basis of prophets in whom he has not believed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative is attracted into the case of its antecedent προφητῶν. “From prophets whom he has not believed” is also possible.

passages.text: “As for us, who have inherited from our ancestors both the worship of the God who created everything and, further, the mystery of the books capable of deceiving, he will be able to accomplish nothing. But among those from the nations, who have the polytheistic conception as a companion from their upbringing and do not know the false elements in the Scriptures, he will be capable of much—not only he; even if someone else presents to those from the nations, against God, some empty, ornamented myth resembling a sumptuous dream, that person too will be believed, because from childhood their mind has been accustomed to accept the things said against God. Yet there will indeed be some rare ones among them—few out of a multitude—who, through good sense, will not be willing even so much as merely to hear an evil word against the God who created everything. For these alone, though they are from the nations, it will come about that they are saved. Therefore, let none of you blame Simon at all, or anyone else either, for nothing happens unjustly, seeing that even the false elements in the Scriptures turn out reasonably to serve as a test.”

source_issues.source_quote: τὴν πολύθεον ὑπόληψιν· σύντροφον ἔχουσιν
source_issues.issue: The printed high point interrupts the construction in which σύντροφον is the complement of ἔχουσιν with τὴν πολύθεον ὑπόληψιν as its object. The translation provisionally repunctuates without changing the surviving words.

source_issues.source_quote: κακὸν. λόγον αὐτὸ κἂν ἀκοῦσαι μόνον
source_issues.issue: The printed full stop separates κακόν from λόγον and is syntactically intrusive. The neuter αὐτό is also unusual if taken as an adjective modifying masculine λόγον, but it can defensibly be read adverbially or intensively. The translation therefore provisionally repunctuates but adopts no lexical emendation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: κακὸν λόγον αὐτὸ κἂν ἀκοῦσαι μόνον

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ἀπατᾶν δυναμένων βίβλων τὸ μυστήριον
lexical_decisions.chosen: the mystery of the books capable of deceiving
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the books’ stated capacity to deceive and the unexplained “mystery” associated with them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have the polytheistic conception as a companion from their upbringing
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύντροφος can describe something reared together with a person and thus ingrained from upbringing, not merely a temporary companion. The printed high point is provisionally treated as intrusive.

lexical_decisions.chosen: ornamented ... resembling a sumptuous dream
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλούσιος is rendered “sumptuous” to convey a richly furnished dream; “a rich dream” is the more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through good sense
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐγνωμοσύνη here denotes sound or fair-minded judgment; “upright-mindedness” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κακὸν. λόγον αὐτὸ κἂν ἀκοῦσαι μόνον
lexical_decisions.chosen: even so much as merely to hear an evil word
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed stop is provisionally treated as intrusive, and αὐτό is understood adverbially or intensively with “hear merely.” If it were construed as agreeing directly with λόγον, masculine αὐτόν would be expected.

lexical_decisions.chosen: blame ... at all
lexical_decisions.rationale: With the negative imperative, παντελῶς can mean “at all”; “blame altogether” or “blame utterly” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: turn out reasonably to serve as a test
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom presents the false elements as having a rationally explicable testing function.

passages.text: And when I, Clement, heard this, I said, “What do you mean, lord, by saying that even the false elements in the Scriptures reasonably serve to test human beings?” He answered, “The false elements of the Scriptures were permitted to be written, at wickedness’s request, for a certain just reason. Here is what I mean by ‘reasonably’: In matters concerning God, the evil one, though loving God no less than the good one does, falls short of the good one in only one respect: he does not pardon even those who act impiously because of ignorance; out of affection for what is being treated impiously, he desires the destruction of those who act impiously and does not even offer them healing. For the good one wants to heal everyone through changes of heart, but saves only those who have come to know God. Yet he does not heal those who do not know—not because he does not want to, but because it is not permissible to grant the good things prepared for the sons of the kingdom to those who, because of their lack of discernment, have been likened to irrational animals.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: The false elements of the Scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjective refers to what is false within the Scriptures; “the falsehoods of the Scriptures” is possible but can imply that the Scriptures as a whole are characterized as false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at wickedness’s request
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive presents wickedness as the source or possessor of the request; the personification is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for a certain just reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος here can denote reason, rationale, or account; the dative states the just rationale under which the writing was permitted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: In matters concerning God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural can denote discourses, teachings, or matters concerning God. “In theological discussions” is a more narrowly discursive alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν ταῖς θεολογίαις ὁ πονηρὸς τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ τὸν θεὸν οὐκ ἔλαττον ἀγαπῶν ἑνὶ μόνῳ ἀπολείπεται τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: In matters concerning God, the evil one, though loving God no less than the good one does, falls short of the good one in only one respect
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjectives are retained as the labels “the evil one” and “the good one” without identifying their bearers. The possible continuity of ὁ πονηρός with “the evil one” in 3.3, together with the subsequent healing and saving actions, supports reading them as personal agents. The generic alternative “a wicked person ... a good person” remains grammatically possible, while specific identifications are not supplied by this wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: out of affection for what is being treated impiously
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized neuter participle denotes the object against which impiety is directed without explicitly identifying it as a person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς ἰᾶσθαι πάντας θέλει ταῖς μεταμελείαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the good one wants to heal everyone through changes of heart
lexical_decisions.rationale: The deponent infinitive ἰᾶσθαι has active force here and presents the good one as the agent who wants to heal everyone. The plural μεταμέλειαι can denote regrets, reconsiderations, or changes of heart.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through changes of heart
lexical_decisions.rationale: μεταμέλεια can denote regret, reconsideration, or a change of mind or heart. “Changes of heart” fits the healing context while keeping this term distinct from μετανοέω and μετάνοια.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of their lack of discernment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjective denotes an undiscerning condition or inability to distinguish rightly.

passages.text: The nature of the one and only God, who made the world, created us, and provided everything, is naturally such that, whenever anyone at all is within the bounds of reverence for God and does not blaspheme his holy spirit, it carries that person’s soul toward him by affection for him, in the form of an innate longing for him. Even if that person is a sinner, after being punished as his deeds deserve, it is in his nature to be saved. If someone denies him or in some other way speaks impiously against him, then reorients himself, he will indeed be punished for the ways in which he sinned against him, but he will be saved, because after turning back he loved him. Perhaps, however, if there is an extraordinary degree of reverence and supplication, he will even be released from punishment, having presented his ignorance together with his reorientation as grounds for forgiveness of the sin. Those, however, who have not reoriented themselves will also meet their end through the punishment of fire, even if they are most devout in every other respect. But, as I said, after being punished with age-long fire for one fifth of a measured age, they will be extinguished. For those who have acted impiously against the eternal and only God can no longer exist forever.

source_issues.source_quote: παντὸς οὐδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος
source_issues.issue: The selected print has smooth-breathed οὐδήποτε, which ordinarily means “never” and does not fit the genitive construction with παντός and ὄντος. The translation provisionally understands it as the genitive indefinite οὑδήποτε, “of anyone whatsoever.” This is a proposed interpretation of a confirmed printed orthographic oddity, not a claim that the print was unverified.
source_issues.proposed_reading: παντὸς οὑδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος

source_issues.source_quote: ἐμφύτου εἰς αὐτὸν ἔρωτος · ἰδέᾳ.
source_issues.issue: The confirmed printed raised dot interrupts the natural construction in which ἰδέᾳ governs the preceding genitive phrase. Treating it as sentence-final would leave ἰδέᾳ isolated before the full stop. The translation therefore provisionally treats the raised dot as anomalous internal editorial punctuation and attaches ἰδέᾳ to the preceding words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is naturally such
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the repeated nature language of πέφυκεν and φύσις while allowing the following infinitive to express what this nature characteristically does.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his holy spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the possessive expression and descriptive wording without using English capitalization to settle personhood beyond what the Greek itself marks.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ὧν ἔπραξεν κολασθῆναι σώζεσθαι φύσιν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished as his deeds deserve, it is in his nature to be saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ ἀξίαν expresses punishment corresponding to the worth or deserts of the deeds, while φύσιν ἔχει continues the passage’s emphasis on nature.

lexical_decisions.chosen: reorients himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes moral-spiritual redirection here. No destination is added because God has already been named, and the distinct ἐπιστρέψας is separately rendered “after turning back.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συγγνώμης τῆς ἁμαρτίας μετὰ τῆς μετανοίας δεδωκὼς τὴν ἄγνοιαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: having presented his ignorance together with his reorientation as grounds for forgiveness of the sin
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compact construction presents ignorance and reorientation in relation to pardon. It may alternatively be understood as offering ignorance as an excuse for the sin, but the chosen wording preserves both elements without making ignorance itself absolve him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μεμετρημένου αἰῶνος τὸ πέμπτον πυρὶ αἰωνίῳ κολασθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished with age-long fire for one fifth of a measured age
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Age-long” preserves the relation between αἰωνίῳ and αἰῶνος and fits the explicitly measured duration. “Eternal fire” is a possible lexical alternative, in which case the fire rather than each person’s punishment would be described as eternal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they will be extinguished
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the image of something being put out rather than replacing it with an interpretive abstraction such as “annihilated.”

passages.text: Affection for God on the part of human beings is therefore sufficient for salvation. The evil one, however, knowing this, while we are eager to sow in the souls of those from the nations who are about to believe the immortality-giving affection that human beings direct toward the one and only God, himself strives, while possessing against the ignorant a weapon sufficient for destruction, to sow the notion of many gods, or even of one as superior, so that, having conceived and become jointly convinced of things that are unlawful, after dying as though under a charge of adultery they may be cast out of his kingdom.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is therefore sufficient for salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτάρκης denotes being sufficient or adequate in oneself; the rendering preserves the passage’s explicit claim about affection and salvation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰδὼς δὲ ὁ πονηρός, ἡμῶν σπευδόντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: The evil one, however, knowing this, while we are eager
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive absolute ἡμῶν σπευδόντων is rendered circumstantially, while the unexpressed object of εἰδώς is supplied as “this,” referring to the preceding claim that affection for God is sufficient for salvation. Alternatively, the effort expressed by the genitive absolute may be understood as the inferred content of his knowledge: “knowing that we are eager.” The chosen rendering more directly preserves the circumstantial construction, but both interpretations are contextually viable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those from the nations who are about to believe
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the source’s “from the nations” wording rather than automatically importing the conventional label “Gentiles.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀθανατοποιὸν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀνθρώπων στοργήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the immortality-giving affection that human beings direct toward him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀθανατοποιός describes the affection as producing immortality, not merely as immortal in quality; πρὸς αὐτόν marks its direction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλῶν θεῶν ἢ καὶ ἑνὸς ὡς κρείττονος
lexical_decisions.chosen: many gods, or even one as superior
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ellipsis after ἑνός is retained: one god is implied, but the Greek does not restate whom that one is superior to.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having conceived
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean “grasped” or “accepted,” but “conceived” continues the preceding image of seed being sown and anticipates the adultery image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: become jointly convinced of things that are unlawful
lexical_decisions.rationale: The συν- element indicates shared persuasion, though the Greek does not specify whether the sharing is with the evil one or with others who accept the notion. “Come to share belief in” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his kingdom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronoun is preserved. The argument points to God’s kingdom, although the evil one is the nearest explicitly named masculine referent.

passages.text: Everyone, therefore, is worthy of exclusion who has so much as wished to hear anything of that kind against God’s sole rule. But if anyone, emboldened by the Scriptures, dares even to hear something directed against God, let him first reflect with me on this: if someone constructs for himself a plausible doctrine in whatever way he wishes and then studies them closely, he will be able to cite from them many testimonies in support of the doctrine he fashioned. How, then, can anyone confidently rely on these writings against God, when everyone’s chosen view can be found in them?

lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s sole rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: μοναρχία denotes rule by one. “Sole rule” preserves its theological force more transparently than the modern political term “monarchy.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸ μόνον κἂν ἀκοῦσαί τι τοιοῦτον θελήσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: who has so much as wished to hear anything of that kind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording stresses that the mere willingness even to listen is enough for the stated condemnation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: emboldened by the Scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: γραφαί may be rendered generically as “writings,” but the continuing references to scriptural testimonies and passages support “the Scriptures” here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὔλογον ἑαυτῷ δόγμα ὡς βούλεται ἀναπλάσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: constructs for himself a plausible doctrine in whatever way he wishes
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὔλογον can mean reasonable or plausible. “Plausible” suits the argument that a person first fabricates a position and then seeks supporting texts.

lexical_decisions.chosen: studies them closely
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐγκύπτω literally suggests bending over or peering into something and idiomatically denotes close examination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν αἷς ἡ πάντων βουλὴ εἰσευρίσκεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: when everyone’s chosen view can be found in them
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουλή can mean counsel, purpose, will, or opinion. The context concerns finding textual support for whatever doctrine one wants, so “chosen view” is adopted; “everyone’s counsel” would be more formally literal but less clear in context.

passages.text: Therefore, before everything else, one ought to know that one finds it nowhere except from a prophet of truth. A true prophet is one who always knows everything, including the thoughts of everyone, and is sinless, as one fully assured concerning God’s judgment. Therefore, we ought not to consider his foreknowledge superficially, but to ask whether his foreknowledge can subsist without any other basis. For physicians foretell things while having the sick person’s pulse as material laid before them; some do so by means of birds, others by means of sacrificial victims, and still others foretell while having many other different materials laid before them—and they are not prophets.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun’s antecedent lies outside the supplied passage; “it” preserves the unresolved reference, probably to truth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a prophet of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the source’s genitive expression rather than replacing it with the interpretive “true prophet,” which appears explicitly in the next sentence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as one fully assured concerning God’s judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πεπληροφορημένος denotes being fully convinced or assured; “fully informed concerning God’s judgment” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: without any other basis
lexical_decisions.rationale: In context πρόφασις denotes an external ground, occasion, or means on which prediction depends; “pretext” is the more usual alternative in other contexts.

lexical_decisions.chosen: material laid before them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase presents the pulse and divinatory objects as supplied material underlying the predictions.

passages.text: Therefore, he confidently gave an account of what was going to happen—I mean sufferings, places, and limits. For, being an unerring prophet, surveying everything with the boundless eye of the soul, he knows it all while himself escaping notice. But if we too admit, as most people do, that even the true prophet has foreknowledge not always but only at times—when he has the spirit and, for that reason, foreknows, but when he does not have it, is ignorant—if we suppose this, we will both deceive ourselves and lay snares for others. For such a thing belongs to those madly inspired by a spirit of disorder, those becoming drunk beside altars and being filled with the reek of burnt fat.

lexical_decisions.chosen: sufferings, places, and limits
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὅροι can denote boundaries, limits, or termini; “limits” preserves the term without conflating it with the explicitly named times in 3.15.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the boundless eye of the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the singular eye image and ἄπειρος in its sense of boundless or unlimited.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he knows it all while himself escaping notice
lexical_decisions.rationale: λανθάνων most naturally describes the prophet as remaining unnoticed while knowing; “he knows secretly” is a possible but less formally precise alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: lay snares for others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνεδρεύω denotes lying in wait for or entrapping someone, not merely leading someone into an intellectual error.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being filled with the reek of burnt fat
lexical_decisions.rationale: κνίσα is the smoke, steam, or odor of sacrificial fat; “being filled with sacrificial fumes” is a less vivid alternative.

passages.text: For if someone wishing to profess prophecy is allowed to be believed, in the matters in which he is caught as a liar, that at that time he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge, he will not be easy to expose, though he is a prophet who is a liar. For in the cases where, while saying many things, he hits upon a few, he is then believed to have the spirit. Moreover, he speaks of first things as last and last things as first, things that have happened as things that will happen, and things that will happen as though they had already happened. He also says other, incoherent things, things stolen from others and transformed, and some things curtailed, shapeless, senseless, ambiguous, crooked, and unclear, all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τῆς προγνώσεως ἅγιον οὐκ εἶχεν πνεῦμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s attributive relation between the holy spirit and foreknowledge without imposing a later doctrinal identification.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while saying many things, he hits upon a few
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιτυγχάνει describes occasionally hitting the mark or obtaining a correct result among numerous claims.

lexical_decisions.chosen: things stolen from others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφαιρέω can mean taking something away secretly; “appropriated from others” is a less pointed alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: curtailed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive describes things reduced, diminished, or mutilated; “curtailed” fits the treatment of allegedly defective predictions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shapeless
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed spelling supports ἀνειδής, “without form, shapeless, unsightly,” rather than ἀναιδής, “shameless.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience
lexical_decisions.rationale: κεκραγότα vividly portrays the statements as openly betraying or proclaiming something; δυσσυνειδησία can denote a bad or guilty conscience and, by extension, unscrupulousness.

passages.text: But our teacher resorted to no such trickery. Rather, as I said earlier, being a prophet who always knew everything by an innate and ever-flowing spirit, he confidently set things out, clearly foretelling sufferings, places, fixed times, ways, and limits. For example, when foretelling about the sanctuary, he said, “Do you see these buildings? Amen, I tell you, not one stone upon another will be left here that will not be torn down,” and, “This generation will certainly not pass away, and the demolition will have its beginning. For they will come and encamp here and throw up an encircling stockade and slaughter your children here.” Likewise, he spoke what follows in a clear voice, things that we are able to see with our own eyes, so that, in the matters about which the word was spoken, the deed might also occur. For the prophet of truth frames the statement of proof to produce faith in those who hear.

lexical_decisions.chosen: resorted to no such trickery
lexical_decisions.rationale: γοητεύω can denote practicing sorcery, bewitching, or deceiving as a charlatan; “trickery” preserves the polemical accusation without requiring a claim of literal magic.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by an innate and ever-flowing spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same expression as in 3.12, apart from the printed spelling ἐμφύτῳ, is rendered consistently; “by an innate and unceasing spirit” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fixed times
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective describes times set or bounded in advance; “appointed times” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: about the sanctuary
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁγίασμα denotes a holy place or sanctuary; “temple” would make the contextual identification more explicit than the source does.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Amen, I tell you
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the distinctive introductory formula rather than replacing it with the familiar interpretive rendering “Truly, I tell you.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: encamp here
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future form conveys sitting or settling down; in the military context, “encamp” is natural, while “sit down here” is the more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: throw up an encircling stockade
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes enclosing with a palisade or stockade. The Greek supplies no explicit object, so the English likewise avoids specifying whom or what is enclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Likewise
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb can mean “equally” or “all the same.” “Nevertheless” is possible, but continuation by similarity best fits the immediate context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα ἐφ᾽ ὧν ὁ λόγος ἐρρέθη, καὶ τὸ ἔργον γένηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that, in the matters about which the word was spoken, the deed might also occur
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ἐφ᾽ ὧν as neuter and topical, referring to the matters about which the statement was made. If ὧν is understood personally and interpreted temporally from the generational context, an alternative is “so that the deed too might occur in the days of those in whose days the word was spoken.” The topical reading avoids supplying an unexpressed noun meaning “days,” while the personal-temporal alternative remains contextually possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς γὰρ πίστιν ἀκουόντων τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀποδείξεως ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας ποιεῖται προφήτης
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the prophet of truth frames the statement of proof to produce faith in those who hear
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγον ποιεῖσθαι can mean formulating or delivering an account, while πρὸς πίστιν states its intended effect. “Gives an account of the demonstration for the faith of the hearers” is a more formal alternative.

passages.text: Nevertheless, there are many heralds of error, all having one leader of wickedness. For that reason there is one herald of the truth, himself also the leader of piety, who in their proper times will have as prophets all who are found pure. The chief reason people have gone astray has been this: they did not first understand the principle of pairing, which I will not cease setting out for you separately, on each occasion, in outline; for speaking point by point is a lengthy task. Therefore, be truth-loving judges for me of what is said.

source_issues.source_quote: ἰδία
source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints ἰδία, a morphologically unexpected form in this adverbial position. The translation provisionally understands it as “separately” or “privately”; the printed form is preserved and is not treated as an OCR error.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For that reason there is one herald of the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular noun is implicit from the preceding κήρυκες; “for that reason” renders the causal ᾧ λόγῳ.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in their proper times
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is taken with the prophets as referring to their respective times; attachment to the singular herald remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the principle of pairing
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος denotes an account or principle, while συζυγία is the work’s technical language for a paired relation; “doctrine of the pairs” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on each occasion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb indicates recurrence on every relevant occasion, rather than merely occurring from time to time.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in outline
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb indicates a summary treatment by principal points rather than a full exposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολὺ γὰρ τὸ κατ᾽ εἶδος λέγειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: for speaking point by point is a lengthy task
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ᾽ εἶδος means treating the matter specifically or item by item, while πολύ indicates its considerable extent.

passages.text: I will now begin speaking. If someone refuses to grant that the great and holy spirit of the foreknowledge of God, who made all things, was infused into the man brought to term by his hands, how does the person who assigns it to another—one born from a foul drop—not sin most gravely? I do not think that person obtains forgiveness, even if he is deceived by spurious scripture into thinking dreadful things against the father of all. For anyone who insults an image—and an eternal king’s image at that—commits that sin against the one in whose likeness the image happened to be. “But,” he says, “the divine spirit left him after he sinned.” Then it sinned along with him. And how is the one who says this not in danger? “No, he had received the spirit after he sinned.” Then it has been given to unrighteous people. And where is justice? “But it is supplied to righteous and unrighteous alike.” This is the most unjust thing of all. Thus every falsehood, even if supported by ten thousand contrivances, is bound to meet its refutation even within a short time.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ὑπὸ χειρῶν αὐτοῦ κυοφορηθέντι ἀνθρώπῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: into the man brought to term by his hands
lexical_decisions.rationale: κυοφορέω carries a gestational image, here paradoxically associated with God’s hands; “formed by his hands” would suppress that image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: refuses to grant that ... was infused
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction leaves the agency of the active infinitive ἐγχέναι implicit. The passive English keeps the spirit as what is infused without supplying an explicit agent; “grant that God infused” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by spurious scripture
lexical_decisions.rationale: νόθος marks the writing as illegitimate or inauthentic, and γραφή in this context can denote a purported scriptural writing; “spurious writing” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and an eternal king’s image at that
lexical_decisions.rationale: καὶ ταῦτα is an emphatic idiom highlighting the especially serious identity of the person represented by the image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἁμαρτίαν εἰς ἐκεῖνον ἀναφερομένην ἔχει, οὗπερ καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν ἡ εἰκὼν ἐτύγχανεν οὖσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: commits that sin against the one in whose likeness the image happened to be
lexical_decisions.rationale: The sin is directed against the person represented by the insulted image; the wording does not transfer the offender’s culpability to that person. More literally, one “has the sin referred against that one.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Then it sinned along with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound verb presents the spirit as sharing in the man’s sin, which is the reductio advanced by the author.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even if supported by ten thousand contrivances
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves μυρίαις as “ten thousand,” though it can idiomatically mean “countless,” and takes ἐπίνοιαι as devised arguments or contrivances.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἔλεγχον κἂν ἐν μικρῷ χρόνῳ λαβεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: is bound to meet its refutation even within a short time
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχει with the infinitive expresses an assured outcome, and ἔλεγχος here is exposure or refutation.

passages.text: Do not be deceived. Our father was ignorant of nothing, since even the law laid down publicly, while concealing him beneath a veil of allegory because of the unworthy, refers those who yearn for truth back to him, saying, “Examine your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will report to you.” It was this father one had to seek, these elders one had to seek out. But you did not seek to learn to whom the time of the kingdom belongs, or to whom the chair of prophecy belongs, even though he disclosed himself by saying, “The scribes and the Pharisees sat on Moses’ chair. Everything they tell you, listen to them.” He said “them” because they had been entrusted with the key of the kingdom, which is knowledge. It alone can open the gate of life, and through it alone it is possible to enter eternal life. “But yes,” he says, “they possess the key, yet they do not provide it to those who wish to enter.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: our father
lexical_decisions.rationale: The designation is retained without inserting a name or capitalizing it, since the immediate wording does not make the referent explicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: beneath a veil of allegory
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐγκάλυμμα is a covering or veil, and the law is depicted as concealing the father through allegorical presentation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: refers ... back to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναπέμπω can mean sending or referring someone back to another person or authority.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνος ἐστὶν ὁ τῆς βασιλείας χρόνος, τίνος ἡ τῆς προφητείας καθέδρα
lexical_decisions.chosen: to whom the time of the kingdom belongs, or to whom the chair of prophecy belongs
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated genitive τίνος asks whose these prerogatives are; the English supplies “belongs” without identifying the person.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they had been entrusted with the key of the kingdom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive perfect of πιστεύω here means being entrusted with something, not merely believing it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥτις ἐστὶν γνῶσις, ἡ μόνη τὴν πύλην τῆς ζωῆς ἀνοῖξαι δύναται, δι’ ἧς μόνης
lexical_decisions.chosen: which is knowledge. It alone can open the gate of life, and through it alone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated feminine forms are taken as referring to knowledge. Because πύλη is also feminine and nearer to δι’ ἧς, “through which gate alone” remains grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: But yes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The emphatic response concedes possession of the key before contrasting the refusal to provide it.

passages.text: For this reason, I say, he himself rose from the chair. Like a father acting on behalf of children, he proclaimed what had from eternity been handed down secretly to the worthy; he extended mercy even to the nations and had compassion on the souls of all, while disregarding his own blood. For he, having been deemed worthy to be king of the coming age, against the one who had now received the kingdom under a time-limited law.... And the greatest thing, which distressed him intensely, is this: those on whose behalf he waged the battle as for children were themselves fighting against him because of ignorance. And yet he loved even those who hated him, wept for those who disobeyed, blessed those who reviled him, and prayed for those who treated him as an enemy. He did not do only these things as a father, but also taught his own disciples to do similar things with the attitude they would have toward brothers. This is a father; this is a prophet; this is what is fitting: for him to reign over his own children, so that through the affection that goes from a father to children and the children’s heartfelt honor toward their father, eternal peace might be able to arise. For when the fitting ruler reigns, genuine joy concerning the ruler comes upon those who are ruled.

source_issues.source_quote: τὴν βασιλείαν.... καὶ
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly four dots after βασιλείαν, leaving the preceding construction without its unavailable continuation. The English retains all four dots, and no restoration has been supplied.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐνπροθέσμῳ
source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints ἐνπροθέσμῳ, apparently an unassimilated or irregular spelling of the compound ordinarily written with μ before π. Its meaning remains recoverable, but this interpretation is provisional and the form is not treated as an OCR error.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he himself rose from the chair
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording continues the chair imagery of the preceding section; ἐγερθείς is rendered as rising from it rather than merely being raised up.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἀπὸ αἰῶνος ἐν κρυπτῷ ἀξίοις παραδιδόμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: what had from eternity been handed down secretly to the worthy
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπὸ αἰῶνος may also mean “from of old” or “from the beginning of the age”; the rendering retains its broad temporal force without supplying a starting event.

lexical_decisions.chosen: disregarding his own blood
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal image is retained. It may refer to accepting the shedding of his blood or, more generally, neglecting his own life and safety.

lexical_decisions.chosen: under a time-limited law
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound denotes something governed by a fixed term or deadline; “under a law with a fixed term” is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were themselves fighting against him because of ignorance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb depicts him as the object of their hostility, while ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ gives ignorance as its cause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς αὐτοῦ μαθηταῖς ὡς πρὸς ἀδελφοὺς ἔχοντας τὰ ὅμοια ποιεῖν ἐδίδασκεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: taught his own disciples to do similar things with the attitude they would have toward brothers
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering understands ἔχειν πρός relationally, with ὡς preserving the comparison to conduct toward brothers. Alternatively, ἔχοντας with the infinitive may express obligation: “taught his disciples that they had to do similar things as toward brothers.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτο εὔλογον ... τοῦ γὰρ εὐλόγου βασιλεύοντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: this is what is fitting ... when the fitting ruler reigns
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated εὔλογος language can mean reasonable, fitting, or rightful. “Fitting” connects the claim that he should reign with the character of his rule; “when a reasonable ruler reigns” is also possible.

passages.text: Nevertheless, I return to the first argument concerning the truth. If someone does not grant that the man brought to term by God’s hands has the Messiah’s holy spirit, how is he not committing the greatest impiety by granting that some other person, born from a foul drop, has it? Rather, he acts with the greatest piety if he does not grant that another has it, but says that that one alone has it—the one who, from the beginning of the age, changing forms together with names, courses through the age until, having reached his own times and having been anointed by God’s mercy because of his labors, he will have rest forever. That one has been honored with ruling and exercising dominion over everything in air, on earth, and in waters. In addition, he received the breath of the very one who made man—an unbreakable covering for the soul—so that he might be able to be immortal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Messiah’s holy spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: χριστός functions independently as a title, so it is rendered “Messiah.” The genitive relates the spirit to the Messiah without deciding whether possession, identity, or source is foremost; “the holy spirit of Christ” is an alternative form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ὑπὸ χειρῶν θεοῦ κυοφορηθέντι ἀνθρώπῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the man brought to term by God’s hands
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the unusual gestational force of κυοφορηθέντι together with the explicit image of God’s hands.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς αἰῶνος ... τὸν αἰῶνα τρέχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the beginning of the age ... courses through the age
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated rendering preserves the source’s repetition of αἰών and its portrayal of movement throughout the age.

lexical_decisions.chosen: changing forms together with names
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both changing forms and corresponding names are retained without identifying particular manifestations not named here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τοὺς καμάτους θεοῦ ἐλέει χρισθείς
lexical_decisions.chosen: having been anointed by God’s mercy because of his labors
lexical_decisions.rationale: χρισθείς is rendered “anointed” to preserve its relation to the title Messiah, while διά with the accusative gives the labors as the reason; “on account of his toils” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: has been honored with ruling and exercising dominion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two infinitives preserve the distinction between governing and holding dominion as the honor granted to him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πνοὴν ἔσχεν, ψυχῆς ἄρρηκτον περιβολήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he received the breath ... an unbreakable covering for the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: The second phrase is taken in apposition to the breath. The genitive ψυχῆς may alternatively be rendered “an unbreakable covering of the soul,” but the context supports a covering bestowed upon and protecting the soul.

passages.text: Let there be, then, two generic prophecies for us: the masculine one (and let it be specified that the first, being male, has thereafter been placed second according to the principle of progression, whereas the second, being female, was appointed to come first in the procession of the pairs)—the one, then, who is “among those born of women,” making promises as the female belonging to the present world, wants to be believed to be masculine. Therefore, stealing the male’s seeds and covering them with her own seeds of the flesh, she brings forth the offspring together as though they were all her own—that is, the words. And she promises to give present earthly wealth as a dowry, wishing to exchange the slow for the quick, the brief for the greater.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ μὲν ἀρσενικὴ ... ἡ μὲν οὖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the masculine one ... the one, then
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the Greek construction’s interruption and resumption around the parenthesis rather than supplying a new contrast absent from the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: according to the principle of progression
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος denotes the governing principle or rationale, while πρόοδος describes progression or procession.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the procession of the pairs
lexical_decisions.rationale: συζυγίαι are paired counterparts; “sequence of the pairs” is also possible for προέλευσις.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς ἰδίοις τῆς σαρκὸς σπέρμασιν ἐπισκέπτουσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: covering them with her own seeds of the flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπισκέπτω here has the sense of covering over; the pronoun “them” represents the previously mentioned male seeds.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ταχεῖ τὸ βραδύ, τὸ βραχὺ τῷ μείζονι ὑπαλλάξαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to exchange the slow for the quick, the brief for the greater
lexical_decisions.rationale: Treats the accusatives as what is exchanged for the dative counterparts. The direction of exchange can be construed in reverse with ὑπαλλάσσω, but this rendering follows the most direct case pattern.

passages.text: This first and abundant, foul and rough substance, then, they say was swallowed by Cronus—that is, Time—in a natural sense, because of its downward descent. After the first sediment, they named the water that had flowed together and floated upon the first deposit Poseidon. The remaining third portion, the purest and uppermost, since it was transparent fire, they named Zeus because of the boiling nature within it. For since fire rises upward, it was not swallowed in the regions below by Time, Cronus; rather, as I said, the fiery substance, being life-giving and upward-moving, flew up into the air itself, which is also the most intelligent because of its purity. By his own heat, therefore, Zeus—that is, the boiling substance—draws up the most rarefied and divine breath left within the underlying moisture, which they called Metis.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by Cronus—that is, Time
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the author’s identification and wordplay between Κρόνος and χρόνος rather than treating τοῦ χρόνου as an unrelated genitive.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a natural sense
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb signals the physical or natural-philosophical interpretation of the myth; “by natural processes” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of its downward descent
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπονόστησις denotes movement or return downward; “downward retreat” would preserve its etymological coloring but is less natural here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the first sediment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποστάθμη denotes matter settled at the bottom; the related ὑποστάσει later in the sentence is rendered “deposit.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ζῆνα ὠνόμασαν διὰ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ ζέουσαν φύσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they named Zeus because of the boiling nature within it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conventional name “Zeus” is used while the explicit sound association between Ζῆνα and ζέουσαν is retained through “boiling.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἰσχνότατον καὶ θεῖον ἀνιμᾶται πνεῦμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: draws up the most rarefied and divine breath
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this physical account, ἀνιμᾶται describes drawing up or vaporizing, and ἰσχνότατον means exceedingly fine or tenuous rather than literally lean.

passages.text: When that breath reaches the crown of the ether itself and is drunk up by it, like liquid mixed with heat, it produces an ever-moving pulsation and gives birth to understanding, which they also call Pallas because it pulses: a most skillful intelligence, by whose use the etherial craftsman fashioned the entire cosmos. From Zeus himself, who permeates everything—the hottest ether—the air reaches as far as the regions here; this they call Hera. And since it has descended beneath the purest substance of the ether and is feminine in purity by comparison with what is superior, it was reasonably regarded as Zeus’s sister, since it had been generated from the same substance, but as his wife because it lies beneath him as a woman does.

source_issues.source_quote: ὁ ἀὴρ μέχρι τῶν ἐνταῦθα διικνεῖται τόπων, ἣν ἐπονομάζουσιν Ἥραν
source_issues.issue: The masculine antecedent ὁ ἀήρ is followed by the feminine relative ἣν. This can defensibly be understood as an anticipatory shift to the personified feminine name Hera rather than as omitted content, so the translation uses the gender-neutral demonstrative “this” without emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ κορυφῆς δὲ αὐτοῦ ἐλθὸν τοῦ αἰθέρος
lexical_decisions.chosen: When that breath reaches the crown of the ether itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The implicit subject is the divine πνεῦμα from 6.7. κορυφή can denote the top, crown, or head, preserving both cosmological height and the mythic head imagery.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and is drunk up by it
lexical_decisions.rationale: συμπωθέν carries an ingestion or drinking image, here depicting the breath’s uptake by the ether; rendering it as physical compression would lose that image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it produces an ever-moving pulsation
lexical_decisions.rationale: παλμός denotes a throbbing, quivering, or pulsation; this wording also supports the following association with Pallas.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἣν καὶ Παλλάδα ἐπονομάζουσιν διὰ τὸ πάλλεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: which they also call Pallas because it pulses
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves the author’s wordplay between Παλλάδα and πάλλεσθαι without asserting that it is a historical etymology.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the etherial craftsman
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective identifies the craftsman with or as belonging to the ether; “craftsman of the ether” is possible but may imply that ether is merely his material.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Zeus himself, who permeates everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: διήκω means to extend or pass through; “permeates everything” reflects the description of Zeus as universally diffused.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς θήλεια τὴν καθαρότητα, πρὸς σύγκρισιν τοῦ κρείττονος
lexical_decisions.chosen: is feminine in purity by comparison with what is superior
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative τὴν καθαρότητα marks respect: the air is characterized as female with respect to purity relative to the superior ether. “Less pure, and therefore female” would make the implication more explicit than the Greek does.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γαμετὴ δὲ διὰ τὸ ὡς γυναῖκα ὑποκεῖσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: but as his wife because it lies beneath him as a woman does
lexical_decisions.rationale: γαμετή means a wedded woman or wife, and ὑποκεῖσθαι retains both the physical placement of air beneath ether and the author’s gendered analogy.

passages.text: Hera is taken to represent a temperate balance of airs, and for that reason she is also exceedingly fertile. Athena, whom they also call Pallas, was regarded as a virgin because, on account of the extreme heat, she could not produce the generation of anything. Artemis is interpreted similarly: they take her to represent the lowest recess of the air and, because she is barren through the extremity of the cold, they likewise called her a virgin. As something that clouds the mind, they name the turbid and intoxicating compound of vapors from above and below Dionysus. The water beneath the earth, though one in nature, passes through all the channels in the land and is divided into many parts—as though cut into pieces—so they called it Osiris. They also take Adonis to represent ripe fruits, Aphrodite sexual union and generation, Demeter the earth, Kore seeds, and some take Dionysus to represent the vine.

source_issues.source_quote: Ἀφροδίτην εἰς μίξιν καὶ γένεσιν
source_issues.issue: The noun μίξις permits both physical “mixture” and “sexual union.” The pairing with Aphrodite and generation supports the sexual rendering adopted in the text, while the surrounding natural-philosophical interpretation leaves physical mixture as a viable alternative. This is ordinary lexical ambiguity and does not require emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παραλαμβάνεται δὲ ἡ μὲν Ἥρα πρὸς ἀέρων εὐκρασίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Hera is taken to represent a temperate balance of airs
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραλαμβάνεται introduces an allegorical identification, while εὐκρασία is a well-balanced or temperate mixture rather than merely pleasant weather.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ ἄκρως θερμὸν γένεσίν τινος ποιῆσαι μὴ δυναμένη
lexical_decisions.chosen: because, on account of the extreme heat, she could not produce the generation of anything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the extreme heat and the explicit inability to cause γένεσις; “bring anything into being” is a smoother alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν κατώτατον μυχὸν τοῦ ἀέρος
lexical_decisions.chosen: to represent the lowest recess of the air
lexical_decisions.rationale: μυχός is an innermost or remote recess; “lowest depth” is possible, but “recess” preserves the spatial image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: As something that clouds the mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: φρένες can denote the mind, understanding, or faculties, and θολωτικός means making turbid or confused.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω ἀτμῶν θολερὰν καὶ μεθύουσαν σύστασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the turbid and intoxicating compound of vapors from above and below
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύστασις here is a combination or compound; μεθύουσαν may describe it as intoxicating or as itself drunken.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ πάντων τῶν χερσαίων πόρων διείρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: passes through all the channels in the land
lexical_decisions.rationale: διείρον depicts passage or threading through, and χερσαίων specifies channels belonging to the land.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λαμβάνουσι δὲ καὶ Ἄδωνιν εἰς ὡραίους καρπούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: They also take Adonis to represent ripe fruits
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡραῖος means produced in its proper season and hence ripe; “seasonal fruits” is an equally possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Aphrodite sexual union and generation
lexical_decisions.rationale: μίξις can denote mixture generally or sexual union. Its association here with Aphrodite and generation favors “sexual union,” while “mixture” remains possible within the passage’s physical allegory. The same sexual sense is explicit in the plural μίξεις with males in 6.10.

passages.text: Understand all such things for me as likewise possessing some such allegory. Regard Apollo as the sun that makes its circuit, an offspring of Zeus, which they also called Mithras, completing the circuit of a year. Let these transformations be understood by you as the many changes of Zeus, who permeates everywhere, and conceive of his countless women as years or generations. For the power that passes through the air from the ether itself, consorting with every year and generation, changes it in different ways and thus produces or destroys the things of the season. The ripe fruits are called children, while the unions with males are the periods of barrenness that occur at certain seasons.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Understand ... for me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ethical dative μοι adds a personal appeal such as “take it from me”; retaining “for me” preserves it without making the phrase overly colloquial.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀπόλλωνα δὲ ἥλιον τὸν περιπολοῦντα εἶναι νόμιζε
lexical_decisions.chosen: Regard Apollo as the sun that makes its circuit
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιπολεῖν denotes going around or patrolling a circuit, fitting the sun’s recurring course.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an offspring of Zeus
lexical_decisions.rationale: γονή can mean birth, offspring, or generative seed; the personal genealogy favors “offspring,” though “product of Zeus” is possible in the physical allegory.

lexical_decisions.chosen: which they also called Mithras
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine relative most naturally refers to the sun identified with Apollo, though its proximity to Zeus permits momentary grammatical ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be understood by you as the many changes
lexical_decisions.rationale: τροπαί can be turnings, changes, or seasonal revolutions; “changes” distinguishes it from the preceding μεταμορφώσεις while retaining the sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς δὲ μυρίας αὐτοῦ γυναῖκας ἐνιαυτοὺς ἢ γενεὰς ἐπινόει
lexical_decisions.chosen: conceive of his countless women as years or generations
lexical_decisions.rationale: μυρίας means countless or innumerable, and γενεάς may denote generations, ages, or successive periods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑκάστῳ ἐνιαυτῷ καὶ γενεᾷ συνουσιάζουσα διαφόρως αὐτὸν τρέπει
lexical_decisions.chosen: consorting with every year and generation, changes it in different ways
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνουσιάζουσα preserves the sexual language underlying Zeus’s unions. The masculine αὐτόν can refer to the air or to each year; “it” retains that referential ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: produces or destroys the things of the season
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ ὡραῖα denotes things belonging to or ripening in their proper season, including seasonal produce; “ripe things” would be narrower.

passages.text: While Appion was interpreting these things allegorically, I was deep in thought and appeared not to be following what he was saying. So he broke off his discourse and said to me, “If you are not following what I am saying, why am I even having this discussion in the first place?” I replied, “Do not suppose that I am insensible to what you are saying, for I understand it very well, since this is not the first time I have heard it. To let you know that I am not ignorant of what you are saying, I will summarize what you have stated; and as for what you have omitted, I will complete the allegories in sequence, just as I heard them from others.” Appion said, “Do as you say.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: I was deep in thought
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύννους describes being absorbed or pensive, which explains why Clement merely appeared not to be following.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ λεγομένοις μὴ παρακολουθεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to be following what he was saying
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρακολουθέω here denotes following or comprehending the course of an argument.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will summarize what you have stated
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιτέμνομαι means to abridge or summarize; the dative σοι is understood as identifying the person by whom the preceding statements were made.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν δὲ παραλειφθέντων σοι κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: as for what you have omitted, I will complete the allegories in sequence
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν is taken as describing an orderly continuation; “by logical consequence” is also possible.

passages.text: And I replied, “I now pass over giving a detailed account of the living egg brought forth from the chance blending of boundless matter. When it burst, according to some, a male-and-female being, Phanes, sprang out. I also summarize all those matters up to the point when the ruptured shell assumed its harmonious structure, while marrow-like matter from it remained; then, in outline, I run through the account of the things produced inwardly by that matter, together with what follows. For, as you say, from Cronus and Rhea—that is, by time and matter—were born first Pluto, as the sediment that settled below; second Poseidon, who is the middle, moist substance floating above the nature with the strongest downward pull; and third the highest substance, which is aether, namely Zeus. This third substance was not swallowed, but, being a hot force and having a nature that rises upward, it flew up, as if driven by some gust, into the most sovereign aether above.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: And I replied
lexical_decisions.rationale: The narrative introduction explicitly identifies the following account as Clement’s reply and is retained before the direct speech.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀπείρου ὕλης κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν κράσεως ἀποκυηθὲν ἔμψυχον ὠόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the living egg brought forth from the chance blending of boundless matter
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔμψυχον is rendered “living” rather than the more technical “ensouled”; κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν presents the blending as occurring by chance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a male-and-female being, Phanes, sprang out
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter compound ἀρρενόθηλυ denotes an androgynous or male-and-female entity, while ἐξέθορεν conveys a sudden springing forth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ῥαγὲν κύτος τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the ruptured shell assumed its harmonious structure
lexical_decisions.rationale: κύτος can denote a hollow vessel, casing, or shell; τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν indicates acquiring an ordered or harmonious arrangement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the sediment that settled below
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποστάθμη denotes sediment or dregs, and παραχωρήσασα depicts it giving way or moving to the lower position.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the nature with the strongest downward pull
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual ὀλκοτάτῃ is understood from the idea of drawing or pulling, while κάτω specifies a downward tendency. “The lowest, most attractive nature” is a possible alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν ἄνω ἡγεμονικώτατον ἀνέπτη αἰθέρα
lexical_decisions.chosen: it flew up into the most sovereign aether above
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἡγεμονικώτατον characterizes the upper aether as ruling or preeminent; “most ruling” would be less idiomatic English.
