passages.text: Cronus’s bonds are the fastening together of heaven and earth, as I have also heard from others who give allegorical interpretations. The cutting off of his parts is the separation and differentiation of the elements, because all things were cut away from their own natural substance and set apart, each to be arranged by itself. Time no longer begets; instead, the things begotten through it carry on the succession by nature’s law. Aphrodite, who rose from the depth, is the generative substance arising from moisture. When the hot spirit mingles with it, it produces the desire for their union and brings the beauty of the world to completion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the fastening together of heaven and earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύμπηξις denotes a joining, compacting, or solid fastening together.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the cutting off of his parts
lexical_decisions.rationale: μορίων is the source’s euphemistic “parts”; the possessive “his” refers contextually to Cronus.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντα ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀπετμήθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: all things were cut away from their own natural substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκ is retained as marking source or separation. “Were divided according to their respective natures” is contextually possible but renders ἐκ less directly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ γεννηθέντα δι’ αὐτοῦ νόμῳ φύσεως ποιεῖται τὰς διαδοχάς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the things begotten through it carry on the succession by nature’s law
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb; διαδοχάς may denote successive generations or succession more generally.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it produces the desire for their union
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔρως can mean desire or erotic impulse, while τῆς μίξεως may describe either desire for the mixture or desire generated by it; the former fits the generative context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: brings the beauty of the world to completion
lexical_decisions.rationale: τελεσιουργέω means to accomplish, perfect, or bring something fully into effect.

passages.text: The wedding banquet, where Zeus was holding the feast for the Nereid Thetis and the beautiful Peleus, has the following allegory—so that you may know, Appion, that we have heard such things even without you. The banquet, then, is the world; the twelve are the Fates’ heavenly encircling supports, which they call zodiacal signs; Prometheus is forethought, through which all things came to be; Peleus is mud, conceived from earth for the making of a human being and mixed with the Nereid—that is, with water. From the mixture of the two, water and earth, the first human was not begotten but molded, and was complete; because he had not brought his lips to breasts, he was called Achilles. He himself also represents the prime of life. If that prime desires Desire—Polyxena—who is alien and foreign to truth, it is killed by serpent venom, by an arrow to the heel, as death creeps in along the footprint.

source_issues.source_quote: ἔστι δὲ αὐτὸς καὶ ἀκμήν, ἥτις
source_issues.issue: The printed ἀκμήν is formally accusative or adverbial, whereas a predicate after ἔστι and the feminine nominative relative ἥτις would ordinarily call for ἀκμή. The context supports reference to the prime of life, but that interpretation remains provisional and is disclosed rather than treated as though the supplied Greek already contained the nominative form.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἔστι δὲ αὐτὸς καὶ ἀκμή, ἥτις

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δεῖπνον ἐτέλει Ζεὺς ὑπέρ τε τῆς Νηρηΐδος Θέτιδος καὶ τοῦ καλοῦ Πηλέως
lexical_decisions.chosen: Zeus was holding the feast for the Nereid Thetis and the beautiful Peleus
lexical_decisions.rationale: τελεῖν a feast means to conduct or celebrate it; ὑπέρ identifies those for whom or in whose honor it is held.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Fates’ heavenly encircling supports
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιστηρίγματα is rare and denotes structures set or supporting something around a circumference; “surrounding fixtures” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Prometheus is forethought
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves the explicit etymological wordplay between Προμηθεύς and προμήθεια.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Πηλεὺς πηλὸς ὁ ἀπὸ γῆς εἰς ἀνθρώπου γένεσιν περινοηθεὶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Peleus is mud, conceived from earth for the making of a human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: πηλός preserves the wordplay with Peleus. περινοηθείς is taken in its mental sense, “conceived” or “devised,” though “selected” is also contextually possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ πρῶτος οὐ γεννηθεὶς ἀλλὰ πλασθεὶς τέλειος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the first human was not begotten but molded, and was complete
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine ὁ πρῶτος resumes the preceding ἀνθρώπου. τέλειος can mean complete, perfect, mature, or full-grown.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ μαζοῖς χείλη μὴ προσενεγκεῖν Ἀχιλλεὺς προσηγορεύθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: because he had not brought his lips to breasts, he was called Achilles
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source supplies an allegorical etymology linking Achilles with the absence of nursing at the breast; the explanation is preserved without replacing it with a modern etymology.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥτις ἐὰν ἐπιθυμίαν (Πολυξένην) ὡς ἀληθείας ἀλλοτρίαν οὖσαν καὶ ξένην ἐπιθυμῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: If that prime desires Desire—Polyxena—who is alien and foreign to truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ὡς with οὖσαν descriptively, characterizing Desire as alien and foreign to truth. More explicitly it could be rendered “desires Desire as being alien and foreign to truth”; ὡς with the participle can also present this characterization as the represented reason or ground, yielding a causal sense such as “because she is alien and foreign to truth.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἰῷ ὄφεως ἀναιρεῖται βέλει κατὰ πτέρναν καὶ κατὰ ἴχνος ἐνέρποντος τοῦ θανάτου
lexical_decisions.chosen: it is killed by serpent venom, by an arrow to the heel, as death creeps in along the footprint
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads both ἰῷ and βέλει instrumentally, attaches κατὰ πτέρναν to the arrow, and takes ἴχνος as a footprint or track with death’s creeping entrance. The instruments may instead be appositional or describe venom conveyed by the arrow. Moreover, ἴχνος can mean the sole or foot, and both coordinated κατὰ phrases may go with death’s entrance: “with death creeping in at the heel and at the sole of the foot.”

passages.text: Hera, then, and Athena and Aphrodite and Eris and the apple and Hermes and the judgment and the shepherd hint at some such meaning: Hera is dignity; Athena, courage; Aphrodite, pleasures; Hermes, interpreting reason; and Paris the shepherd, the unreasoning and barbarous impulse. So if, at the prime of life, the reasoning faculty that shepherds the soul happens to be barbarous and, passing over what is beneficial—thrusting aside both courage and self-control—chooses pleasures alone and awards victory to desire alone, as though receiving delightful things from her in return, then the one who judged wrongly will receive enjoyment to the destruction of both himself and all that is his. Eris is contentious vice. The golden apple of the Hesperides would be wealth, which sometimes knows how to lead even the self-controlled—as Hera—toward idleness, makes the courageous—as Athena—more contentious over things unfitting for them, and, under the pretext of luxury, destroys beauty of soul—as Aphrodite. I will put it briefly: wealth provokes everyone to evil strife.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hermes, interpreting reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος here belongs to the psychological allegory and is therefore rendered “reason”; ἑρμηνευτικός also sustains the wordplay with Hermes. “Interpretive discourse” is possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ποιμὴν Πάρις ἡ ἀλόγιστος ὁρμὴ καὶ βάρβαρος
lexical_decisions.chosen: Paris the shepherd, the unreasoning and barbarous impulse
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁρμή denotes impulse or drive, while ἀλόγιστος marks it as lacking rational deliberation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the reasoning faculty that shepherds the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the shepherd image in ποιμαίνων and distinguishes λογισμός as the faculty of calculation or reasoning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς παρ’ αὐτῆς τὰ τέρποντα ἀντιλαμβάνων
lexical_decisions.chosen: as though receiving delightful things from her in return
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀντιλαμβάνων expresses receiving something in exchange or return; ὡς allows the motivation to be presented as the reasoner’s supposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπ’ ὀλέθρῳ ἑαυτοῦ τε καὶ τῶν αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to the destruction of both himself and all that is his
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival τῶν αὐτοῦ is broad. In the Paris allegory it may refer to his people or household, but it can also denote his possessions; “all that is his” is intended to leave both personal and nonpersonal referents open.

lexical_decisions.chosen: contentious vice
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλονεικοῦσα characterizes vice as loving disputes or strife.

lexical_decisions.chosen: under the pretext of luxury
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις is a pretext or professed ground, while τρυφή denotes luxury, indulgence, or soft living.

passages.text: But the Heracles who killed the serpent, the ruler and guardian of wealth—the true Heracles—is also the philosophical mind. Naked of every vice, it ranges throughout the world, visiting souls and bringing those it meets to sound judgment; I mean people resembling bold lions, cowardly deer, wild boars, or many-sided hydras. Likewise, all the other things Heracles is said to have accomplished as labors are riddles of intellectual virtue. For now, let what has been said suffice, for not even all of time will be enough to speak about each one.

source_issues.source_quote: Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς
source_issues.issue: The attachment of ὁ γνήσιος and force of καί are interpretively ambiguous. The main rendering attaches “true” appositionally to Heracles and understands καί as “also,” but ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφος may instead jointly characterize νοῦς, yielding “Heracles is the genuine and philosophical mind.” This is an attachment ambiguity, not evidence of a defective source.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν τοῦ πλούτου ἡγεμόνα καὶ φύλακα ὄφιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the serpent, the ruler and guardian of wealth
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both roles attributed to the serpent and the genitive relation to wealth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the true Heracles—is also the philosophical mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes ὁ γνήσιος as identifying the true Heracles and καὶ φιλόσοφος with νοῦς, with καί represented by “also.” A material alternative coordinates γνήσιος and φιλόσοφος as qualifications of νοῦς: “Heracles is the genuine and philosophical mind.” The main rendering is retained because the article in ὁ γνήσιος naturally permits an appositional identification of Heracles, while the surrounding allegory identifies the genuine Heracles with mind.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bringing those it meets to sound judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονίζω can mean making someone prudent, self-controlled, or sound-minded; this wording suits the philosophical context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: many-sided hydras
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολύτροπος can mean manifold, versatile, devious, or many-natured; “many-sided” preserves its breadth without choosing only the moral sense “wily.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: intellectual virtue
lexical_decisions.rationale: νοερός concerns mind or intellect, matching the passage’s allegory of the philosophical mind.

passages.text: Still, I wonder how those who concealed these things in oblique riddles and veiled them over with wicked myths are called intelligent and wise by you, when the things could have been disclosed clearly, reverently, and beneficially by the uncovered, straight way. As though driven on by an evil demon, they laid snares for almost all humanity. For either these are not riddles but true sins of the gods—in which case they ought not to have exposed the gods or, in the first place, set those sins before human beings for imitation—or the things falsely presented as having been done by the gods were told in riddling form. And the men you call wise sinned, Appion, because by covering solemn things with indecent myths they encouraged human beings to sin, and did this while insulting those whom they even believed to be gods.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα
source_issues.issue: ψευδῶς may be heard as modifying the alleged performance itself (“falsely done”) or the presentation of the deeds as divine. The surrounding contrast between true sins and riddling falsehood supports “falsely presented as having been done.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by the uncovered, straight way
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s contrast between an unveiled direct route and oblique, concealing riddles.

lexical_decisions.chosen: laid snares for ... humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνεδρεύω evokes lying in ambush or entrapping, rather than merely misleading.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to have exposed the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐλέγχω can mean expose, convict, or censure; “exposed” fits the argument that their sins should not have been publicized.

lexical_decisions.chosen: or, in the first place
lexical_decisions.rationale: Under negation, τὴν ἀρχήν idiomatically means “at all” or “in the first place,” not merely “at the beginning.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the things falsely presented as having been done by the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context contrasts actual divine sins with false mythic representations. A more formally literal alternative is “the things falsely done by the gods.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: solemn things
lexical_decisions.rationale: σεμνός may mean solemn, venerable, august, or dignified; the contrast is with indecent myths.

passages.text: Therefore regard such people not as wise men but as evil demons, for they put forward wicked storylines for noble deeds, so that those wishing to become imitators of their betters might emulate the actions of the so-called gods. When speaking on the previous day I did not conceal those actions: I mean patricides, murders of children, impious unions with mothers, daughters, and sisters, unseemly adulteries, male-male intercourse, and defiled acts unfit to name, besides ten thousand other unlawful unions of this kind. Still more impious are those who want these things to be regarded as true, so that they may do the like without shame. In this matter, if they had really wished to act reverently, they ought—as I just said—even if the gods had in fact committed the evils sung about them, out of honor for the gods to have covered the indecent things with myths of a more seemly kind, and not the reverse: as you claim, when good deeds had been performed by them, to wrap them in evil and indecent forms. Such forms, when allegorized, can be understood only with labor and scarcely at that; and whenever some people understand them, they have given those people, in exchange for their great toil, the benefit of not being led astray, though the toil could have been avoided, while they have utterly destroyed those who were led astray. Nevertheless, I approve those who allegorize them toward the more dignified sense, such as those who intimated in a riddle that practical wisdom sprang from the head of Zeus. But perhaps this is more plausible to me: once wicked men had won the reputation of gods, those outrages were dared.

source_issues.source_quote: ὧν ἀσεβέστεροι οἱ ταῦτα ἀληθῆ δοκεῖν εἶναι θέλοντες
source_issues.issue: The antecedent and force of comparative ὧν are not fully explicit. It may mean “more impious than these” or introduce a subgroup, “among whom the more impious are.” The main text uses the defensible contextual sense “still more impious” without forcing an antecedent.

source_issues.source_quote: τοὺς εἰς τὸ σεμνότερον ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτὰς
source_issues.issue: The feminine pronoun αὐτάς may refer back to the actions or accounts implicit in the argument; its precise antecedent is not explicit. The English “them” preserves that referential openness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wicked storylines for noble deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόθεσις may denote a subject, underlying premise, or dramatic plot; “storylines” fits myths that clothe supposedly good deeds in wicked narratives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their betters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative can refer to those superior to the imitators, here especially the beings called gods.

lexical_decisions.chosen: male-male intercourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound directly denotes sexual intercourse between males; the rendering avoids importing a broader modern identity category.

lexical_decisions.chosen: defiled acts unfit to name
lexical_decisions.rationale: μιαρός marks pollution or defilement, while the rare ἀρρητουργία denotes the doing of things that are unspeakable or not to be named.

lexical_decisions.chosen: out of honor for the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative phrase expresses the honor owed or directed toward the gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκείνοις μὲν ἀντὶ τοῦ πολλοῦ μόχθου παρέσχον τὸ μὴ πλανηθῆναι, ἐξὸν μὴ μοχθῆσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: they have given those people, in exchange for their great toil, the benefit of not being led astray, though the toil could have been avoided
lexical_decisions.rationale: The benefit is identified as not being led astray, while μέν sets up the contrast with those who were led astray; the Greek does not expressly make this their only benefit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that practical wisdom sprang
lexical_decisions.rationale: φρόνησις is prudent or practical understanding, while ἀναπηδάω supplies the vivid image of springing forth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: had won the reputation of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποφέρομαι with δόξαν can mean carrying off, gaining, or winning a reputation.

passages.text: But we do not find the poetic allegory concerning all the gods consistent. To take an immediate example, in the ordering of the universe the poets say at one time that nature became the originator of the whole creation, and at another that mind did. For they say that the first motion and mingling of the elements arose from nature, but that this was ordered by the providence of mind. Although they declare that the universe was fashioned by nature, because they cannot demonstrate this beyond objection on account of the artistry of creation, they also interweave the providence of mind, thinking themselves able to sweep along even those who are very discerning. But we say to them: If the world came into being from spontaneous nature, how has it acquired proportion and order? These can be brought about only by surpassing intelligence and can be comprehended by knowledge, which alone is capable of determining these things precisely. But if all things received their combination and ordering through intelligence—which necessarily cannot be otherwise—how could these things then possibly have happened to come into being spontaneously?

lexical_decisions.chosen: the poetic allegory
lexical_decisions.rationale: ποιητικός can mean poetic or belonging to poets; “the poets’ allegory” is a viable alternative, but the adjective is preserved directly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: nature ... mind ... the originator
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passage contrasts nature and mind as competing explanatory first principles; lowercase English avoids imposing personification beyond the context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on account of the artistry of creation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔντεχνος denotes what is artful, skillfully made, or governed by craft.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even those who are very discerning
lexical_decisions.rationale: σαφής applied to people can describe those who are clear-minded, perspicacious, or discerning, while πάνυ marks a high degree, represented by “very” rather than a superlative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: only by surpassing intelligence
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here φρόνησις concerns the intelligence responsible for cosmic proportion and order, while μόνης restricts what can bring them about.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καταληφθῆναι ὑπὸ ἐπιστήμης τῆς μόνης ταῦτα ἀκριβοῦν δυναμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: can be comprehended by knowledge, which alone is capable of determining these things precisely
lexical_decisions.rationale: The second μόνης belongs to the attributive phrase describing knowledge as alone capable of precise determination; it does not directly restrict the passive verb “can be comprehended.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: spontaneously
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase can also be rendered “by chance” or “of itself”; “spontaneously” maintains the connection with ἐξ αὐτομάτου φύσεως earlier in the argument.

passages.text: Therefore, those who wished to allegorize divine matters in the more shameful direction—for example, that Metis was swallowed by Zeus—have fallen into perplexity. They do not understand that those who gave oblique accounts of nature concerning the gods have also abolished their very existence as gods, dissolving their forms by allegory into the substances of the world. It is more plausible, then, to say that the gods celebrated by them were certain evil magicians. Though wicked human beings, they assumed different forms by magic, broke up marriages, and ruined lives; yet to people of old, who did not know what magic even was, they seemed to be gods because of what they did. In city after city, both their deaths and their tombs are evident.

source_issues.source_quote: φυσιολογήσαντες ·περὶ θεῶν
source_issues.issue: The supplied, image-checked print has a raised point before περὶ. This verified editorial punctuation leaves περὶ θεῶν capable of being associated either with the oblique account of nature or more loosely with the following claim about abolishing the gods. The translation provisionally takes it with the participial phrase while retaining the supplied reading; the punctuation is not treated as an OCR defect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to allegorize ... in the more shameful direction
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative phrase describes the direction or resulting sense of the allegorical interpretation, not simply its method.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Metis
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the mythic example Μῆτις is the conventional name Metis, although the name itself also means counsel or cunning intelligence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gave oblique accounts of nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: φυσιολογέω means discoursing or theorizing about nature, while πλαγίως marks the indirect or oblique manner.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ εἴδη αὐτῶν ... εἰς τὰς τοῦ κόσμου οὐσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: their forms ... into the substances of the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the philosophical contrast between the gods’ forms or identities and the cosmic substances into which allegory resolves them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were certain evil magicians
lexical_decisions.rationale: μάγος here denotes practitioners of magic; the following μαγείᾳ confirms that sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they assumed different forms
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle or passive participle can mean transforming themselves or being transformed; the context presents magical changes of appearance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their deaths
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόρος can mean death, doom, or allotted fate; its pairing with tombs favors “deaths,” though “fates” remains possible.

passages.text: Indeed, to take an immediate example (as I also said on another occasion), in the Caucasus Mountains the tomb of a certain Cronus, a man, is pointed out—the tomb of a savage tyrant and killer of his children. His son, named Zeus, became worse; appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic, he breaks up many marriages and punishes his father together with his uncles. When he then died, the Cretans point out his tomb. In Mesopotamia, a certain Helios lies at Hatra and a certain Selene at Carrhae; a certain Hermes, a human being, lies in Egypt; Ares in Thrace; Aphrodite in Cyprus; and Asclepius in Epidaurus. Tombs of many other such figures are also visible.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως τελευτήσαντος τὸν τάφον Κρῆτες ἐπιδεικνῦσιν
source_issues.issue: The genitive absolute does not explicitly identify the person who died. The continuing focus and the Cretan tomb tradition favor Zeus; Cronus is grammatically possible but contextually less likely.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the tomb of a certain Cronus, a man, is pointed out
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although σῆμα can mean a sign or monument, the burial context and the subsequent τάφον and τάφοι support “tomb.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the alleged magical means and ἀναφανείς, which presents his world-rule as an appearance or emergence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν πατέρα σὺν τοῖς θείοις κολάζει
lexical_decisions.chosen: punishes his father together with his uncles
lexical_decisions.rationale: The family and mythological context supports the substantival sense “uncles,” with the father and uncles as joint objects. “Punishes his father together with the divine ones” is lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a certain Helios lies at Hatra
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἄτροις is treated as the dative plural place-name referring to Hatra in Mesopotamia.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a certain Hermes, a human being, lies in Egypt
lexical_decisions.rationale: The apposition explicitly identifies Hermes as a human being; the verb “lies” is carried forward from κεῖνται.

passages.text: Thus it has been plainly acknowledged by those who think correctly that they were human beings. Those who were their contemporaries, perceiving that they had proved mortal, paid less attention to them after they died; but the long passage of time clothed them with the reputation of gods. Do not be amazed if those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles were deceived, or those in the days of Dionysus or anyone else of that period, since the people in those places worship even Hector at Ilium and Achilles on the island of Leuce, the Opuntians worship Patroclus, and the Rhodians worship Alexander the Macedonian.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it has been plainly acknowledged that they were human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The implied subjects are the allegedly divine figures discussed in the preceding section; the perfect construction identifies them as having been human.

lexical_decisions.chosen: perceiving that they had proved mortal
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can express noticing, apprehending, or suspecting, while the completed deaths demonstrate the figures’ mortality.

lexical_decisions.chosen: clothed them with the reputation of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the image of time placing divine repute around them without asserting that they truly became gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ κατὰ Ἀσκληπιὸν καὶ Ἡρακλέα γενόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles
lexical_decisions.rationale: The surrounding argument concerns contemporaries and the effect of elapsed time. “Those associated with Asclepius and Heracles” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since the people in those places worship even Hector
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ὅπου introduces a striking supporting circumstance; the worshipers are supplied later by οἱ ἐκεῖ.

passages.text: But among the Egyptians, even now, a man is worshiped as a god before his death. This, at least, is a lesser act of impiety, because the Egyptians accord divine honors while a man is alive; but the most ridiculous thing of all is that they worship birds and reptiles and all animals. For most human beings neither understand nor do anything with judgment. Now observe what is most shameful of all: the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans, whom most people call Zeus, they depict on a panel as a goose coupled with Leda and set up publicly. As retribution for this outrage, I would have liked it if they had portrayed their present king in a shameful coupling and, having done the same thing they have dared to do in Zeus’s case, had set it up publicly, so that, even if only through the anger of their temporary king—and he a human being—they might learn through punishment how due honor must be rendered. I tell you these things not as one who has already recognized the God who truly is, but, being fair-minded, I confess: Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists.

source_issues.source_quote: ἤθελον εἰ
source_issues.issue: The construction continues with aorist indicatives and is compressed. It defensibly expresses an unreal wish, “I would have liked it if they had ...”; “I wanted to see whether they had ...” is grammatically conceivable but fits the argument less well. No textual correction is required.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Egyptians accord divine honors
lexical_decisions.rationale: Νομίζω can denote customary observance or acknowledgment; here it concerns treating a living person as entitled to divine honors.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν δι’ αὐτῶν ὄντα πατέρα θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase δι’ αὐτῶν is literally “through them.” In context it can mark Zeus’s status as established through their own representation or claim; “through their agency” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as a goose coupled with Leda
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χῆνα explicitly means “goose,” not the familiar “swan.” The participle describes Zeus as joined or correspondingly formed with Leda and, in this sexual context, is rendered “coupled with.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a shameful coupling
lexical_decisions.rationale: Πλοκή can denote entwining or entanglement; the preceding sexual image involving Zeus and Leda supports “coupling.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: their temporary king
lexical_decisions.rationale: Πρόσκαιρος emphasizes that the earthly ruler lasts only for a limited time.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰ καὶ τί θεὸς οὐκ οἶδα, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε σαφῶς ὅτι θεός, νομίζω εἰδέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between not knowing what God is and knowing that God exists. “What sort of god” and “that he is God” are grammatically possible but fit the immediate contrast less directly.

passages.text: To take an immediate example, the first four elements—things brought into being by another—cannot be God; neither can mixing, blending, coming-to-be, the visible vessel that encompasses the whole, the sediment collecting in Hades, the water floating on top, the boiling substance, or the air extending from it as far as the things here. For whether the four elements had stood apart from one another—in which case they could not have been mixed for the generation of a living creature without some great craftsman—or had always been joined to one another, even so they are fitted together by a craftsman mind to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature, so that it may be able to preserve the proportion of each to each and may possess a well-bounded constitution, and so that all the things within may receive the appropriate harmony. Likewise, the craftsman mind precisely fashions the proper places of each with complete beauty. To sum up: of all the other things that a living creature must ever have, nothing was lacking in this great living creature of the whole circuit.

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα τὴν ἑκάστου πρὸς ἕκαστον ἀναλογίαν ἀποσώζειν δύνηται καὶ τὴν ἕξιν εὐπερίγραφον ἔχῃ
source_issues.issue: The singular verbs leave their subject implicit. The resulting organized whole or living creature is the best contextual referent; the neuter plural elements can also govern singular verbs in Greek, so they remain a grammatical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ πρῶτα τέσσαρα στοιχεῖα θεὸς εἶναι οὐ δύναται τὰ ὑπὸ ἄλλου γενόμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the first four elements—things brought into being by another—cannot be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The final participial phrase characterizes the four elements and supplies the reason they cannot themselves be God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the visible vessel that encompasses the whole
lexical_decisions.rationale: Κύτος denotes a hollow body, cavity, or vessel. “Vessel” preserves the cosmological container image without identifying it more specifically.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἐν τῷ ᾄδῃ συρρέουσα ὑποστάθμη
lexical_decisions.chosen: the sediment collecting in Hades
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ὑποστάθμη denotes sediment, dregs, or what settles at the bottom, while συρρέουσα presents it as flowing or gathering together.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐξ αὐτῆς μέχρι τῶν ἐνταῦθα διήκων ἀήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the air extending from it as far as the things here
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun most naturally refers to the immediately preceding “boiling substance,” though another feminine item in the list is grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον τῶν τοῦ ζῴου μελῶν καὶ μερῶν συναρμόζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: are fitted together to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes an intelligent fitting of the elements to the proper constitution or requirements of the creature’s members and parts.

lexical_decisions.chosen: may possess a well-bounded constitution
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἕξις here denotes condition or constitution, while εὐπερίγραφος suggests being readily circumscribed or clearly bounded. “A well-defined constitution” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ μεγάλῳ τούτῳ ζῴῳ τῆς ὅλης περιφορᾶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: in this great living creature of the whole circuit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The cosmos is presented as a great living creature. Περιφορά can denote revolution, circular motion, or the circuit produced by it; “of the whole revolution” is also possible.

passages.text: Thus there must be some unoriginated craftsman mind that either gathered the elements when they were apart or, when they were together with one another, skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature and completed a single work from them all; for it is impossible for an exceedingly wise work to be completed without some greater mind. Nor indeed can love be the craftsman of all, nor desire, nor force, nor anything else of that kind, since such things are passions and naturally come and go. Nor is whatever is borne by another a god, nor indeed whatever is altered by time or nature and dissolved into no longer existing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unoriginated craftsman mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἀγέννητος means not generated or not brought into being. “Unoriginated” suits the contrast with elements produced by another; “unbegotten” is possible but carries stronger traditional theological associations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb emphasizes artful or craftsmanlike arrangement, while the prepositional phrase states its purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an exceedingly wise work
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase presents the work as embodying extraordinary wisdom or skill; “a work of surpassing skill” is an idiomatic alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: love can be the craftsman of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἔρως can denote love as a cosmic principle and may evoke personified Eros. Lowercase “love” avoids requiring personification.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάθη ὄντα συμβαίνειν καὶ ἀποβαίνειν πέφυκεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: such things are passions and naturally come and go
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired verbs describe the proposed principles as contingent passions that arise and depart.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου φερόμενόν ἐστιν θεὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever is borne by another is a god
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation is negated by the preceding οὐδὲ. Φέρω in the passive can mean carried, borne, or moved; “moved by another” is also viable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ὑπὸ χρόνου ἢ φύσεως ἀλλοιούμενον καὶ εἰς τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι ἀναλυόμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever is altered by time or nature and dissolved into no longer existing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the alteration, the image of dissolution, and its stated outcome of nonexistence.

passages.text: While I was discussing these things with Appion, Peter arrived from Caesarea, and crowds converged in Tyre, hurrying to meet him and thank him for coming. Appion withdrew with only Anubion and Athenodorus, but all the rest of us set out to meet Peter. I was the first to welcome him in front of the gates, and I led him to the lodging. When we arrived there, we dismissed the crowds. When he asked me to tell him what had happened, I held nothing back; instead, I reported Simon’s slanders, the monstrous apparitions he had produced, how many illnesses he had sent after the feast arising from the ox sacrifice, and that, of those who were ill, some had remained right there in Tyre, while the others had gone away with Simon to Sidon at the same time as my arrival, in expectation of being healed by him. I also reported that I had learned that none of them had obtained healing from him, and I recounted to Peter the discussion I had had with Appion. Then, to show affection and offer encouragement, he praised and blessed me. After partaking of salt, because of the exertions of the journey, he gave himself over to the most necessary rest of sleep.

lexical_decisions.chosen: crowds converged
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes crowds running or gathering together, not merely static assemblies.

lexical_decisions.chosen: thank him for coming
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιδημία can denote an arrival, presence, or visit; the immediate context favors Peter’s coming to Tyre.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to the lodging
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία may denote hospitality or guest quarters; here it functions as the destination where Peter would stay.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τερατώδεις φαντασίας ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γεγενημένας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the monstrous apparitions he had produced
lexical_decisions.rationale: φαντασίαι can be appearances, apparitions, or illusions; “apparitions” preserves their presented visual character without deciding whether they were real or deceptive.

lexical_decisions.chosen: how many illnesses he had sent
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὅσας preserves the emphasis on their number or extent; it could also be rendered “all the illnesses that he had sent.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βουθυσίας ἑστίασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: after the feast arising from the ox sacrifice
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουθυσία is an ox sacrifice, while ἐκ presents the feast as proceeding from or resulting from it; “the feast from/of the ox sacrifice” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at the same time as my arrival
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction expresses simultaneity; the alternative “as soon as I arrived” would give it a stronger sequential force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in expectation of being healed by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς with the future participle presents the travelers’ purpose or expectation rather than endorsing the expected healing as fact.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to show affection and offer encouragement
lexical_decisions.rationale: χάριν marks the purpose of Peter’s praise and blessing; προτροπή may also be rendered “exhortation.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: after partaking of salt
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves the explicit salt image; the phrase may contextually imply sharing or eating food more generally.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ ἀναγκαιοτάτῃ ἡσυχίᾳ τοῦ ὕπνου ἑαυτὸν ἐπέτρεπεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he gave himself over to the most necessary rest of sleep
lexical_decisions.rationale: This retains the superlative force of ἀναγκαιοτάτῃ and the image of entrusting or yielding oneself to sleep.

passages.text: On the fourth day of our stay in Tyre, toward dawn, when Peter had come forward, not a few inhabitants of the neighboring places and very many from Tyre itself met him and cried out, saying, “May God have mercy on us through you; may he heal us through you.” Peter stood on a certain high stone so that he could be seen by everyone and, after greeting them in accordance with the law that reveres God, began as follows:

lexical_decisions.chosen: of our stay in Tyre
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἐπιδημία denotes a temporary residence or stay, not an epidemic or an official visitation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: toward dawn
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase locates the event near the approach of daybreak.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when Peter had come forward
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle presents Peter as having gone out or come forward; “come forward” fits his subsequent public address without specifying an unmentioned building.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after greeting them in accordance with the law that reveres God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσαγορεύω means greet or address, while the dative θεοσεβεῖ νόμῳ expresses the God-revering rule or manner governing the greeting; “with a God-revering greeting” is also possible.

passages.text: God, who created heaven and the universe, does not lack an occasion for the salvation of those who wish to be saved. Therefore, no one should rashly accuse him of lacking benevolence toward humanity, even on account of things that appear bad. For the outcomes of what happens to a human being are unknown to humans and are suspected of tending toward evil, but they are known to God as things that will turn out well. Take Simon as an immediate example: being God’s left-hand power and holding authority over those who do not know God for the purpose of doing harm, he was able to surround you with diseases. These diseases, having been permitted to arise through God’s good providence, compelled you, after you had looked around for and found the one able to heal, to accept, on the pretext of treatment of the body, the things that seem good to God and to be persuaded to set your minds on them, so that in this way, together with your bodies that are to be saved, you might also have your souls safe.

lexical_decisions.chosen: does not lack an occasion for the salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Occasion” preserves πρόφασις as grounds or an opportunity for action and also makes visible its lexical connection with the later προφάσει. In the later occurrence, bodily treatment is the ostensible basis on which the hearers accept divine instruction, so the context supports the more pointed rendering “pretext” there.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν μηδὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς δοκοῦσιν φαύλοις ὑπὸ προπετείας τις αὐτὸν ὡς μὴ φιλάνθρωπον αἰτιάσθω
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore, no one should rashly accuse him of lacking benevolence toward humanity, even on account of things that appear bad
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering treats ὑπὸ προπετείας as the rash manner or impulse behind the accusation and preserves the emphatic force of μηδέ with “even.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: of lacking benevolence toward humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλάνθρωπος describes one who is humane or benevolent toward people; the rendering preserves the negation without importing a specialized theological title.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτίκα γοῦν Σίμων ἀριστερὰ τοῦ θεοῦ δύναμις ὢν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Take Simon as an immediate example: being God’s left-hand power
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτίκα γοῦν introduces a concrete immediate example, and ἀριστερὰ τοῦ θεοῦ δύναμις directly identifies Simon as the left-hand power of God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν τὸν θεὸν οὐκ εἰδότων ἐπὶ κακοποιΐᾳ τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: holding authority over those who do not know God for the purpose of doing harm
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive marks those over whom the authority operates, while ἐπὶ κακοποιΐᾳ states its harmful purpose or function.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the pretext of treatment of the body
lexical_decisions.rationale: This repeats the πρόφασις wording used earlier. Here bodily healing functions as the ostensible basis or occasion for accepting what pleases God; “on the occasion of bodily treatment” is possible, but “on the pretext” better preserves the distinction between the immediate bodily aim and the further saving outcome.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ θεῷ δοκοῦντα ἀναδεξαμένους πεισθῆναι φρονεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to accept the things that seem good to God and to be persuaded to set your minds on them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes accepting what is pleasing to God, followed by persuasion in thought. More literally, the final words can be rendered “to be persuaded to think,” but English benefits from making the contextually supplied object explicit.

passages.text: I learn, then, that after sacrificing an ox he gave you a feast in the middle of the marketplace, and that in this way, carried away by much wine, you joined the evil demons in showing hospitality to their ruler. Thus most of you were seized by afflictions, because in ignorance you drew against yourselves, with your own hands, the sword of destruction. For the demons would not have had authority against you if you had not first shared a meal with their ruler. From the beginning, God, who created everything, laid down this law for the two rulers in every instance—the ruler of the right and the ruler of the left: neither of them is to have authority unless he first becomes the table companion of someone whom he wishes to benefit or harm. As, then, by partaking of the sacrifices dedicated to demons you were enslaved to the leader of evil, so, if you cease from these things and take refuge in God through the good, right-hand leader, honoring him without sacrifice by doing what he wishes, know well that along with the healing of the body you will also have healthy souls. For he alone, destroying through the left hand, can give life through the right hand; likewise, he can both strike and raise up one who lies fallen.

source_issues.source_quote: ·ἀθύτοις τιμαῖς
source_issues.issue: An isolated raised point is printed immediately before ἀθύτοις despite the preceding comma. It appears to be stray or redundant punctuation and contributes no lexical content; that interpretation remains provisional.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that after sacrificing an ox he gave you a feast
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουθυτέω denotes sacrificing an ox or cattle. The unexpressed subject is most naturally Simon from the preceding context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅμα τοῖς πονηροῖς δαίμοσιν τὸν ἄρχοντα αὐτῶν ἐφιλοφρονεῖσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: you joined the evil demons in showing hospitality to their ruler
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλοφρονέομαι can mean welcome, entertain, or treat graciously. “Showing hospitality” preserves the banquet setting, though “paying court to” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you had first shared a meal
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμοδίαιτος can describe living or dining together. The surrounding references to sacrifices and table fellowship support the meal-related rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσὶν ἑκάστοτε ἄρχουσι, δεξιῶν τε καὶ εὐωνύμων
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the two rulers in every instance—the ruler of the right and the ruler of the left
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑκάστοτε indicates each recurring instance, while the genitives distinguish the right-hand and left-hand sides or powers. “For each pair of rulers, of right and left” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honoring him without sacrifice by doing what he wishes
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀθύτοις describes honors not involving sacrifice. The rendering takes doing what God wishes as the form of those non-sacrificial honors.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸς γὰρ μόνος διὰ τῆς ἀριστερᾶς ἀναιρῶν διὰ τῆς δεξιᾶς ζωοποιῆσαι δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: For he alone, destroying through the left hand, can give life through the right hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle ἀναιρῶν describes destruction through the left, while the infinitive ζωοποιῆσαι with δύναται states his ability to give life through the right.

passages.text: For this reason, after first being deceived by Simon the forerunner, you died to God in your souls, and your bodies were struck. But in the same way you can, a second time, through reorientation—as I said—accept the things pleasing to God and both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls. What pleases God is this: to pray to him; to make requests of him as the one who gives everything according to a judicial law; to abstain from “the table of demons”; not to taste dead flesh; not to touch blood; and to wash oneself clean of every pollution. As for the rest, hear it, all of you, in one saying, just as the Jews who revere God have heard it, taking up one mind in many bodies: “Whatever good things each person wants for himself, he should plan the same things for his neighbor as well.” Each of you would understand what is good in this way, if he were to reason with himself as follows: “You do not want to be murdered; do not murder another. You do not want another to commit adultery with your wife; do not commit adultery with another man’s wedded wife. You do not want any of your possessions to be stolen; do not steal anything belonging to another.” And so, recognizing from your own case what is reasonable and doing it, you will become dear to God and obtain healing; for otherwise you will be tormented in your bodies in the present age and punished in your souls in the age to come.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after first being deceived by Simon the forerunner
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόδρομος explicitly calls Simon a forerunner, while προαπατάω presents the deception as prior; the translation does not specify whose forerunner he is.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context concerns moral and spiritual redirection expressed by accepting what pleases God. “Through repentance” is the traditional alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τὰ σώματα ἀναρρῶσαι καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀναλαβεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναρρωννύω denotes renewed bodily strength, while ἀναλαμβάνω here presents the souls as regained or recovered; “take up your souls again” would be more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸν αἰτεῖν ὡς πάντα νόμῳ κριτικῷ διδόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: to make requests of him as the one who gives everything according to a judicial law
lexical_decisions.rationale: κριτικός can mean discriminating or judicial. “According to a law of discernment” is possible, but the surrounding emphasis on consequences and punishment favors “judicial.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: not to taste dead flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording directly prohibits tasting flesh that is dead; it has not been generalized to a familiar dietary formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν πολλοῖς σώμασιν μίαν γνώμην ἀναλαβόντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: taking up one mind in many bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the author’s image of bodily plurality united in a single judgment or disposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ θέλεις τὴν σὴν ὑφ’ ἑτέρου μοιχευθῆναι γυναῖκα, τὴν ἑτέρου μὴ μοίχευε γαμετήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: You do not want another to commit adultery with your wife; do not commit adultery with another man’s wedded wife
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English changes the first clause from passive to active to avoid implying sexual coercion while preserving the participants and the repeated adultery terminology. The distinction between γυναῖκα, “wife,” and γαμετήν, “wedded wife,” is also retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐν τῷ παρόντι αἰῶνι βασανισθήσεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: for otherwise you will be tormented in your bodies in the present age
lexical_decisions.rationale: After an exhortation or stated favorable outcome, ἐπεί can introduce the consequence that follows otherwise. The formally possible “since indeed you will be tormented” would obscure the warning contrast supplied by the context.

passages.text: After being instructed in such things by Peter over a few days and being healed, they were baptized. Then, all deeply grieved by his further wonders, they sat together as a whole populace in the middle of the marketplaces on ashes and sackcloth, reorienting themselves over the sins they had previously committed. When those in Sidon heard these things, they did the same and sent suppliants to Peter, since they themselves were unable to come to him because of their diseases. Peter, after staying in Tyre for not many days, instructing everyone in it, freeing them from every kind of affliction, forming a church, and appointing for them a bishop from among the elders who followed him, set out for Sidon. On learning that Peter was coming, Simon immediately fled to Beirut with Appion and his companions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοιαῦτα ὑπὸ τοῦ Πέτρου ἐν ὀλίγαις ἡμέραις κατηχηθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: After being instructed in such things by Peter over a few days
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατηχέω here means to instruct orally; “catechized” would preserve the later technical term but would be less accessible in modern English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: deeply grieved by his further wonders
lexical_decisions.rationale: περίλυπος takes the dative as the cause or occasion of grief, and λοιπός can mean remaining, other, or further. “Deeply grieved at his other wonders” is a close alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πανδημεὶ ἐπὶ σποδοῦ καὶ σάκκου ἐκαθέζοντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: they sat together as a whole populace ... on ashes and sackcloth
lexical_decisions.rationale: πανδημεί means collectively or with the whole populace, while ἐπί with the genitive presents ashes and sackcloth as what they sat upon.

lexical_decisions.chosen: reorienting themselves over the sins they had previously committed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes moral reorientation in response to earlier sins, while ἐπί identifies those sins as its occasion. “Repenting over their former sins” is the traditional alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: forming a church
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the context of appointing a bishop from among elders, ἐκκλησία denotes an organized congregation or church, and συνίστημι denotes forming or establishing it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: On learning that Peter was coming
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the narrative sequence Peter has just set out for Sidon, so the present participle is best understood as his approach. Because ἥκω can also have a perfect-like sense, “had arrived” remains grammatically possible.

passages.text: As Peter entered Sidon, people carried many in on beds and laid them before him. But he said to them, “Then do not suppose that I can do anything for your healing, since I am myself a mortal man capable of falling prey to many sufferings. But I do not begrudge showing you the way by which you will be able to be saved, for I myself learned from the prophet of truth the determinations of God, foreordained ‘before the foundation of the world.’ I mean the evil actions for which he appointed human beings to be afflicted by the ruler of wickedness, and likewise the good actions for which he determined that those who first believed in him as he healed the bodies would be saved, and afterward that their souls too would be restored to imperishability.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Μὴ τοίνυν νομίσητε ἐμέ τι δύνασθαι πρὸς ὑμετέραν ἴασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Then do not suppose that I can do anything for your healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive construction expresses what the hearers must not suppose; πρὸς ὑμετέραν ἴασιν indicates ability directed toward their healing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς προωρισμένους τοῦ θεοῦ „πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου“ ὁρισμούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the determinations of God, foreordained ‘before the foundation of the world’
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Foreordained determinations” preserves the source’s repetition of the ὁρίζω word group rather than replacing it with unrelated English terms.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil actions for which
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἐπί with the dative introduces the actions or conditions on account of which the stated consequence was appointed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥρισεν πρότερον πιστεύσαντας αὐτῷ ἰωμένῳ τὰ σώματα σώζεσθαι, ἔπειτα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐπανορθοῦσθαι πρὸς τὸ ἀνώλεθρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he determined that those who first believed in him as he healed the bodies would be saved, and afterward that their souls too would be restored to imperishability
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes τὰ σώματα as the object of the immediately preceding ἰωμένῳ. Alternatively, τὰ σώματα may specify the bodily scope of σώζεσθαι: “he determined that, after first believing in him who heals, they should be saved in body, and afterward that their souls too should be restored to imperishability.” That attachment makes the parallel between bodies and souls explicit. The immediate position of τὰ σώματα after ἰωμένῳ supports the chosen attachment, but the alternative remains syntactically viable; αὐτῷ may likewise be represented as “in him” or “him.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to imperishability
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjective denotes the imperishable or indestructible state toward which the souls are restored.

passages.text: Knowing, then, both these good and evil actions, I announce them to you beforehand as two roads, showing you along which one people perish as they walk and along which one they are saved as they travel, guided by God. The road of those who perish is broad and very smooth, but it brings destruction without toil; the road of those who are saved is narrow and rough, but at the end it saves those who have traversed it laboriously. At the head of these two roads sit unbelief and faith. Those who have preferred pleasures travel by way of unbelief; because of those pleasures . . . . they did not even continue to seek what is beneficial. Yet they do not know that God’s purposes are not like human purposes. For first of all, he knows everyone’s thoughts, and each person is held accountable not only for undertaking something but also for intending it. Those who try to think what is good and fail act far less impiously than those who do not attempt good things at all. For God himself saw fit that the person who lapses despite knowing what is good should, after being punished moderately in proportion to human transgressions, be saved. But those who have neglected even to begin to know what is better—even if they do countless other good things—but do not adopt the religious observance he himself prescribed will, having incurred a charge of negligence, be utterly extinguished by the greatest punishment.

source_issues.source_quote: δι’ ἃς . . . . οὐδὲ ζητεῖν τὸ συμφέρον οὐ διεφύλαξαν
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints exactly four dots between the surviving opening causal phrase and the surviving negative clause. The unavailable wording leaves the complete causal statement fragmentary, and no restoration has been supplied. The image-checked transcription verifies the printed gap but does not recover its content. Under the selected-edition coverage scope, the translation preserves the exact gap marker and defensibly represents all surviving words, so the unavailable content does not itself block publication.

source_issues.source_quote: ἄνευ του πόνου
source_issues.issue: The article is printed as του without the expected circumflex. This is an accentual feature and does not affect the meaning.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐνχειρῆσαι
source_issues.issue: The print has the orthographic form ἐνχειρῆσαι where the assimilated compound spelling ἐγχειρῆσαι is more usual. The supplied form remains intelligible as the aorist infinitive of “undertake.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: At the head of these two roads sit unbelief and faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: προκάθημαι depicts unbelief and faith as positioned before or at the head of their respective roads.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δι’ ἃς . . . . οὐδὲ ζητεῖν τὸ συμφέρον οὐ διεφύλαξαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of those pleasures . . . . they did not even continue to seek what is beneficial
lexical_decisions.rationale: δι’ ἃς refers back to the pleasures, while διαφυλάσσω with the infinitive is understood as maintaining or continuing an activity. The two negatives are treated as emphatic negative concord; a strictly logical double-negative reading is possible in isolation but is contextually less likely. The exact four-dot gap is preserved because its unavailable wording prevents recovery of the complete causal statement.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐν τῷ ἐνχειρῆσαι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἐννοῆσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: not only for undertaking something but also for intending it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast extends accountability from beginning an action to conceiving or intending it; “something” and “it” represent the implicit object shared by the two infinitives. “Conceiving it” is also possible for ἐννοῆσαι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ ἐγχειροῦντες καλὰ νοεῖν καὶ ἀποτυγχάνοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who try to think what is good and fail
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves νοεῖν as mental activity rather than adding an action not explicitly stated; “try to understand good things” is a viable lexical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ λόγον τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων παραπτωμάτων μετρίως κολασθέντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished moderately in proportion to human transgressions
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ λόγον is attached to the punishment and expresses proportion. It could instead qualify the person’s lapse as occurring according to the measure or character of human transgressions, but its placement before μετρίως κολασθέντα permits the chosen attachment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν ᾗ δὲ αὐτὸς ὥρισεν θρησκείᾳ μὴ γένωνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but do not adopt the religious observance he himself prescribed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, they do not “come to be in” the θρησκεία he determined. “Religious observance” preserves the practical cultic or devotional sense; “religion” or “worship” is also possible in this context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will be utterly extinguished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb retains the image of quenching or extinguishing rather than being generalized to “will be punished” or “will perish”; “utterly” represents παντελῶς.

passages.text: The religious observance appointed by him is this: to worship him alone; to believe the one prophet of truth; to be baptized “for forgiveness of sins” and thus, through the purest immersion, to be born anew to God through the water that saves; not to partake of “a table of demons” (I mean things sacrificed to idols, animals found dead, strangled animals, animals caught by wild beasts, and blood); not to live in impurity; to bathe after intercourse with a woman, while women themselves must also observe menstrual separation; for everyone to practice self-control, do good, and not act unjustly; and to await eternal life from the all-powerful God, asking through continual prayers and petitions to receive it. As Peter gave such exhortations also in Sidon, within a few days many there too reoriented themselves, believed, and were healed. He established a church, appointed one of the elders accompanying him as their overseer, and departed from Sidon.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας μόνῳ πιστεύειν προφήτῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to believe the one prophet of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνῳ characterizes the prophet as the sole or one prophet of truth. The phrase could also be rendered “to believe only the prophet of truth,” with the exclusivity attached adverbially to believing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through the purest immersion
lexical_decisions.rationale: βαφή denotes dipping or immersion and here refers to the preceding baptism; the superlative force of ἁγνοτάτης is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀναγεννηθῆναι θεῷ διὰ τοῦ σώζοντος ὕδατος
lexical_decisions.chosen: to be born anew to God through the water that saves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the God-directed dative θεῷ and the source’s direct description of the water as saving.

lexical_decisions.chosen: animals found dead, strangled animals, animals caught by wild beasts
lexical_decisions.rationale: These substantivized plurals occur in a list of prohibited foods. “Animals found dead” expresses νεκρῶν contextually; more literally it is simply “dead things.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to bathe after intercourse with a woman
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοίτη γυναικός literally refers to a woman’s bed but in this purity context denotes sexual intercourse.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while women themselves must also observe menstrual separation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄφεδρος is a term for menstruation or the associated period of separation. The phrase may also be rendered “observe the menstrual period”; the source does not explicitly repeat the preceding command to bathe.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοιαῦτα καὶ ἐν τῇ Σιδῶνι τοῦ Πέτρου παραινοῦντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: As Peter gave such exhortations also in Sidon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The additive καί is preserved with “also,” explicitly stating that Peter gave such exhortations in Sidon as well. This is distinct from the later κἀκεῖ, rendered “there too,” which characterizes the people’s response.

lexical_decisions.chosen: reoriented themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context describes moral and religious redirection accompanying belief; the traditional alternative is “repented.” No Godward phrase is added because the Greek does not state one here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: overseer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The word designates the supervisory office assigned to the elder; “bishop” is a possible institutional rendering but may imply a later fixed title.

passages.text: As soon as he set foot in Berytus, an earthquake occurred. The crowds approached Peter and said, “Help us! For we are afraid,” they declared, “that perhaps we may all be utterly destroyed.” Then Simon, taking courage, together with Appion, Anubion, Athenodorus, and the rest of his companions, publicly shouted to the crowds against Peter: “Flee from this man, men! He is a magician—believe it! He himself brought the earthquake upon us and stirred up the diseases, so that he might overawe you as though he himself were a god.” Simon’s party made many such false claims against Peter, alleging that he possessed power beyond human capacity. But when the crowds fell silent for him, Peter gave a slight smile and said with startling boldness, “Men, I acknowledge that, if God wills, I am able to do the very things these men say. What is more, if you do not heed me in what I say, I am ready to tear your entire city up from its foundations.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα ὑμᾶς καταπλήξεται
source_issues.issue: The purpose clause is printed with the future indicative καταπλήξεται after ἵνα rather than the more classically expected subjunctive. The selected edition’s reading is construed provisionally as later Greek syntax supporting a purpose clause; no emendation is required for a defensible translation, and the feature is not treated as an OCR defect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: set foot in Berytus
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιβαίνω with the genitive can denote entering or setting foot in a place; “Berytus” preserves the ancient city name rather than modernizing it to Beirut.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τὸν σεισμὸν αὐτὸς ἐποίησεν ἡμῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: He himself brought the earthquake upon us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative ἡμῖν presents the earthquake as something caused for or against the speakers; “upon us” conveys the hostile result.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that he might overawe you
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταπλήσσω can denote terrifying, stunning, or overwhelming with amazement. “Overawe” fits the accusation that Peter is using wonders to induce a false perception of divinity. The purpose interpretation of the printed future indicative after ἵνα is contextually defensible but remains provisional.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though he himself were a god
lexical_decisions.rationale: The anarthrous predicate θεός permits “a god,” while “God” is also possible in the work’s monotheistic setting. The chosen wording preserves the accusers’ comparison without identifying Peter with the supreme God unambiguously.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ὑπὲρ δύναμιν ἀνθρωπίνην δυναμένου τοῦ Πέτρου
lexical_decisions.chosen: alleging that he possessed power beyond human capacity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ὡς construction presents this superhuman ability as the content or guise of Simon’s party’s false allegations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with startling boldness
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρρησία denotes open, confident speech, while καταπληκτική marks its astonishing or overwhelming effect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to tear your entire city up from its foundations
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκβαθρεύω evokes uprooting or razing down to the foundations, an image stronger than simply “destroy.”

passages.text: When the crowds became frightened and promised to act otherwise as they might be commanded by him, Peter said, “None of you is to associate with these sorcerers or mingle with them.” As soon as the crowds heard the brief command, they picked up sticks and pursued them until they had driven them completely out of the city. Then the sick and demon-possessed among them came in and threw themselves at Peter’s feet. But when he saw this and wished to dispel their consternation, he said to them:

source_issues.source_quote: ἑτέρως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται
source_issues.issue: The printed adverb ἑτέρως (“differently” or “otherwise”) produces a compressed connection with the following relative clause, but it can defensibly mean that the crowds promised to change their conduct in conformity with his commands. The smoother ἑτοίμως (“readily”) is only a possible conjecture and has not been used in the translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἑτοίμως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: promised to act otherwise as they might be commanded by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἑτέρως is taken in its normal sense, “differently” or “otherwise,” indicating a promised change of conduct in accordance with Peter’s commands. The connection with the following relative clause is compressed but yields a defensible contextual sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with these sorcerers
lexical_decisions.rationale: γόης can denote a sorcerer, charlatan, or impostor. “Sorcerers” fits the immediately preceding accusation of magic, though “charlatans” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the brief command
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύντομος characterizes the command as concise or terse; “brief” preserves its form without adding an emotional tone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they picked up sticks
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξύλα literally denotes pieces of wood; in the pursuit scene, “sticks” expresses their likely use without specifying weapons more precisely than the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the sick and demon-possessed among them
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτῶν most naturally refers to the crowds, though grammatically it could be heard as a possessive “their.” “Among them” avoids implying that the crowds owned or controlled the afflicted people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to dispel their consternation
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατάπληξις can be amazement, shock, or terror. In the aftermath of Peter’s threat and the people’s prostration, “consternation” preserves both alarm and astonishment.

passages.text: If I were able to cause earthquakes and to do anything at all I wish, I am not saying that I would annihilate Simon together with his companions—for I have not been sent to bring destruction on human beings—but I would make him my friend, so that, by slandering my true proclamation, he might not hinder many on their way to salvation. But if you believe me, he himself is a magician, he himself a slanderer, he himself a servant of evil against those who do not know the truth. And for this reason he can produce diseases in those who sin, having those who sin as partners in the power directed against them. But I am a servant of God, who made all things, and a disciple of his right-side prophet. Therefore, as that prophet’s apostle, I speak the truth. For in serving what is good, I also drive diseases away. For I was sent second, since disease goes first and healing follows. Thus, through that magician who does evil, having disbelieved God, you became ill; but through me, if you believe him, you will be healed. For in this way, having experienced power and turned to doing good, you might also be able to be saved in your souls.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐάν τε αὐτῷ πιστεύσητε
source_issues.issue: The postpositive τε has no explicit correlative in the printed construction. It can provisionally be read as a weak connective whose force is absorbed into the coordinated contrast, so no correction is required.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Σίμωνα οὐ λέγω ὅτι μετὰ τῶν αὐτοῦ ἑταίρων ἐξωλόθρευον
lexical_decisions.chosen: I am not saying that I would annihilate Simon together with his companions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect ἐξωλόθρευον functions as the unreal result of the preceding condition; “annihilate” preserves its intensive destructive force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he himself a slanderer
lexical_decisions.rationale: διάβολος can mean “slanderer” or “devil.” The nearby cognate διαβάλλων (“slandering”) supports the common-noun sense, while “he himself a devil” remains a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he can produce diseases in those who sin
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁμαρτάνουσι is taken as a dative plural participle, anticipated by τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας. Morphologically it could instead be finite—“they sin”—with a sentence break after it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συνεργοὺς ἔχων τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας τῆς κατ’ αὐτῶν δυνάμεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: having those who sin as partners in the power directed against them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The sinners paradoxically cooperate in the power exercised against them; the rendering preserves both the partnership and the hostile direction of the power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a disciple of his right-side prophet
lexical_decisions.rationale: δεξιοῦ modifies “prophet” and marks him as right or right-sided. “Right-hand prophet” is possible, but may suggest merely a trusted assistant; replacing it with “true prophet” would erase the printed wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as that prophet’s apostle
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκείνου most naturally refers to the immediately preceding prophet. Reference to God is grammatically possible but less immediate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For in serving what is good
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival ἀγαθῷ may denote goodness or a good person, including “the Good One.” The neutral wording preserves the contrast with serving evil without fixing the referent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For I was sent second
lexical_decisions.rationale: δεύτερος indicates his position in the sequence subsequently explained: disease precedes and healing follows.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if you believe him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronoun is retained in English. God is the most likely antecedent because this belief contrasts with τῷ θεῷ ἀπιστήσαντες, though the magician is grammatically nearer.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having experienced power
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival δυνατοῦ can denote what is powerful or “the Powerful One.” The main rendering expresses the experience of power without fixing a personal referent; “having experienced the Powerful One” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you might also be able to be saved in your souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνασωθῆναι is passive, so the addressees do not actively save their own souls. The rendering takes τὰς ψυχὰς as an accusative of respect—“as regards your souls”—and preserves the contrast with the preceding bodily healing; “you might also be able to have your souls rescued” is a possible but less direct English formulation.

passages.text: As he was saying these things, they all lay kneeling at his feet. He, however, raised his hands toward heaven, prayed to God, and healed them all by prayer alone. After remaining with the people of Beirut for quite a few days, accustoming many to monarchical worship and baptizing them, and appointing as their bishop one of the elders who followed him, he departed for Byblos. When he arrived there and learned that Simon had not stayed with them for even one day but had immediately hurried to Tripolis, he stayed with them for a few days, healed quite a few people, and trained them in the books; then he traveled to Tripolis in Simon’s tracks, having chosen to pursue him rather than flee from him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γονυπετεῖς πρὸ τῶν αὐτοῦ ἔκειντο ποδῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they all lay kneeling at his feet
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves both ἔκειντο, “lay,” and γονυπετεῖς, “kneeling” or “fallen on the knees.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: accustoming many to monarchical worship
