lexical_decisions.rationale: θρησκεία can mean worship, religious observance, or religion, while μοναρχική evokes sole rule or sovereignty. “The religion of sole rule” is a possible more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: appointing as their bishop one
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίσκοπος literally denotes an overseer, but “bishop” fits the explicitly appointed community office in this historical narrative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the people of Beirut
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek uses the civic demonym rather than the city name; the rendering makes that reference explicit in conventional English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: trained them in the books
lexical_decisions.rationale: The definite plural βίβλοις is retained as “the books”; the source does not explicitly identify them as Scripture.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in Simon’s tracks
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the source’s physical trail or footprint image rather than reducing it to the abstract “after Simon.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to pursue him rather than flee from him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between continuing the pursuit and withdrawing or slipping away; “flee from him” gives the natural English opposition.

passages.text: As Peter was entering Tripolis, many of those more eager to learn, from Tyre and Sidon as well as Beirut and Byblos and the neighboring districts, were entering with him. Especially, too, crowds from the city itself were converging, wishing to question him. So in the suburbs we were met by the brothers whom he had sent out to ascertain precisely both the other matters concerning the city and what Simon was doing, so that they might return and give an account. They welcomed him and led him to the house of Maroones.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those more eager to learn
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative describes people especially fond of learning; “the more inquisitive” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wishing to question him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορεῖν with a personal object can mean to inquire of or question someone, rather than merely to learn about that person.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what Simon was doing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative may denote Simon's activities or affairs; “what was happening with Simon” is a viable broader rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they might return and give an account
lexical_decisions.rationale: The motion is understood contextually as coming back to Peter after their fact-finding mission; more literally, “so that, having come, they might explain.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: led him to the house of Maroones
lexical_decisions.rationale: Μαροόνου is treated as the genitive of the personal name Μαροόνης, transliterated Maroones.

passages.text: When he had already reached the very gate of the guesthouse, he turned to the crowds and promised to speak with them about reverence for God after the coming night. When he entered, the advance party prepared lodging for those who had gathered. Nor did those who received and hosted them fall short of the eagerness of those asking to host them. Peter knew nothing of these arrangements, and when we invited him to partake of food, he said that he himself would not partake before those who had come with him had found rest. We answered, “This has already been accomplished as follows: making their affection for you their plea, people received all of them with such eagerness that those who had obtained no one to host were exceedingly grieved.” When Peter heard this, he was delighted; and after blessing them for their prompt kindness, he went out, bathed in the sea, came back inside, partook of food with the advance party, and, as evening came on, went to sleep.

source_issues.source_quote: μετὰ τὴν ἐπιοῦσαν
source_issues.issue: The omitted noun creates a genuine temporal ambiguity. Supplying the conventional ἡμέραν gives “after the following day,” while the narrative sequence supports supplying νύκτα, “after the coming night.” No textual alteration is proposed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπ’ αὐτῷ τῷ τῆς ξενίας πυλῶνι
lexical_decisions.chosen: at the very gate of the guesthouse
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία can denote hospitality, lodging, or guest quarters; the mention of a gate favors a place of lodging.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after the coming night
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine adjective has an omitted noun. Although ἡ ἐπιοῦσα often means “the following day,” the subsequent evening, sleep, and expectation of an address “today” favor understanding an ensuing night here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the advance party
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes those sent ahead, identified later as the twelve who had gone in advance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the eagerness of those asking to host them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object of ἀξιούντων is unstated. The subsequent grief of people who obtained no guests supports understanding these as prospective hosts asking to receive travelers. Alternatively, the phrase may mean “the eagerness of those requesting hospitality or lodging,” referring to travelers or those arranging lodging for them; “those who considered it an honor” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who had come with him had found rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative αὐτῷ is taken as associative with συνεληλυθότας, identifying those who had accompanied or joined Peter, rather than people assembled for his benefit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: making their affection for you their plea
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can mean a pretext, plea, or stated reason; “plea” preserves the expressed motive without necessarily implying insincerity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for their prompt kindness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “keen” or “swift benevolence”; the context emphasizes the speed and eagerness of their hospitality.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as evening came on, went to sleep
lexical_decisions.rationale: The image is of evening overtaking or coming upon the situation; idiomatic English uses “came on.”

passages.text: At about the second crowing of the roosters, he awoke and found us awake. All of us with him numbered sixteen: Peter himself, I, Clement, Nicetas and Aquila, and the twelve who had gone ahead. After greeting us, he said, “Today, since we are not devoting our time to those outside, we are free for one another. Therefore I will recount to you what happened after the departure from Tyre, and you tell me what Simon has done here and explain it in greater detail.” After we had exchanged our accounts in turn, one of the companions presented a report to Peter, saying, “Simon, having learned that you had arrived, set out on the road toward Syria. The crowds have regarded this one night as a year's span and are unable to wait for the time appointed by you. They are standing before the doors in clusters and gatherings, talking with one another about Simon's slander. They say that after raising their expectations and promising that, when you came, he would expose you as guilty of many evils, he learned that you had arrived and fled by night. But as they long to hear you, a certain rumor—I do not know from where—has fallen upon them that you are going to speak with them today. Therefore, so that they do not wear themselves out for a long time only to disperse to no purpose, you yourself know what you ought to do.”

source_issues.source_quote: εἰσήγει τις τῶν συνήθων ἀπαγγέλλων Πέτρῳ
source_issues.issue: The verified print reads εἰσήγει. It is provisionally analyzed as the imperfect of εἰσηγέω, “introduce” or “present,” rather than silently normalized to εἰσῄει, “was coming in.” Because the object of εἰσήγει is implicit, “presented a report” is contextual; “introduced the matter, reporting to Peter” is a viable alternative.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῦ-Σίμωνος
source_issues.issue: The supplied print has a hyphen between the article and the name. It has no evident syntactic or lexical function and is provisionally treated as an editorial or line-division feature rather than as part of the name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ δὲ τὰς δευτέρας τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων φωνὰς
lexical_decisions.chosen: At about the second crowing of the roosters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural phrase refers to the second cockcrow or round of rooster calls; ὑπό here marks approximate time.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since we are not devoting our time to those outside
lexical_decisions.rationale: σχολάζω with the dative means to be occupied with or devote time to someone; τοῖς ἔξω may mean outsiders generally or, in context, the people physically outside.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀμειψαμένων οὖν ἀλλήλους ταῖς ἐν μέρει διηγήσεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: After we had exchanged our accounts in turn
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν μέρει indicates narration by turns, with each side giving its account.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰσήγει τις τῶν συνήθων ἀπαγγέλλων Πέτρῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: one of the companions presented a report to Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed εἰσήγει is taken as an imperfect of εἰσηγέω, “introduce” or “present,” while ἀπαγγέλλων Πέτρῳ identifies the action as reporting to Peter. The object of εἰσήγει is implicit; “introduced the matter, reporting to Peter” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: set out on the road toward Syria
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπί with the accusative expresses direction toward Syria; ὁρμάω conveys setting out energetically.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Simon's slander
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαβολή can mean slander, accusation, or calumny; the ensuing claim against Peter supports “slander.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: raising their expectations
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετεωρίζω can mean to lift up, excite, or keep in suspense; the promised confrontation has heightened their expectations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: expose you as guilty of many evils
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐλέγχειν may mean expose, convict, or refute, while ἐπὶ πολλοῖς κακοῖς states the alleged wrongs on which the exposure would rest.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a certain rumor ... has fallen upon them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves the source's image of a rumor falling upon or overtaking the crowd; “has reached them” would be more idiomatic.

lexical_decisions.chosen: disperse to no purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀλόγως can mean unreasonably, pointlessly, or without due cause; the concern is that their prolonged waiting might prove futile.

passages.text: And Peter, marveling at the crowds' eagerness, answered, “See, brothers, how our Lord's words are visibly being fulfilled. For I remember him saying, ‘Many will come from east and west, north and south, and will recline in the bosoms of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.’ But he also says, ‘Many are called, but few are chosen.’ Thus the part about their coming when called has been fulfilled. But since this is not their own doing, but God's—‘the one who called’ them and caused them to come—they have no reward for this alone, because it is not their own doing but belongs to the one who brought it about. But if, after being called, they do good deeds, which is their own doing, then they will have a reward for this.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν λόγοι ἐμφανῶς τελοῦνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: our Lord's words are visibly being fulfilled
lexical_decisions.rationale: τελοῦνται denotes being accomplished or fulfilled, while ἐμφανῶς stresses that the fulfillment is evident.

lexical_decisions.chosen: north and south
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄρκτος, literally “the Bear,” denotes the north, while μεσημβρία, literally “midday,” denotes the south.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will recline in the bosoms
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the banquet image of reclining and the unusual plural κόλπους; “at the breastsides” or “in the embraces” would interpret the image more strongly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ μὲν οὖν ἐλθεῖν αὐτοὺς κληθέντας πεπλήρωται
lexical_decisions.chosen: the part about their coming when called has been fulfilled
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive identifies their coming in response to being called as the element already fulfilled.

lexical_decisions.chosen: this is not their own doing
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιον marks what belongs distinctively to them; “doing” fits the contrast with God's action and their later good deeds.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who called
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source itself marks this phrase as a quotation, so the quotation is retained rather than absorbed into the surrounding clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who brought it about
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνεργέω here refers to the agent who effected their coming, not merely one who was active in a general sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: do good deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase refers to performing morally good actions, in contrast with merely responding to the divine call.

passages.text: “For not even Hebrews who believe Moses while not keeping what was said through him are saved, unless they keep what was said to them. For even the fact that they believed Moses did not arise from their own decision, but from God, who said to Moses, ‘Look, I myself am coming to you in a pillar of cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking to you and may believe you forever.’ Therefore, since for both Hebrews and those called from the nations, believing teachers of truth has come from God, while good deeds have been left to each person to perform according to that person's own judgment, the reward is rightly paid to those who do good. For there would have been no need either for Moses or for Jesus's coming, if indeed they were willing to understand what is reasonable on their own; nor does salvation come about by believing teachers and calling them lords.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δι’ αὐτοῦ ῥηθέντα μὴ φυλάσσοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: while not keeping what was said through him
lexical_decisions.rationale: φυλάσσω here means to observe or obey what was spoken, while διά presents Moses as the one through whom it was communicated.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the fact that they believed Moses
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive makes their belief in Moses the subject of the clause; πιστεύω with the dative can mean believe or trust someone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: did not arise from their own decision
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουλή may mean counsel, purpose, or decision; “decision” best expresses the contrast with God's initiative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a pillar of cloud
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording specifically presents a pillar of cloud and is not replaced by a more familiar rendering from another textual form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those called from the nations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase identifies people called from among the nations; “Gentiles who were called” is a viable idiomatic alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: believing teachers of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative construction denotes placing belief or trust in teachers characterized as teachers of truth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν καλῶν πράξεων ἰδίᾳ κρίσει ἑκάστῳ ποιεῖν ἀπολελειμμένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: good deeds have been left to each person to perform according to that person's own judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction contrasts divinely produced belief with actions left to each individual's κρίσις, which may also be rendered “choice” or “decision.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Jesus's coming
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρουσία can denote presence, arrival, or coming; the contrast with the need for Moses favors Jesus's historical coming, though “the presence of Jesus” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what is reasonable
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective used substantivally denotes what accords with reason; “the reasonable course” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calling them lords
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural κυρίους may mean lords or masters. “Lords” preserves the source's title-like wording and its application to the teachers under discussion.

passages.text: For this reason, Jesus is concealed from the Hebrews who have received Moses as teacher, while Moses is hidden from those who have trusted Jesus; for since the teaching through both is one, God accepts the person who has trusted either of them. But trusting a teacher is for the sake of doing the things spoken by God. That this is so, our Lord himself says: “I praise you, Father of heaven and earth, because you hid these things from wise elders and revealed them to nursing infants.” Thus God himself hid a teacher from some, since they already knew what must be done, but revealed one to others, since they did not know what they ought to do.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have trusted Jesus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect of πιστεύω with a personal object can denote placing trust in someone; “believed Jesus” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I praise you
lexical_decisions.rationale: In an address to God, ἐξομολογοῦμαι can express praise or thanksgiving rather than confession; “I give thanks to you” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wise elders
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both terms are retained as printed rather than harmonized with a familiar form of the quotation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since they already knew
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context contrasts prior knowledge of what to do with ignorance; the more formally temporal “since they had known beforehand” remains possible.

passages.text: As Peter was saying these things, the crowds entered the place where he was, as though summoned by someone. When he saw the large crowd flowing gently in like the quiet current of a river, he said to Maroones, “Where around here do you have a place better able to hold the crowds?” When Maroones led him on to an outdoor place laid out as a garden, the crowds followed. Peter took his stand on the not very high pedestal of a statue and, immediately upon greeting the crowd according to a devout custom, knowing that many among the crowds present had for many years been tormented by demons and numerous afflictions, gnashing their teeth amid wailing and falling down in supplication, he rebuked them and ordered them to remain quiet. Then, after promising healing once he had delivered his discourse, he began to speak as follows:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ ποταμοῦ ἥσυχον ῥεῦμα πράως προσρέοντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: flowing gently in like the quiet current of a river
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparison presents the approaching crowd as a calm river current rather than as a violent rush.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Maroones
lexical_decisions.rationale: The name is transliterated from its dative form; the corresponding nominative is Μαροόνης.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an outdoor place laid out as a garden
lexical_decisions.rationale: κεκηπευμένον describes a place cultivated or arranged as a garden; “a cultivated open-air place” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gnashing their teeth amid wailing
lexical_decisions.rationale: βρύχω commonly describes gnashing, though “roaring” or “growling” is lexically possible in this depiction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once he had delivered his discourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive-form verb is used in the deponent sense of speaking or discoursing; “after he had spoken” is a less specific alternative.

passages.text: As I begin to deliver the discourse concerning reverence for God to people who know nothing at all and whose minds have been stained by the slanders of Simon, our opponent, I have thought it necessary first to deliver a discourse on why one must not blame God, who made everything. I begin nowhere else than from the very occasion that he himself providentially presented at the opportune moment, so that it may be known that with good reason many people have been held fast by many demons and overtaken by strange afflictions, in order that in this too God’s justice may become apparent; and so that those who blame him through ignorance, even now, after learning how they ought to think, may call themselves back from their former accusation by speaking well and doing good, offering ignorance—the cause of their wicked audacity—as grounds for pardon.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἀντικειμένου ἡμῖν Σίμωνος διαβολῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by the slanders of Simon, our opponent
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive construction identifies Simon as the one opposing the speakers and as the source of the slanders.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπ᾽ αὐτῆς τῆς κατὰ πρόνοιαν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ εὐκαίρως ὑποβληθείσης προφάσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the very occasion that he himself providentially presented at the opportune moment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις here can denote an occasion or starting point, not necessarily a deceptive pretext; αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with good reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb asserts that the demonic and physical afflictions occurred on reasonable or justifiable grounds, rather than merely describing them as intelligible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: may call themselves back from their former accusation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording can depict withdrawal from their prior accusation against God. Alternatively, ἔγκλημα may denote the charge or culpability they incurred, yielding “extricate themselves from their former charge.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by speaking well and doing good
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the parallel between favorable speech and beneficial action; “through praise and good works” is also possible.

passages.text: The matter is as follows: when the only good God had made everything well and handed it over to the human being who had come into being according to his image, the one who had come into being, breathing the divinity of the one who made him, being a true prophet and knowing all things, in honor of the father who had given him everything and for the salvation of the sons who came from him, as a genuine father preserving his goodwill toward the children brought into being by him, and wishing them, for their own benefit, to love God and be loved by him, revealed the road that leads to friendship with him. He taught by what human actions the sole God and Master of all rejoices; and, after declaring the things pleasing to him, he established an eternal law for all, one that cannot be burned up by war, is not secretly adulterated by any impious person, and is not hidden in a single place, but can be read by everyone. Consequently, through obedience to the law, everything was abundant for them: the finest fruits, the full span of years free from pain and disease, all securely bestowed along with every temperate condition of the air.

source_issues.source_quote: μήτε ἐνὶ τόπῳ ἀποκεκρυμμένον
source_issues.issue: The supplied print has smooth-breathing ἐνὶ, which can be the extended preposition “in,” giving “not hidden away in a place.” The main rendering provisionally takes it in the contextual numeral/locative sense “in a single place,” for which the usual numeral form would be ἑνὶ. The contrast with “but can be read by everyone” supports that interpretation, but does not make it certain. This is a disclosed printed orthographic and lexical ambiguity, not an asserted OCR defect or an unresolved loss of source content.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παραδεδωκότος τῷ κατ᾽ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ γενομένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: handed it over to the human being who had come into being according to his image
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραδίδωμι here denotes handing over or entrusting the created order, while κατ᾽ εἰκόνα is retained as “according to his image.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ πεποιηκότος αὐτὸν πνέων θειότητος
lexical_decisions.chosen: breathing the divinity of the one who made him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual genitive construction is preserved without resolving whether πνέων means breathing in, breathing forth, or manifesting the maker’s divinity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the sons who came from him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase uses ἐξ αὐτοῦ to express origin from him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ γενομένους παῖδας
lexical_decisions.chosen: toward the children brought into being by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Unlike the preceding ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ marks agency, so the observable distinction is retained without implying that the phrases necessarily identify different groups.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πρὸς φιλίαν αὐτοῦ ἄγουσαν ἐξέφηνεν ὁδόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: revealed the road that leads to friendship with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to God; “his friendship” is possible but less explicit about the direction of the road.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he established an eternal law for all
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῖς ὅλοις may refer to all people or to the whole created order; the inclusive “for all” preserves that breadth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μήτε πολέμῳ ἐμπρησθῆναι δυνάμενον μήθ᾽ ὑπὸ ἀσεβοῦς τινὸς ὑπονοθευόμενον μήτε ἐνὶ τόπῳ ἀποκεκρυμμένον, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ἀναγνωσθῆναι δυνάμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: one that cannot be burned up by war, is not secretly adulterated by any impious person, and is not hidden in a single place, but can be read by everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The inability expressed by δυνάμενον is attached explicitly to being burned, while the next two participles describe separately negated states. The final δυνάμενον expressly states the law’s ability to be read by everyone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is not secretly adulterated by any impious person
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπονοθεύω denotes covert falsification, adulteration, or interpolation; “is not covertly tampered with” is a broader alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a single place
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering provisionally understands printed ἐνὶ in the numeral/locative sense associated with ἑνί, because concealment in one particular place contrasts directly with the law’s being readable by everyone. As printed, however, ἐνὶ can instead be the extended preposition “in,” yielding “in a place”; that alternative remains viable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ τῶν ἐτῶν τέλεια καὶ ἄλυπα καὶ ἄνοσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the full span of years free from pain and disease
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression is elliptical; it can denote complete years or a full lifetime, characterized as painless and healthy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ πάσης τῆς τῶν ἀέρων εὐκρασίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: along with every temperate condition of the air
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐκρασία denotes a favorable balance or temperateness, while the plural ἀέρων can encompass atmospheric or climatic conditions.

passages.text: But because they had not first experienced evils, they were insensible to the gift of good things and, through plentiful nourishment and luxury, were turning toward ingratitude, so that they thought there was no providence at all, since they had received the good things as a reward without first laboring for righteousness. For none of them had fallen under any affliction, sickness, or other necessity, so that—as people are inclined to do when distressed by grievous misfortune—they might look around for the God able to heal them. But in fact, immediately after the contempt born of their fearlessness and carefree luxury, a just punishment met them, as though following from a certain harmoniously ordered sequence: it thrust away the good things as having harmed them and brought in the evils in exchange as having benefited them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ μὴ πρότερον καμόντες ἐπὶ δικαιοσύνης· ὡς μισθὸν τὰ ἀγαθὰ εἰλήφεσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: since they had received the good things as a reward without first laboring for righteousness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed punctuation and word order favor taking μή with καμόντες: the good things were received without prior righteous labor. A broader scope for μή, “since they had not received the good things as a reward after first laboring for righteousness,” is also grammatically possible and likewise emphasizes that the benefits were unearned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when distressed by grievous misfortune
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαμαρτία can denote a failure, reverse, or misfortune; “grievous misfortune” fits the affliction-and-healing context without specifying its nature more narrowly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ ἐξ ἁρμονίας τινὸς ἀκολούθως ἐφηρμοσμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: as though following from a certain harmoniously ordered sequence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording depicts punishment as emerging in due succession from an arrangement whose parts have been fitted together harmoniously.

passages.text: For among the spirits inhabiting heaven, the angels dwelling in the lowest region, distressed at humanity’s ingratitude toward God, ask to enter human life, so that, by becoming humans in reality and exposing through their higher way of life those who had been ungrateful to him, they might there and then subject each one to the punishment deserved. When, then, they received what they had asked for, they changed themselves into every kind of nature, since they were of a more divine substance and could readily turn themselves into anything. They became a precious stone, a much-admired pearl, perhaps the most beautiful purple, renowned gold, and every sort of costly material. They fell into the hands of some people and into the laps of others and willingly allowed themselves to be stolen by them. They also changed into four-footed animals, reptiles, swimming creatures, winged creatures, and anything else they wished. Your poets also sing of these things at random because they have no fear, attributing to a single being the many and varied deeds of them all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν γὰρ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἐνοικούντων πνευμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: For among the spirits inhabiting heaven
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial γάρ explicitly presents the angels’ intervention as an explanation of the punishment introduced in the preceding section.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through their higher way of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here denotes conduct or a way of life, and the following section says that the angels intended to demonstrate the possibility of pious conduct. The comparative may alternatively mean “more extensive” rather than “higher.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: perhaps the most beautiful purple
lexical_decisions.rationale: πορφύρα may denote purple material or dye, while εἰ τύχοι introduces it as a possible example, literally “if it should happen.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: sing of these things at random because they have no fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀφοβία literally denotes fearlessness but can imply brazen audacity here; ὡς ἔτυχεν means without careful discrimination, “as it happens” or “at random.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνὶ τοίνυν τὰς πάντων πολλὰς καὶ διαφόρους πράξεις ἀπονέμοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: attributing to a single being the many and varied deeds of them all
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνί means “to one”; “being” is supplied only to make the otherwise unspecified singular referent intelligible in English.

passages.text: However, when by becoming these things they had exposed as greedy those who seized them, they changed themselves into human nature so that, after living piously and showing that such conduct was possible, they might subject the ungrateful to an accounting. But because they truly became human in every respect and acquired human desire, they were overcome by it and slipped into intercourse with women. Once entangled with them, congealed by defilement, and completely emptied of their original power, they were not strong enough to recombine their limbs, which had been transformed from fire, into the original undefiled state of their own nature. For under the weight of their fire, which through desire had ended in flesh, they traveled the impious road downward. Fettered by bonds of flesh, they have been held down and tightly bound; for this reason they could no longer ascend into the heavens.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον· μετασυγκρῖναι οὐκ ἐξίσχυσαν.
source_issues.issue: The supplied edition prints a high stop before the delayed infinitive μετασυγκρῖναι. The translation provisionally treats this as an editorial or rhetorical break rather than as a boundary preventing εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον from expressing the state into which they could not recombine their limbs. The printed punctuation is verified and is not treated as an OCR defect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ ὄντως τὰ πάντα ἄνθρωποι ἐγίνοντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: because they truly became human in every respect
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative τὰ πάντα functions adverbially, indicating complete rather than merely apparent participation in human nature.

lexical_decisions.chosen: congealed by defilement
lexical_decisions.rationale: παγέντες evokes being fixed, congealed, or solidified. “Made fast by defilement” remains a viable less specific alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἐκ πυρὸς τραπέντα μέλη εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον· μετασυγκρῖναι οὐκ ἐξίσχυσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they were not strong enough to recombine their limbs, which had been transformed from fire, into the original undefiled state of their own nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English makes restoration into the original state the unaccomplished result of μετασυγκρῖναι, not the result of the earlier transformation from fire. The supplied high stop before μετασυγκρῖναι makes the attachment visually unusual, so this interpretation remains provisional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ γὰρ βάρει τῷ ὑπὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας εἰς σάρκα τελευτήσαντος αὐτῶν τοῦ πυρός
lexical_decisions.chosen: For under the weight of their fire, which through desire had ended in flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive participle τελευτήσαντος qualifies τοῦ πυρός: their fire had ended in flesh through desire, and its resulting weight bears them downward. The repeated article links the genitive qualification to “weight”; the wording does not make that weight the cause of the transformation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have been held down
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect middle-passive form is understood from κατέχω, “hold” or “restrain.” In context it parallels being fettered and tightly bound.

passages.text: For after intercourse, when they were asked for what they had become at first and were no longer able to furnish it—because after defilement they could not turn themselves into anything else—and because they wished to please their beloved women, they showed them, in place of themselves, the marrows of the earth, by which I mean the blooms from mines: gold, copper, silver, iron, and the like, together with all the most precious stones. So to those bewitched by these stones they also handed down the crafts for the operations relating to each one; they disclosed practices of magic, taught astronomy, the powers of roots, and whatever could never be discovered by human thought, and furthermore the casting of gold, silver, and similar materials, as well as the many-colored dyeing of garments. Simply put, everything that serves women’s adornment and pleasure is an invention of the demons bound in flesh.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For after intercourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial γάρ explicitly presents this account as an explanation and elaboration of the loss of transformative power described in the preceding section.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when they were asked for what they had become at first
lexical_decisions.rationale: The request concerns their former transformations into precious materials, which they could no longer reproduce after their defilement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the marrows of the earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal anatomical image is retained and immediately explained by the author as metals and precious stones extracted from mines.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὖν τούτοις δὲ τοῖς μαγευθεῖσιν λίθοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: So to those bewitched by these stones
lexical_decisions.rationale: The article with μαγευθεῖσιν is taken substantivally for the recipients, while τούτοις λίθοις identifies the stones by which they were bewitched. A less likely alternative makes all the dative forms one phrase, “these enchanted stones,” but that leaves the dative’s relationship to “handed down” less clear.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τέχνας τῶν πρὸς ἕκαστα πραγμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the crafts for the operations relating to each one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed phrase refers to technical arts associated with working or using what had just been listed; “each one” may refer to each material or to each corresponding operation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάνθ’ ἁπλῶς ὅσαπερ πρὸς κόσμου καὶ τέρψεώς ἐστι γυναικῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Simply put, everything that serves women’s adornment and pleasure
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόσμος here means ornament or adornment rather than the physical world.

passages.text: And so the humans associated with them then sought for the first time to do the same. Thus we are not born either good or evil; rather, we become so, and once habituated, we are hard to draw away. When the nonrational animals then ran out, the humans of mixed birth also tasted human flesh. For destroying their own flesh was no longer far removed from them, since they had previously tasted it in other forms.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ δὲ οὖν αὐτοῖς ἄνθρωποι τὸ ὅμοιον τότε πρῶτον ποιεῖν ἐζήλωσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the humans associated with them then sought for the first time to do the same
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes αὐτοῖς with ἄνθρωποι, marking the humans’ association with the previously mentioned beings. Alternatively, αὐτοῖς may identify the model of τὸ ὅμοιον: “And so humans then first sought to do the same as they did.” The associative reading is retained because of the placement of αὐτοῖς beside ἄνθρωποι, but the comparative attachment is also viable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once habituated, we are hard to draw away
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression depicts established habits as difficult to break; more literally, “having become accustomed, we are in a state difficult to detach.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the humans of mixed birth
lexical_decisions.rationale: νόθοι denotes illegitimate or mixed parentage here, referring to the hybrid origin described in the surrounding narrative; “bastard humans” would be more blunt.

lexical_decisions.chosen: destroying their own flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves the source’s image. In context, “their own flesh” likely means human flesh belonging to their own kind rather than their individual bodies.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since they had previously tasted it in other forms
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronoun refers back to flesh, presenting animal flesh as that same flesh under different forms; the unusual conceptual identification is retained.

passages.text: Because of the great outpouring of blood, the pure air was defiled by an impure exhalation and became diseased, making those who breathed it sickly, so that thereafter people died prematurely. The earth, being severely defiled by these things, then for the first time spewed out venomous and destructive creatures. Since everything had consequently moved toward the worse because of the beastlike demons, God planned to remove them like bad leaven, lest, from evil seed, each successive generation should become like the one before it, act impiously in the same way, and empty the coming age of men who would be saved. For precisely this reason, after announcing beforehand to one righteous man that he was to be preserved in a chest with the three born from him, together with their wives and all the rest, God sent water flooding in as a deluge, so that, once everything had been destroyed, the world, thoroughly purged, might be returned clean to the one preserved in the chest for a second beginning of life. And indeed, so it happened.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by an impure exhalation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναθυμίασις denotes vapor or exhalation; “impure” preserves the contrast with the previously “pure” air.

lexical_decisions.chosen: died prematurely
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄωρος describes death occurring before its proper time; “died young” is possible but more narrowly age-specific.

lexical_decisions.chosen: venomous and destructive creatures
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰοβόλα literally suggests creatures that cast or inject venom, while λυμαντικά describes those that ravage or cause harm.

lexical_decisions.chosen: men who would be saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle can denote men receiving preservation or salvation. “Surviving men” is possible in the flood context, but the coming-age language supports the broader rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a chest
lexical_decisions.rationale: λάρναξ is a chest, coffer, or container and is not the usual Septuagint term for Noah’s ark. “In an ark” is contextually possible but would obscure the source’s distinct word choice.

lexical_decisions.chosen: together with all the rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source leaves the referent of “the rest” unstated, likely the other beings preserved in the flood vessel; the translation does not supply an explicit noun.

passages.text: Since the souls of the dead giants were larger than human souls—since the giants also surpassed humans in bodily size—they were designated, as a new race, by a new name as well. For these newcomers to the world, a law prescribing how they must live was laid down by God through an angel. For since they were hybrid in origin, from the fire of angels and the blood of women, and for that reason were destined to desire a certain race of their own, they were forestalled by a certain just law. For an angel was sent out to them by God, disclosing his will and saying:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἱ τῶν τεθνεώτων γιγάντων ψυχαὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπείων ψυχῶν μείζους ἦσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the souls of the dead giants were larger than human souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: μείζους may mean “greater” or “larger”; the following appeal to bodily size favors the spatial sense while retaining the author’s unusual claim about souls.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτε δὴ καὶ τοῖς σώμασιν ὑπερέχουσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the giants also surpassed humans in bodily size
lexical_decisions.rationale: Grammatically the feminine participle refers to the souls, yielding the more literal but difficult “since they also surpassed them with respect to bodies.” The contextual rendering understands the bodily comparison as one between giants and humans.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς καινὸν γένος καινῷ καὶ τῷ ὀνόματι προσηγορεύθησαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they were designated, as a new race, by a new name as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσηγορεύθησαν concerns being called or designated; the source does not state the new name in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for these newcomers to the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπήλυτος denotes one who has come from elsewhere, hence an alien, immigrant, or newcomer; “newcomers” best fits their newly arising race.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were destined to desire a certain race of their own
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένος can mean race, kind, or class. The object of their anticipated desire remains unusual and underspecified, so the translation retains “race” rather than supplying what that desire entails.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they were forestalled by a certain just law
lexical_decisions.rationale: προλαμβάνω here presents the law as acting beforehand to anticipate or restrain their intended conduct; “were anticipated by” is more literal but less clear.

passages.text: For the temporary king once approached the king of our piety, not using force (for that was not permitted), but exhorting and persuading, because being persuaded lies within each person’s own power. So he approached as king of present things and said to the king of things to come, “All the kingdoms of the present world are subject to me; moreover, the gold and the silver and all the luxury of this world are under my authority. Therefore, fall down and worship me, and I will give you all these things.” He said this knowing that, with that act of worship, he would also have authority over him, and so the latter would deprive himself of the glory and kingdom to come. Knowing these things, the latter not only did not worship him, but did not even wish to take any of the things that had been given by him. For he would thereby have pledged himself as security together with what was his own—that is, from then on he would no longer be permitted even to touch any of the things returned to him. He therefore answered, “It is written: ‘You shall fear the Lord your God and serve him alone.’”

source_issues.source_quote: ταῦτα δὲ ἔλεγεν εἰδὼς ὅτι μετὰ τοῦ προσκυνῆσαι καὶ τὴν κατ’ αὐτοῦ εἶχεν ἐξουσίαν καὶ οὕτως τῆς μελλούσης δόξης καὶ βασιλείας ἑαυτὸν ἀφῄρει
source_issues.issue: The unexpressed subject of ἀφῄρει is materially ambiguous. The main text takes it to be the future king, who would deprive himself of the coming glory and kingdom by worshiping; alternatively, the subject may continue to be the temporary king from εἶχεν, despite the resulting contextual difficulty. This is a provisional contextual interpretation, not a correction of the supplied text.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δεδομένων λαβεῖν τι ἠθέλησεν
source_issues.issue: The perfect passive δεδομένων describes the things as already given by the temporary king, although his preceding direct speech promises, “I will give you all these things.” The translation preserves this shift in presentation rather than changing “given” to “offered.” The discourse relation is uncertain, but the printed wording is translatable without emendation.

source_issues.source_quote: ἑαυτὸν γὰρ σὺν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ κατενεχύραζεν, ὅπερ ἐστὶν μὴ ἐξεῖναι τοῦ λοιποῦ τῶν αὐτῷ ἀποδοθέντων μηδὲ ψαῦσαι ἔτι
source_issues.issue: The subject of κατενεχύραζεν and the referent of αὐτῷ are not explicit. The translation continues the future king as the implied subject and takes αὐτῷ as referring to him; alternatively, one or both may refer to the temporary king. The substantival τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ may denote his own things, possessions, or those belonging to him. The supplied construction is translatable without emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ γὰρ τῆς εὐσεβείας ἡμῶν βασιλεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the king of our piety
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the unusual genitive description rather than replacing it with a familiar Christological title.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the temporary king
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόσκαιρος marks limited duration and contrasts this ruler with the king of things to come.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τοῦ προσκυνῆσαι καὶ τὴν κατ’ αὐτοῦ εἶχεν ἐξουσίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: with that act of worship, he would also have authority over him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes the temporary king as the one who would have authority and the future king as the one placed under it; κατ’ αὐτοῦ can express authority directed against or over someone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως τῆς μελλούσης δόξης καὶ βασιλείας ἑαυτὸν ἀφῄρει
lexical_decisions.chosen: and so the latter would deprive himself of the glory and kingdom to come
lexical_decisions.rationale: Supplies the future king as the subject of ἀφῄρει because worship would cost him the coming glory and kingdom, although the Greek does not explicitly mark a change of subject.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δεδομένων λαβεῖν τι ἠθέλησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: but did not even wish to take any of the things that had been given by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the perfect passive gift-language of δεδομένων rather than replacing it with “offered,” despite the preceding promise being expressed in the future.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑαυτὸν γὰρ σὺν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ κατενεχύραζεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For he would thereby have pledged himself as security together with what was his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: Renders the security or pledge imagery of κατενεχύραζεν while leaving τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ broad enough to include his own things or those belonging to him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: You shall fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: Follows the supplied Greek rather than harmonizing the quotation with a familiar temptation narrative using “worship.”

passages.text: Nevertheless, after the king of the impious had tried in many ways to draw the king of the devout toward his own will and was unable, he ceased his effort to ensnare him in the remaining areas of his way of life. But you, because you were ignorant of the law laid down beforehand, came under his authority through evil deeds. Therefore, you were defiled in body and soul, and in the present you are abused by both sufferings and demons, while in what is to come you will have souls destined to be punished. You are not the only ones who have suffered this through ignorance, but so have some from our own nation. Having been seized beforehand for evil deeds by the ruler of wickedness, they were then invited as though to a banquet by a father celebrating a wedding for his son, but they did not obey. In place of those who disobeyed because of that prior seizure, the father celebrating the wedding for his son commanded us through the prophet of truth, when we had gone to the outlets of the roads (that is, toward you), to put a clean wedding garment around you (which is baptism, performed for forgiveness of the evil deeds you have committed) and to bring into God’s banquet those who have become good through a change of heart, even if they had at first been left out of the feast.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπαύσατο, πρὸς τὰ λοιπὰ τῆς πολιτείας θηρεύειν αὐτὸν ἐπιχειρῶν
source_issues.issue: The present participle ἐπιχειρῶν may describe the effort that ceased or an attendant attempt made before or while he ceased. The translation takes the attempt to ensnare him as the effort that ceased; the alternative attachment does not require a textual correction.

source_issues.source_quote: καθαρὸν ἔνδυμα γάμου περιβαλεῖν
source_issues.issue: The person around whom the garment is to be placed is not expressed. The translation supplies “you” from the immediately preceding parenthesis and the following reference to deeds committed by the audience; “those encountered at the roads” is a broader possible referent.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς εἰς τὸ θεοῦ δεῖπνον εἰσάγειν ἐκ τῆς μεταμελείας
source_issues.issue: The attachment of ἐκ τῆς μεταμελείας is not explicit. The main text takes it with τοὺς ἀγαθούς, describing people who have become good through a change of heart. Alternatively, it may modify εἰσάγειν, so that their change of heart or regret provides the grounds for bringing the good into God’s banquet. Both readings are possible without altering the supplied Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the remaining areas of his way of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here denotes conduct or manner of life, not a political constitution.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the law laid down beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the prior determination expressed by προορισθέντα without importing a later doctrinal sense of predestination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τοῦ τῆς κακίας ἡγεμόνος προληφθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: having been seized beforehand by the ruler of wickedness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb depicts prior capture or preemption and prepares for the related noun πρόληψιν.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to put a clean wedding garment around you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The person being clothed is implicit; the parenthetical identification with baptism for the audience’s past deeds supports taking the audience as the recipient.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς εἰς τὸ θεοῦ δεῖπνον εἰσάγειν ἐκ τῆς μεταμελείας
lexical_decisions.chosen: and to bring into God’s banquet those who have become good through a change of heart
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text relates ἐκ τῆς μεταμελείας to τοὺς ἀγαθούς, understanding the people as good through moral reconsideration. μεταμέλεια may denote change of heart, regret, or reconsideration. The phrase may instead modify εἰσάγειν, yielding “to bring the good into God’s banquet on account of their change of heart.”

passages.text: On the following day, then, Peter went out with his companions, came to the place where they had been the day before, stood there, and began to say: “God destroyed with water all the people of old who had acted impiously. Yet, finding among them all one godly man, he caused him to be saved in an ark together with his three sons and the women. From this one can perceive his nature: it takes no account of a crowd of people acting impiously, but it does not neglect the salvation of one godly person. The greatest impiety of all, then, is to abandon the sole Master of all and revere many nonexistent gods as though they existed.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in an ark
lexical_decisions.rationale: λάρναξ can denote a chest or coffer; the flood setting supports “ark.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τριῶν αὐτοῦ υἱῶν καὶ γυναικῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: together with his three sons and the women
lexical_decisions.rationale: γυναικῶν can mean “women” or “wives.” The rendering avoids specifying whose wives they were, since the Greek does not make that relationship explicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it takes no account of a crowd of people acting impiously
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle refers back to God’s “nature”; the collective construction is represented naturally in English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλοὺς τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας ὡς ὄντας σέβειν θεούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: revere many nonexistent gods as though they existed
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves both the denial that these gods exist and the contrast introduced by ὡς ὄντας.

passages.text: “If, then, while I am instructing you and showing that this is the greatest sin, one that can destroy you all, the thought should steal into your mind that you will not be destroyed because you are many crowds, you have been deceived. For you have the example of the world that was flooded long ago. And yet their sin was much less than yours: they acted impiously against those like themselves, either by murdering or by committing adultery, but you act impiously against the God of all by revering lifeless images instead of him, or even alongside him, and by casting his divine name upon all insentient matter. In the first place, then, you have suffered misfortune by failing to recognize the difference between rule by one and rule by many: rule by one produces concord, whereas rule by many produces wars. For the one does not fight itself, but the many have occasion to launch a fight against another.”

source_issues.source_quote: τὸν ὑμέτερον ὑποδράμῃ .νοῦν
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a period between ὑποδράμῃ and νοῦν, separating the adjective and article from the noun within the phrase “your mind.” It appears to be extraneous punctuation rather than a lacuna marker; the construction remains intelligible when the period is disregarded.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the thought should steal into your mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποτρέχω here depicts a thought slipping or stealing into the mind; the printed period is treated separately as a source issue.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because you are many crowds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The deliberately unusual plural image is retained rather than reduced to the smoother but less exact “because you are numerous.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ θεῖον αὐτοῦ ὄνομα πάσῃ ἀναισθήτῳ ὕλῃ ἐπιρρίψαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: by casting his divine name upon all insentient matter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the concrete image of ἐπιρρίπτω, “cast upon,” and takes ὕλη as physical matter rather than merely “material.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: rule by one and rule by many
lexical_decisions.rationale: These expressions convey the contrast without importing the narrower modern political associations of “monarchy” and “polyarchy.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: have occasion
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις may mean a pretext, ground, or occasion; “occasion” fits the claim that plurality creates an opening for conflict.

passages.text: “Indeed, immediately after the flood, Noah lived on for three hundred fifty years and continued in concord with the multitudes descended from him, being a king in the likeness of the only God. But after his death, many of his descendants desired kingship, and in their eagerness to reign, each devised how he might be able to do so. One sought it by war, another by deceit, another by persuasion, and another in some other way. One of them was a certain man from the lineage of Ham, who fathered Mestrem, from whom indeed the tribes of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Persians multiplied.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: lived on for three hundred fifty years
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιζάω denotes continuing to live or surviving beyond an event, here the flood.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ μόνου θεοῦ κατ’ εἰκόνα ὑπάρξας βασιλεύς
lexical_decisions.chosen: being a king in the likeness of the only God
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ εἰκόνα expresses correspondence or likeness; the wording preserves the author’s comparison between Noah’s kingship and God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who fathered Mestrem
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although ποιέω ordinarily means “make,” the genealogical context supports the extended sense “beget” or “father.” The edition’s form Μεστρέμ is transliterated rather than harmonized with a familiar biblical name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐξ οὗπερ τὰ Αἰγυπτίων καὶ Βαβυλωνίων καὶ Περσῶν ἐπλήθυνε φῦλα
lexical_decisions.chosen: from whom indeed the tribes of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Persians multiplied
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nearest antecedent of οὗπερ is Mestrem, which is therefore followed in the main text; reference to Ham remains grammatically possible. The singular verb with the neuter plural φῦλα is an ordinary Greek agreement pattern.

passages.text: “By this lightning bolt, then, which fell from heaven to earth, the magician Nimrod was killed and, because of what had happened, was renamed Zoroaster, since the star’s living stream had been borne against him. But the foolish among the people of that time thought that his soul had been summoned by a thunderbolt because of his friendship with God. After burying what remained of his body, they honored the tomb with a temple among the Persians, where the descent of the fire had occurred, and worshiped him as a god. Following this example, the others there also bury as friends of God those who die by lightning, honor them with temples, and erect statues representing the dead in their own forms. From this, those who gained power in their various regions similarly became imitators. Most of them honored with temples and carved images the tombs of people dear to them even when those people had not died by lightning; they also kindled altars and commanded that the dead be worshiped as gods. Much later, because so much time had passed, later generations came to believe that they really were gods.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ τὴν τοῦ ἀστέρος κατ’ αὐτοῦ ζῶσαν ἐνεχθῆναι ῥοήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the star’s living stream had been borne against him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s proposed wordplay explaining the name Zoroaster through a “living” flow or stream associated with a star.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his soul had been summoned by a thunderbolt
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive of μεταπέμπω commonly means “be sent for” or “be summoned”; “carried away” is possible contextually but is less lexically direct.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν μὲν τάφον ναῷ ἐτίμησαν ἐν Πέρσαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: they honored the tomb with a temple among the Persians
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν Πέρσαις literally locates the action among the Persian people; “in Persia” would be a smoother geographical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν τεθνεώτων ἰδίων μορφῶν ἱστᾶσιν ἀγάλματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: erect statues representing the dead in their own forms
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes images corresponding to the individual forms or likenesses of the deceased.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τῶν κατὰ τόπους οἱ δυναστεύσαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who gained power in their various regions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression τῶν κατὰ τόπους is elliptical; the rendering takes it as referring to people or communities distributed place by place.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with temples and carved images
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξόανα are carved cult images, often specifically wooden, but the material is not made explicit here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: commanded that the dead be worshiped as gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive lacks an explicit accusative subject. The deceased people whose tombs were honored are the contextual referent; taking the tombs or images themselves as the object is less likely but grammatically conceivable.

passages.text: Nevertheless, although the origin was one, many divisions of kingship arose in this way. The Persians were the first to take coals from the lightning that had fallen from heaven and preserve them with fuel of their own. They gave the fire special honor as a heavenly god, and because they were the first to worship it, they were the first to be honored with kingship by that very fire. After them, the Babylonians stole coals from the fire there, brought them safely into their own lands, and worshiped it; they too reigned next in succession. The Egyptians acted likewise and in their own language called the fire Phthae, which is interpreted “Hephaestus”; the one who first reigned among them is also called by his name. Thus those who reigned in each locality followed this practice, made an image, and kindled altars in honor of the fire. Most of them were extinguished from kingship;

lexical_decisions.chosen: although the origin was one
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπαρχή can denote an origin, beginning, underlying basis, or established state. “Origin” fits the following account of how multiple divisions of kingship arose, though “although the underlying basis was one” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: preserve them with fuel of their own
lexical_decisions.rationale: τροφή ordinarily denotes nourishment or sustenance; in relation to coals, “fuel” conveys what feeds and preserves the fire.

lexical_decisions.chosen: into their own lands
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized neuter plural is elliptical and could refer to their own places, territory, or possessions. “Lands” contextually expresses the transfer from the Persian fire to Babylonia.

lexical_decisions.chosen: called the fire Phthae, which is interpreted “Hephaestus”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Egyptian designation is transliterated, while the author’s Greek identification introduced by ἑρμηνεύεται is translated rather than harmonized with another naming tradition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: made an image
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἵδρυμα can denote an erected sacred image, a shrine, or a sacred establishment. “Image” is chosen in view of the ξόανα mentioned immediately afterward, while “made a shrine” remains a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς μὲν βασιλείας οἱ πλεῖστοι ἀπεσβέσθησαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Most of them were extinguished from kingship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The marked extinguishing metaphor is retained because it echoes the preceding fire imagery. The sense is that most lost their kingship, but that smoother wording would erase the wordplay.

passages.text: Yet they did not cease reverencing the carved images, because of the wicked contrivance of the Magi, who devised for them pretexts capable of holding them fast to futile worship. For, after installing the images with magical rites, they appointed festivals for them consisting of sacrifices, libations, flutes, and clapping. Deceived under cover of these things, the senseless—even though their kingship had been taken away—do not abandon the accumulated religious observances. To such an extent, because of their love of pleasure, did they prefer error to truth. These people also, after becoming drunk, raise a ritual cry beside the altar, while their soul, from its depths as if through dreams, foretells to them the punishment that is to come for such deeds of theirs.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the wicked contrivance of the Magi
lexical_decisions.rationale: μάγοι can denote Magi or magicians. “Magi” preserves the historically specific designation, while the magical rites in the context make the polemical sense clear.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὑρόντων αὐτοῖς προφάσεις κρατεῖν αὐτοὺς πρὸς τὴν ματαίαν λατρείαν δυναμένας
lexical_decisions.chosen: who devised for them pretexts capable of holding them fast to futile worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὑρίσκω here concerns finding or devising pretexts, and κρατεῖν conveys keeping the worshipers under control or holding them fast.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἱδρύσαντες γὰρ αὐτὰ μαγικαῖς τελεταῖς ἑορτὰς αὐτοῖς ὥρισαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For, after installing the images with magical rites, they appointed festivals for them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The explanatory γάρ is represented by “For.” The participle is read temporally, while ἱδρύω can denote setting up, installing, or ritually establishing an image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ τε θυμάτων, σπονδῶν, αὐλῶν τε καὶ κρότων
lexical_decisions.chosen: consisting of sacrifices, libations, flutes, and clapping
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρότοι can denote clapping, striking sounds, noisy applause, or clashing. “Clapping” supplies a concrete festival sound, though “clashing sounds” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the accumulated religious observances
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, these are religious observances that have “come together.” “Accumulated” treats them as observances combined in the festivals; “combined religious observances” or “assembled rites” are alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: raise a ritual cry beside the altar
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀλολύζω denotes a loud ritual cry or ululation, while παραβώμιον locates the action beside the altar.

passages.text: For otherwise, while in the present life you are abused by demons with strange afflictions, upon release from the body you will also have your souls punished forever—in truth, not because God condemns them, but because evil deeds carry such a judgment. For the demons, having authority through the food rendered to them, are admitted by your own hands into your own bodies. For, after dwelling in the innermost recesses for a long time, they also become blended with the soul. And because of the negligence of those who do not think to help themselves, or are even unwilling to do so, the soul of these very people, united to the demon when the body is dissolved, must be carried by it to whatever places it wishes. Worst of all, when, at the consummation of all things, the demon is first handed over to the purifying fire, the soul blended with it must itself be punished inexpressibly, while the demon takes pleasure. For the soul, since it comes from light, cannot bear the flame of the fire, which is foreign to its kind, and is tormented; but the demon, being within the substance of its own kind, takes immense pleasure, having become a bond hard to break for the soul that, under its influence, shares its condition.

source_issues.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ δαίμονες, διὰ τῆς αὐτοῖς ἀποδοθείσης τροφῆς ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντες, ὑπὸ τῶν ὑμετέρων χειρῶν εἰς τὰ ὑμέτερα εἰσκρίνεται σώματα
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints the singular verb εἰσκρίνεται with the plural subject οἱ δαίμονες and plural participle ἔχοντες. The English represents the contextually clear plural sense, but a plural Greek form would be a conjectural grammatical normalization rather than the supplied reading.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you are abused by demons with strange afflictions
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνυβρίζω conveys abusive or outrageous treatment, while ἀλλόκοτος denotes what is strange, alien, or extraordinary.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ ἐκ τοῦ σώματος ἀπαλλαγῇ καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς εἰσαεὶ κολασθησομένας ἕξετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: upon release from the body you will also have your souls punished forever
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future passive participle κολασθησομένας states that punishment will actually be inflicted on the souls, not merely that they will face its possibility. The construction with ἕξετε is retained rather than recast as a wholly impersonal prediction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἀληθῆ οὐ θεοῦ καταδικάζοντος, ἀλλὰ κακῶν πράξεων τοιαύτην ἐχουσῶν κρίσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in truth, not because God condemns them, but because evil deeds carry such a judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ ἀληθῆ functions adverbially as “in truth.” The contrasting genitive constructions deny that God’s condemnation is the cause and attribute the judgment to the character of evil deeds; the object “them” is supplied from the souls just mentioned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through the food rendered to them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποδίδω can mean give back, render, or deliver what is due. “Rendered” preserves the implication of food presented to demons rather than ordinary eating alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνδομυχήσαντες γὰρ πολλῷ τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ ἀνακίρνανται
lexical_decisions.chosen: For, after dwelling in the innermost recesses for a long time, they also become blended with the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: “For” represents the explanatory γάρ, and “also” represents καί. ἐνδομυχέω depicts dwelling or making a lair deep within, while ἀνακίρναμαι denotes becoming mixed or blended.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ἑαυτοῖς βοηθεῖν μὴ νοούντων ἢ καὶ μὴ βουλομένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who do not think to help themselves, or are even unwilling to do so
lexical_decisions.rationale: νοέω with an infinitive can concern thinking of, considering, or intending an action. “Do not think to help themselves” avoids narrowing the phrase to ignorance about how to help; “do not intend to help themselves” is also viable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be punished inexpressibly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπορρήτως can mean unspeakably, indescribably, or in a manner that cannot be disclosed. “Inexpressibly” preserves this uncertainty without reducing the punishment to something merely secret.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the flame of the fire, which is foreign to its kind
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀλλόφυλος literally describes something belonging to another race or kind. The flame is represented as foreign to the soul that comes from light, in contrast to the demon’s affinity with the fire.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a bond hard to break
lexical_decisions.rationale: δύσρηκτος describes something difficult to break or rupture without necessarily asserting absolute impossibility.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the soul that, under its influence, shares its condition
lexical_decisions.rationale: συμπαθέω can mean sharing a condition, being affected together, suffering together, or having affinity, while ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ may express agency or causal influence. The rendering takes the soul as sharing the demon’s joined condition under its influence, not necessarily its pleasurable response to the fire. Alternatives include “for the soul that suffers together with it because of it” and “for the soul affected along with it under its power.”

passages.text: As for the demons’ eagerness to slip into human bodies, this is the cause. Being spirits and having desire for foods, drinks, and intercourse, yet being unable to partake because they are spirits and need instruments suited to their use, they enter human bodies so that, obtaining them as instruments that serve them, they may be able to obtain what they want—whether foods through the person’s teeth or intercourse through that person’s genitals. Consequently, to put demons to flight, deprivation, fasting, and hardship are the most fitting aid. For if they enter a human body for the sake of partaking, it is clear that hardship drives them out. But since some are more formidable and, having persisted obstinately, remain in the body undergoing punishment even while they themselves are being punished, it is therefore necessary to take refuge in God with prayers and supplications, while abstaining from every occasion of impurity, so that God’s hand may be able to touch that person for healing, as one who is pure and believes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς δαίμονας γλίχεσθαι εἰς τὰ ἀνθρώπων εἰσδύειν σώματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the demons’ eagerness to slip into human bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: γλίχομαι expresses eager desire or striving, while εἰσδύω depicts entering or slipping into something.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς βρωτὰ καὶ ποτὰ καὶ συνουσίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: for foods, drinks, and intercourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although συνουσία can denote association generally, the later reference to the genitals establishes sexual intercourse here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: obtaining them as instruments that serve them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπουργέω describes rendering subordinate service; the human bodies function as instrumental agents through which the demons satisfy their desires.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἔνδεια καὶ ἡ νηστεία καὶ ἡ κακουχία
lexical_decisions.chosen: deprivation, fasting, and hardship
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔνδεια denotes lack or deprivation, while κακουχία denotes harsh treatment, bodily hardship, or privation; the separate terms are retained rather than collapsed into fasting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having persisted obstinately
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound conveys continued contentious resistance or stubborn persistence; “persisted obstinately” fits demons that remain despite punishment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while abstaining from every occasion of impurity
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can mean pretext, occasion, or ostensible cause. “Occasion” best fits practical abstention, though “every impure pretext” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ τοῦ θεοῦ χεὶρ εἰς ἴασιν αὐτοῦ ἐπιψαῦσαι δυνηθῇ ὡς ἁγνοῦ καὶ πιστεύοντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s hand may be able to touch that person for healing, as one who is pure and believes
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιψαύω takes the genitive αὐτοῦ. Although the pronoun could grammatically look back toward the body, the accompanying “pure and believing” identifies the intended referent as the afflicted person.
